title: Audio Transcription
description: Convert speech audio into timestamped text while preserving timing, language metadata, and source traceability for captions, search, summarization, and extraction.
body: Audio Transcription Description Convert an audio file into structured transcript segments. A useful pipeline preserves timestamps and enough source metadata to trace generated text back to the recording. Transcription is extraction, not independent fact verification. Inputs / Outputs | Item | Type | Required | Notes | |---|---|---:|---| | Audio path | str | yes | Local audio readable by the process | | Model | str | yes | Installed Whisper model identifier | | Language | str or None | no | Omit for model language detection | | Output segments | list[dict] | yes | Start, end, and text per segment | | Output language | str or None | no | Detected language when available | Runnable Example Engineering Rules - Bound maximum file size and duration before processing. - Preserve the source identifier and transcription model in application metadata. - For long recordings, chunk without losing absolute timestamps. - Speaker diarization is a separate component; do not imply speaker identity from plain transcription. - Treat transcript text as extracted data until independently verified. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Wrong language | Automatic detection uncertainty | Supply language when known and retain detected value | | Hallucinated text | Ambiguous or poor audio | Preserve timestamps and verify critical segments | | Truncated recording | Operational limits | Process bounded chunks with absolute time offsets | | Resource exhaustion | Large model or media | Select model size explicitly and enforce limits | Evidence - Whisper implementation: https://github.com/openai/whisper - Whisper transcription implementation: https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/transcribe.py Evidence status: implementation guidance is grounded in the cited primary implementation. title: Barcode and QR Scanning
description: Decode 1D barcodes and QR codes from images into payload text with format detection, orientation handling, and honest confidence reporting for damaged codes.
body: Barcode and QR Scanning Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A barcode or QR code is a machine-readable string with a strict geometry. This skill covers locating candidate code regions in an image, detecting the symbology, decoding the payload, and reporting confidence honestly — including the case where a damaged or partially occluded code decodes to a wrong-but-checksum-valid result. When to Use Use when an image contains barcodes or QR codes whose payload drives a decision — inventory labels, ticket validation, payment codes, hardware serials. Do not treat a successful decode as ground truth without the symbology checksum; low-quality images decode to plausible wrong values more often than they fail outright. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The image containing one or more codes | | | | No | Crop to scan when the code location is known | | | | No | Restrict detection to given symbologies | Procedure 1. Locate candidate code regions before decoding — finder patterns for QR codes, quiet-zone and bar geometry for 1D symbologies. 2. Detect the symbology from the located region rather than trying every decoder and taking the first success. 3. Normalize the region — deskew, binarize, correct perspective — before attempting the decode. 4. Decode the payload and verify the symbology checksum; reject codes that fail their check digit. 5. Report per-code confidence and symbology together with the payload, and flag damaged regions explicitly. 6. Bound the work: cap the number of regions examined per image so pathological images cannot stall the pipeline. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Decoded payloads with symbology and checksum status | | | | Located code regions in image coordinates | | | | Regions that failed to decode, with reasons | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Wrong but valid decodes | Damaged codes decode to checksum-plausible wrong values | Flag low-confidence and damaged regions | | Missed codes | Codes at angles or small scale are not located | Use rotation-tolerant, multi-scale region detection | | Unbounded scanning | Pathological images stall detection | Cap regions and modules examined per image | | Payload taken as fact | A decoded string drives a decision unchecked | Verify the checksum and cross-check the expected format | | Symbology misclassification | The wrong decoder is applied to a region | Detect symbology from geometry before decoding | Security and Authority Boundary Decoded payloads are untrusted input. A QR code can encode a URL or instruction string; payloads must be validated against an expected format before being used to drive navigation, payment, or privileged actions. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The pyzbar barcode decoding library project page (https://pypi.org/project/pyzbar/). 2. The ZXing barcode image processing library GitHub repository (https://github.com/zxing/zxing). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - OCR — the text-recognition counterpart for codes without strict geometry. - Image Understanding — the visual grounding layer that locates code regions. title: Certificate Parsing
description: Parse X.509 certificates into structured fields — subject, issuer, validity, key usage — with explicit expiry checking and stated chain-validation boundaries.
body: Certificate Parsing Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A certificate is a signed claim about an identity, and most TLS mistakes come from reading one field of it in isolation. This skill parses a certificate into its material fields, checks validity windows and key usage against the operation at hand, and states clearly what a leaf certificate cannot tell you: whether its chain actually anchors to a trust store. When to Use Use when a workflow receives a certificate and needs its identity, expiry, or purpose fields — inventory of deployed certificates, pre-flight checks, incident triage of a TLS failure. Do not use field parsing as chain validation; a parsed, unexpired, purpose-matching certificate can still be untrusted, self-signed, or revoked. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The certificate to parse | | | | No | Clock to evaluate validity against; default is now | | | | No | Key usage the operation needs, such as server auth | Procedure 1. Decode PEM or DER into the certificate structure, reporting the encoding and size. 2. Extract the material fields — subject, issuer, serial, validity window, signature algorithm, key usage, subject alternative names. 3. Evaluate the validity window against the reference time and report days remaining, not just a boolean. 4. Check key usage and subject alternative names against the operation the certificate is being assessed for. 5. Report self-signed and wildcard states explicitly; they change what the fields can support. 6. State the boundary: chain building, revocation, and trust-store anchoring are separate validation steps. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Parsed certificate fields | | | | Not-before, not-after, and days remaining at reference time | | | | Self-signed, wildcard, weak-algorithm, and boundary cautions | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Parsing used as validation | An untrusted chain is treated as trusted because fields look correct | Keep chain validation a separate explicit step | | Expiry checked once | A certificate expires between check and use | Report days remaining and re-check at use time | | Weak algorithms missed | A signature algorithm is accepted without review | Flag weak hashes and small keys | | Purpose mismatch | A certificate is used for an operation its key usage forbids | Match key usage and names to the operation | | Encoding errors | Truncated DER is parsed as a shorter record | Verify declared lengths against actual size | Security and Authority Boundary Certificates authenticate identities, not intentions. This skill reports what a certificate claims; it must not be used to grant access, and private keys must never travel through the same parsing path as public certificates. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OpenSSL documentation for certificate handling (https://docs.openssl.org/). 2. The Python ssl module reference (https://docs.python.org/3/library/ssl.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Config File Parsing
description: Parse YAML, TOML, and INI configuration files into typed, validated structures with explicit defaults, unknown-key reporting, and provenance of every effective value.
body: Config File Parsing Category: Perception | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Configuration is where runtime truth comes from. A loader that silently invents defaults or ignores unknown keys turns typos into behavior, and a system that cannot say which file a setting came from cannot audit its own decisions. This skill treats a configuration file as data with a schema: parse it strictly, validate types, surface unknown keys, and record the provenance of every effective value. When to Use Use whenever an agent or service loads settings from YAML, TOML, or INI files — application settings, tool configuration, pipeline definitions — and later decisions depend on those values. Do not treat an unparsable file as empty configuration; a missing file and a broken file are different failures and must not collapse into a silent fall-back to defaults. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The configuration file to load | | | | Yes | yaml, toml, or ini, detected when not supplied | | | | No | Expected keys, types, and ranges for validation | | | | No | Fallback values applied with recorded provenance | Procedure 1. Detect the format from the file extension and content before choosing a parser; refuse ambiguous input rather than guessing. 2. Parse with a strict parser that reports line numbers for syntax errors instead of attempting best-effort recovery. 3. Validate parsed values against the schema — required keys, types, ranges — and collect all violations before failing. 4. Report unknown keys rather than silently dropping them; an unknown key is either a typo or a schema that drifted from the config. 5. Merge defaults only for missing values and record, per key, whether it came from file, default, or environment override. 6. Emit the effective configuration together with its provenance map so later decisions can cite their settings. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The typed, validated effective configuration | | | | The source recorded for each effective value | | | | Schema violations and unknown keys found during load | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent defaults | Unparsable file treated as empty config | Fail closed on parse errors | | Unknown keys dropped | Schema drift or typos stay invisible | Report and list every unknown key | | Type coercion surprises | Values parsed as strings regardless of intent | Validate against a typed schema | | Duplicate keys | Last-wins parsing hides conflicts | Surface duplicate definitions at load time | | Credentials in config | Credential-shaped values committed to files | Keep secrets in the environment or a secret store | Security and Authority Boundary Configuration parsing reads files that often sit next to credentials. Parsed values must not be logged in full, and credential-shaped values found in a config file should be reported as a finding rather than passed through silently. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Python standard library configparser reference (https://docs.python.org/3/library/configparser.html). 2. The twelve-factor guidance on keeping config in the environment (https://12factor.net/config). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. description: Estimate per-pixel depth from a single image or video frame, ranking surfaces by distance with explicit handling of scale ambiguity, occlusion edges, and reflective surfaces.
body: Monocular Depth Estimation Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Depth estimation maps every pixel of an image to a distance from the camera. In the monocular setting there is no stereo baseline and no known camera motion, so the raw output is a relative ordering of surfaces — closer versus farther — unless an external reference converts it to metric units. This skill covers running a depth estimator, aligning its relative output to a known scale when one exists, and reporting the ambiguity honestly. When to Use Use when a single image or video feed must support distance-aware decisions: robot navigation, AR object placement, background separation, or defocus-aware editing. Do not treat monocular depth as surveyed distance. Without a known reference the output is ordering only, and reflective or low-texture surfaces break even the ordering. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Single image or video frame | | | | No | Known size-at-distance pairs used to fit a metric scale | | | | No | (default) or (requires ) | Procedure 1. Normalize the input to the estimator's native resolution while preserving aspect ratio; record the resize factor. 2. Run the estimator and obtain the relative depth map. 3. If a metric scale is required, fit a single scale factor over the reference pairs with a least-squares alignment and report the residual. 4. Post-process with edge-aware smoothing only; hard occlusion boundaries must survive. 5. Produce a confidence channel: flag low-texture regions, mirrors, glass, and thin structures as unreliable. 6. Bound the cost: one estimator pass, no iterative refinement loops on unbounded inputs. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-pixel depth (relative or metric per ) | | | | Per-pixel reliability flags | | | | Fitted scale, residual, or explicit marker | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Relative depth read as meters | No reference was provided or fitted | Always emit ; refuse silent metric claims | | Reflective surfaces | Mirrors and glass return the reflected scene's depth | Flag glossy regions as unreliable | | Occlusion edges smoothed away | Aggressive post-processing | Use edge-aware smoothing and check boundaries | | Thin structures missed | Poles, wires, and cables vanish at low resolution | Report sub-pixel structures as low confidence | | Scale drift across frames | Per-frame independent estimation in video | Use temporal consistency or report per-frame scale | Security and Authority Boundary Depth maps reveal room layout and object placement; treat them as sensitive scene data. Do not route third-party images through estimators that log or retain inputs, and do not use depth output to infer information about identifiable people beyond the task's purpose. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The MiDaS monocular depth estimation project (https://github.com/isl-org/MiDaS). 2. The Depth Anything V2 monocular depth estimation model repository (https://github.com/DepthAnything/Depth-Anything-V2). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Env File Parsing
description: Parse KEY=VALUE environment files into explicit settings with malformed-line and duplicate-key reporting so misconfiguration surfaces at load time instead of at first use.
body: Env File Parsing Category: Perception | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Environment files are a common configuration interface, and they fail quietly: a missing separator, a duplicated key, or an unmatched quote produces a wrong setting long before anyone reads the file back. This skill defines a deterministic parse contract that separates valid settings from reported problems, and it treats quoted values, comments, and blank lines explicitly. It covers parsing only; it does not cover secret storage, rotation, or runtime override precedence. When to Use Use when a service or job loads settings from a dotenv-style file and the failure mode is a misread value discovered late. Do not use for resolving runtime environment variables or managing secret storage; use the dedicated skills for those boundaries. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw file contents preserving every line, including comments | | | | No | Keys that must be present for the load to succeed | | | | No | Per-key coercion such as int or bool applied after parsing | | | | No | When true, duplicate keys fail the load instead of being reported | Procedure 1. Read the file as text and preserve line numbers; do not trim or rewrite the raw input before parsing. 2. Skip blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is a hash; record them as ignored, not as errors. 3. Split each remaining line on the first equals sign; a line without a separator is a malformed entry, not a parse-stopping exception. 4. Validate the key shape and strip one layer of matching surrounding quotes from the value. 5. Detect duplicate keys and record whether the last value wins or the load fails under the declared strictness. 6. Apply the declared per-key type coercion and record coercion failures alongside malformed entries. 7. Return the parsed settings together with the problem list, including line number, kind, and raw line; never return a silent partial result. 8. Fail the load when strict mode is on or when a required key is missing; otherwise surface every problem at load time. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Valid key-to-value map after coercion | | | | Malformed, duplicate, and coercion failures with line numbers | | | | Declared required keys absent from the file | | | | Comment and blank line numbers skipped during parsing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Missing separator | A line has no equals sign | Record as malformed; never guess a separator | | Duplicate key | The same key appears twice | Report duplicates and fail the load under strict mode | | Quote mismatch | An opening quote has no closing partner | Strip only matched pairs and report unmatched quotes | | Coercion failure | A non-numeric value sits where an integer was declared | Coerce during parsing and record the failure with its line | | Required key absent | The file parses but is incomplete | Compare against required_keys and fail the load | Security and Authority Boundary Parsing a configuration file grants no execution authority. Values from environment files are untrusted input: they must be validated before use and must never be evaluated as code. Sensitive values parsed from such files flow only into the runtime’s declared secret storage, and the problem report must never echo those values. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The twelve-factor app guidance on configuration (https://12factor.net/config). 2. Python’s configparser module documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/configparser.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Structured Data Reading — parses structured inputs into typed records; this skill applies that discipline to KEY=VALUE files. - Log Parsing — reports malformed lines with line numbers the same way. - Env Vars — consumes resolved environment variables; this skill only parses the file form. title: IoT Telemetry Parsing
description: Parse IoT telemetry streams — MQTT, CoAP, and device events — into timestamped, typed records with schema validation, unit normalization, and out-of-order handling.
body: IoT Telemetry Parsing Category: Perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Device telemetry arrives as compact binary or JSON payloads over constrained transports, often out of order and sometimes duplicated. This skill turns raw telemetry into analysis-ready records: decode the payload, validate it against the device schema, normalize units and timestamps, and keep malformed messages visible instead of dropping them silently. When to Use Use when consuming device or sensor streams — MQTT topics, CoAP observations, gateway exports — that feed monitoring, alerting, or analysis. Do not assume ordering, uniqueness, or unit consistency across devices; each message carries its own clock, schema version, and encoding. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The raw telemetry message | | | | Yes | mqtt, coap, or gateway export | | | | Yes | Expected fields, types, and units for the device | | | | No | Payload schema version declared by the device | Procedure 1. Identify the device and its schema version from the topic or payload header before decoding. 2. Decode the payload with the schema — field order for binary encodings, key paths for JSON — and record the encoding used. 3. Validate fields for type, range, and unit, converting to canonical units with the conversion recorded. 4. Normalize timestamps to UTC from the device clock and flag messages with implausible clock drift. 5. Handle duplicates and out-of-order arrival explicitly — dedupe by device sequence number, sort by event time, and report reordering. 6. Route malformed messages to a dead-letter record with the raw payload preserved rather than a silent drop. title: Log Parsing
description: Parse bounded application and infrastructure logs into normalized events while preserving malformed records for explicit error handling.
body: Log Parsing Category: perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description Convert log lines or bounded log batches into normalized events that an agent can filter, correlate, summarize, or route. The parser should preserve the original record, make parsing failures explicit, and avoid interpreting arbitrary message text as trusted structure. This skill covers common line-oriented formats such as JSON Lines, simple key-value records, and timestamp/level/message records. It is deliberately format-aware: an agent should not silently treat an unknown format as successfully parsed structured data. When to Use Use log parsing when an agent needs event-level fields from operational logs, incident timelines, audit records, or application diagnostics. Prefer a dedicated parser when the producer publishes a formal schema. Use text reading first when the task is only to inspect or summarize raw log content. Inputs - : a bounded string, iterable of lines, or already-separated log records. - : , , , or . - : positive integer limiting records processed in one call. - : positive integer limiting each record before parsing. - : optional field name for structured formats. Outputs Each input record produces either a normalized event or an explicit parse error. A normalized event has , , , , and . Parse errors contain , , and so callers can decide whether to retry, quarantine, or ignore the record. Contract | Aspect | Contract | |---|---| | Input | Bounded log records; never assume untrusted text is trusted metadata | | Output | Deterministic event/error objects in input order | | Ordering | Preserve source order; do not infer chronology from arrival order | | Limits | Enforce and before expensive parsing | | Unknown data | Preserve unknown fields under ; do not discard silently | | Errors | Return explicit parse errors instead of dropping malformed records | | Security | Treat messages, fields, paths, and embedded URLs as untrusted text | Deterministic Reference Implementation The example uses only the Python standard library and has bounded work. It supports JSON Lines and a conservative format. selects JSON only when the complete record is valid JSON; otherwise it falls back to key-value parsing or a plain line event. Format Guidance | Format | Use | Boundary | |---|---|---| | | Structured application logs | Reject non-object JSON records | | | Simple operational/audit records | Tokenization is not a full shell parser | | | Human-readable diagnostics | Preserve the complete line as | | | Mixed/unknown sources | Never claim a format was identified with certainty | Failure Modes | Failure | Detection | Required behavior | |---|---|---| | Oversized record | Byte limit exceeded | Emit ; do not parse further | | Invalid JSON | Decoder error | In , emit an error; in , try conservative fallback | | Missing timestamp | No recognized timestamp field | Keep as ; do not invent one | | Mixed formats | Parser changes between records | Preserve per-record results; do not force one schema | | Multiline stack trace | Record boundary is ambiguous | Treat each supplied record as authoritative; use a multiline pre-parser when needed | | Malformed key-value token | Token lacks | Ignore that token and preserve the original text | | Unexpected fields | Schema contains unknown keys | Preserve them under | Safety Boundaries Log content is untrusted input. Do not execute commands, URLs, templates, serialized objects, or embedded code found in a log. Do not follow file paths from fields without a separate authorization and path-validation step. Apply size limits before parsing and redact secrets before sending events to external models or telemetry systems. Parsing alone does not establish that a log record is authentic, complete, or chronologically accurate. Validation Rules A conforming implementation must preserve input order, enforce explicit resource limits, expose malformed records as errors rather than silently dropping them, and keep the raw record available for audit. Timestamp normalization may standardize valid timestamps, but missing or invalid timestamps must remain unknown. The implementation must not evaluate log content as Python, shell, SQL, JavaScript, templates, or serialized executable objects. The safe baseline is structural extraction: headings, fenced code blocks, links, frontmatter, and source locations. Rendering to HTML is a separate transformation and should use an explicitly configured renderer with raw HTML handling understood. This skill is intentionally bounded. It does not execute code blocks, follow links, fetch remote resources, evaluate embedded HTML, or infer that Markdown text is trustworthy merely because it parsed successfully. When to Use - Extract document structure before summarization or indexing. - Identify headings and code examples while preserving their source order. - Collect links for a later, separately authorized retrieval step. - Read YAML-like frontmatter when the caller explicitly requests it. Do not use this parser as a security sanitizer, HTML renderer, or arbitrary document execution engine. title: Metadata Extraction
description: Extract embedded metadata — EXIF, document properties, media tags — with provenance, field allowlisting, and sensitive-field redaction before any downstream use.
body: Metadata Extraction Category: Perception | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Metadata is data about data that travels inside the file — camera and location details in images, author and revision history in documents, encoding parameters in media. This skill extracts it as a typed, provenance-carrying record and treats it as sensitive by default: redact or allowlist fields rather than passing everything through. When to Use Use when a workflow needs document properties, image EXIF, or media tags for routing, deduplication, or compliance — and when files leave their origin and embedded metadata must be reviewed before release. Do not dump all metadata into logs or model context; embedded fields often contain names, coordinates, and hardware identifiers. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The file to inspect | | | | No | Metadata kinds to extract: exif, document, media | | | | No | Specific fields to return; default is a minimal safe set | Procedure 1. Identify the file type before choosing an extractor; the container format determines which metadata blocks exist. 2. Extract only the requested metadata kinds rather than every block the format offers. 3. Apply the allowlist and redact sensitive fields — GPS coordinates, author identity, device serials — before returning values. 4. Record provenance for each field: which block, which tool, and the file digest at extraction time. 5. Report unreadable or truncated metadata blocks as findings rather than as empty metadata. 6. Keep the original file unmodified; extraction is a read-only operation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Allowlisted fields with their values | | | | Per-field block and tool provenance | | | | Unreadable blocks and redacted field names | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Metadata leakage | Location or identity fields reach logs or models | Allowlist and redact before use | | Format mismatch | An extractor is applied to the wrong container type | Identify the file type before extracting | | Truncated blocks | Damaged metadata is parsed as empty | Report unreadable blocks as findings | | Encoding surprises | Dates and charset-prefixed strings are misread | Normalize with the declared encoding | | Stale extraction | Fields are cited against a modified file | Record the file digest at extraction time | Security and Authority Boundary Embedded metadata is personal data in most contexts — author names, locations, and device identifiers. Extraction results are sensitive by default; only allowlisted fields leave this skill, and redaction must be reported rather than silent. title: OCR (Optical Character Recognition)
description: Extract text from images and scanned documents. Modern stack: a vision-language model (Claude / GPT-4o) for layout-aware OCR, with Tesseract as the open-source fallback for high-volume / offline runs.
body: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) Description OCR converts an image of text into machine-readable text. Classical OCR (Tesseract, AWS Textract) gives you raw characters with bounding boxes; vision-language model OCR (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini) gives you structured output that respects layout — tables stay tables, columns stay columns, headers stay headers. The two approaches now coexist: VLM for structure-sensitive jobs, classical for high-volume / offline / cost-sensitive batch. This skill returns both the raw text and a structured representation, plus per-page confidence so the caller can route low-confidence pages to a human review queue. When to Use - The source is an image (scanned PDF, photo, screenshot) — not searchable PDF or HTML. - You need text plus layout (forms, invoices, receipts, tables) → use VLM-OCR. - You need raw text at low cost across many millions of pages → use Tesseract / Textract. - Don't use when the file is a digital PDF (use PDF Parsing) or HTML (use HTML Reading) — those have native text already. body: XML Parsing Category: perception | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description XML parsing converts a bounded XML document into a tree and extracts selected elements. The skill is deliberately limited to parsing and querying; transport, authentication, business semantics, and persistence remain outside its boundary. For untrusted XML, use a hardened parser configuration or a maintained safe-XML library rather than enabling external entities. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Complete, bounded XML document | | | | Optional ElementTree-compatible path for local selection | | | | Positive upper bound applied before parsing | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered element records containing tag, text, and attributes | | | | Root element tag for the parsed document | Deterministic Reference Implementation Namespaces ElementTree expands namespace-qualified tags to names. Do not strip namespaces merely to make matching easier; doing so can merge distinct vocabularies. For XPath-like queries, pass an explicit namespace mapping when the selected library supports it. Treat namespace URIs as data, not as permission to fetch network resources. Frameworks | Framework | Role | Security boundary | |---|---|---| | Python | Lightweight deterministic parsing | Keep input bounded; do not assume it is a full security policy | | | Rich XPath and XML features | Use a hardened parser configuration for untrusted input | | LangChain | Loader orchestration | XML security remains the parser's responsibility | Failure Modes | Cause | Observable result | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Malformed XML | | Reject and report location/context to caller | | Input too large | | Enforce before parsing | | Namespace mismatch | Empty selection | Inspect expanded tag names and pass explicit namespaces | | External-entity content | Unsafe or unexpected resolution in unsafe configurations | Disable external entity/network behavior; prefer hardened parsers | | Mixed content | Important text appears in nested nodes | Define extraction rules instead of flattening blindly | Security Boundaries XML is untrusted input. Parsing must not fetch external entities, schemas, stylesheets, DTDs, or URLs as a side effect. Do not evaluate XSLT, XPath supplied by an untrusted caller, or embedded application-specific instructions without a separate policy layer. The parser must not execute code or infer authorization from XML content. Validation Rules - Reject non- / inputs. - Enforce a finite input-size bound before parsing. - Preserve document order in returned records. - Return deterministic results for identical input and query. - Keep network access and transport outside the parsing function. Provenance The reference example uses Python's standard library and makes no claim about external parser CVE status. If or another dependency is selected, its deployed version and security advisories must be validated by the consuming project. title: Argument Structure Analysis
description: Decompose arguments into premises, conclusions, inference links, and explicit gaps so agents distinguish stated evidence from unsupported claims.
body: Argument Structure Analysis Category: reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description Argument structure analysis represents an argument as claims connected by stated or inferred support. The core task is decomposition: identify premises, a conclusion, the relation between them, and missing assumptions. Fallacy detection is a separate judgment and should not be treated as a guaranteed output of parsing. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Bounded natural-language argument | | | | Optional manually extracted premise candidates | | | | Optional explicit conclusion | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered claims offered as support | | | | Best-supported conclusion or null | | | | Explicitly stated missing assumptions; never invented as facts | | | | Support links between claims | Deterministic Reference Implementation Analysis Protocol 1. Preserve the original wording before normalization. 2. Separate explicit premises from conclusions. 3. Record inference markers without treating them as proof. 4. Mark missing assumptions as hypotheses, not recovered facts. 5. Distinguish logical validity from factual truth. 6. Evaluate fallacies only after the argument structure is explicit. Failure Modes | Cause | Observable result | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Implicit premise | Gap in support chain | Label the missing premise explicitly | | Circular reasoning | Conclusion appears in its own support | Check dependency paths for cycles | | Ambiguous pronoun | Unclear claim reference | Preserve ambiguity rather than guessing | | Multiple conclusions | Flat extraction loses hierarchy | Build separate conclusion nodes | | Rhetorical language | False premise detection | Separate rhetoric from propositional content | Validation Rules - Every relation must reference an existing claim. - No missing assumption may be represented as an observed fact. - A conclusion is not automatically valid because it follows an indicator word. - Factual verification is outside the structural parser's boundary. - The same input must produce the same deterministic parse under the reference implementation. Safety Boundaries Do not infer criminal intent, medical diagnosis, legal liability, or other high-impact attributes from argument structure alone. When an argument contains sensitive claims, preserve attribution and uncertainty and require domain-specific review for consequential decisions. Provenance The deterministic example is a structural baseline, not an LLM reasoning benchmark. LLM-based extraction can be layered on top, but its claims require independent validation and source attribution. title: Bayesian Reasoning

body: Bayesian Reasoning Category: reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description Bayesian reasoning updates a prior belief using evidence likelihoods. The posterior is conditional on the chosen model, prior, likelihood, and evidence definition; it is not a measure of certainty by itself. The reference implementation is a scalar binary-hypothesis update so the arithmetic is transparent and deterministic. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | Probability in for hypothesis before evidence | | | | in | | | | in | | | | Whether is observed; means | | Output | Type | Contract | |---|---|---| | | | or in | Deterministic Reference Implementation Interpretation Protocol 1. Define the hypothesis before looking at the evidence. 2. State the prior source or assumption. 3. Define the evidence event precisely. 4. Specify both likelihoods for a binary model. 5. Compute the posterior without rounding intermediate values. 6. Report sensitivity when the prior or likelihood estimates are uncertain. Failure Modes | Cause | Observable result | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Base-rate neglect | Posterior dominated by a vivid observation | Validate the prior against the target population | | Dependent evidence treated as independent | Overconfident posterior | Model joint likelihoods or condition sequentially | | Poor likelihood estimates | Precise-looking but weak result | Report source and uncertainty for likelihoods | | Zero evidence probability | Undefined update | Revisit the model and evidence definition | | Selection bias | Prior does not represent observed population | Re-estimate from the relevant sampling frame | Validation Rules - All probabilities must lie in . - The denominator must be positive. - Posterior must remain in . - Evidence assumptions must be stated before treating multiple observations as independent. - Numerical output must not be presented as stronger evidence than the underlying model. Frameworks | Framework | Role | Boundary | |---|---|---| | Python | Exact scalar arithmetic in the reference example | No uncertainty estimation beyond supplied inputs | | SciPy | Statistical distributions and tests | Validate model assumptions separately | | PyMC | Probabilistic models and posterior inference | Sampling diagnostics are required; not a drop-in replacement for scalar Bayes | Safety Boundaries Do not use an unvalidated posterior as a sole basis for medical, legal, financial, employment, or other high-impact decisions. A Bayesian calculation cannot repair biased evidence, an invalid causal model, or an unrepresentative prior. Provenance The reference example uses elementary Bayes arithmetic and does not claim any external dataset or empirical prior. Framework compatibility is descriptive; consuming projects must verify their installed versions independently. title: Case-Based Reasoning
description: Solve new problems by retrieving and adapting similar past cases, stating what transferred and what differs instead of reasoning from first principles alone.
body: Case-Based Reasoning Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Case-based reasoning treats experience as the primary asset: a new problem is solved by finding the most similar past cases, adapting their solutions, and recording explicitly what transferred and where the analogy breaks. This skill covers case representation, similarity retrieval, adaptation, and the honest boundary where a superficially similar case misleads. When to Use Use when a domain accumulates resolved instances — incidents, designs, diagnoses, negotiations — and a new instance resembles them more than it resembles a clean rule. Do not adapt a past case without stating its differences from the current one; the closest match is not always the most instructive one. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The problem instance to solve | | | | Yes | Resolved past cases with outcomes | | | | No | Explicit comparison dimensions and weights | Procedure 1. Represent the new case with the same fields the case base uses, including context and constraints. 2. Retrieve the nearest cases across explicit dimensions — not overall impressions — and record their distances. 3. Compare the retrieved solutions against the new case and identify which parts transfer and which do not. 4. Adapt the closest solution to the differences, recording each adaptation as a delta from the source case. 5. Test the adapted solution against the new case constraints before accepting it. 6. Store the solved case back into the case base with its outcome so the loop compounds. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The adapted solution with its source case | | | | Which parts of the source solution transferred | | | | Adaptations made and the reason for each | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Superficial match | The nearest case shares surface features but differs in cause | Compare causes and constraints, not just attributes | | Stale cases | Old solutions no longer fit the current system | Record when cases were validated and retire stale ones | | Single-case anchoring | The first retrieved case dominates the answer | Retrieve several and compare adaptations | | Unrecorded adaptation | The delta from the source case is lost | Log every adaptation as an explicit delta | | Base pollution | Failed solutions are stored as good cases | Store outcomes and retain only cases with known results | Security and Authority Boundary Case bases contain history — incidents, personnel decisions, customer interactions. Treat case records as sensitive context with access control, and never expose one customer case details as guidance for another. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on analogy and analogical reasoning (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/reasoning-analogy/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of case-based reasoning (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case-based_reasoning). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Analogical Reasoning — the similarity-mapping foundation this skill operationalizes. - Inductive Reasoning — the generalization discipline that guards against single-case overreach. title: Cost-Benefit Analysis
description: Compare options by monetized and non-monetized effects over a stated horizon, with explicit discounting, distribution of costs and benefits, and named losers.
body: Cost-Benefit Analysis Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A cost-benefit analysis puts options on one comparable footing: what each costs, what it returns, over what horizon, and who pays versus who benefits. This skill structures the comparison — full-cost inventory, effect monetization where honest, explicit discounting, and named distributional effects — and keeps non-monetizable impacts visible instead of treating them as zero. When to Use Use when choosing among options with different cost and effect profiles — build versus buy, adopt versus wait — where a defensible comparison must survive scrutiny. Do not collapse everything into one number; the analysis is the table of costs, benefits, and who bears them, not just the net present value. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Candidate options under comparison | | | | Yes | Analysis period | | | | No | Annual rate used to compare future and present values | | | | Yes | Cost and benefit items per option, monetized where possible | Procedure 1. Inventory the full cost set per option — direct, indirect, transition, and operating — before any benefit is counted. 2. Monetize effects where a defensible basis exists and mark the basis used; leave non-monetizable effects as explicit rows. 3. Convert flows to present values over the stated horizon with the stated discount rate, showing how the rate affects the ranking. 4. Compute per-option summaries — net value, payback, benefit-cost ratio — and compare on the same assumptions. 5. Name the distribution: who pays, who benefits, and when, because net-positive totals can hide transfers. 6. State the decision rule in advance — minimum ratio, maximum payback — and apply it to the computed table. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-option costs, benefits, and present values | | | | Net value, payback, and ratio per option | | | | Who bears which costs and receives which benefits | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Hidden costs | Only direct costs are counted | Inventory indirect, transition, and operating costs | | Forced monetization | Non-monetizable effects get invented numbers | Keep them as explicit non-monetized rows | | Rate silence | The discount rate is unstated or arbitrary | State the rate and show ranking sensitivity to it | | Buried transfers | A net-positive total hides who loses | Name payers and beneficiaries per row | | Post-hoc rule fit | The decision rule is chosen after seeing results | Fix the rule before computing | Security and Authority Boundary Cost-benefit tables over security controls monetize breach risk and can pressure under-investment. Treat security-benefit estimates as decision inputs, not commitments, and never use monetized risk to justify skipping controls required by policy or law. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of cost-benefit analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost%E2%80%93benefitanalysis). 2. Wikipedia's overview of net present value used for time-discounted comparison (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netpresent_value). body: Counterfactual Reasoning Category: Skill Level: Stability: Added: 2025-03 Version: v2 --- Description Reason about hypothetical alternative histories: "What would have happened if X had been different?" Counterfactual reasoning underpins causal inference, debugging, root-cause analysis, and policy evaluation. It requires building a causal model of the world and then intervening on specific variables. --- Counterfactual vs. Hypothetical | Type | Premise | Example | |---|---|---| | Counterfactual | Contrary to known fact | "If I hadn't deployed Friday, the outage wouldn't have happened" | | Hypothetical | Unknown outcome | "If we launch in Q3, will revenue increase?" | | Semifactual | Same outcome under changed antecedent | "Even if the tests had passed, the bug would still ship" | --- Reasoning Steps 1. Identify the factual world — what actually happened 2. Define the intervention — which variable to change 3. Build a causal model — what depends on what (DAG) 4. Propagate the change — follow causal edges forward 5. title: First Principles Thinking
description: Decompose a problem into verified foundational facts, rebuild the solution upward from those facts, and record which borrowed assumptions were kept or dropped so the plan stays auditable.
body: First Principles Thinking Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Plans inherit assumptions by analogy — a design or estimate is carried over because it worked last time — and those assumptions are rarely re-checked. This skill defines a rebuild contract: state the goal, list the facts that are actually verified, list the assumptions being borrowed, and derive the plan from the facts with an explicit verdict for every assumption. It is a reasoning procedure, not a source of new facts; verification still happens through evidence gathering. When to Use Use when a plan, design, or estimate keeps inheriting unexamined defaults and the cost of a wrong inherited assumption is high. Do not use for routine execution where the constraints are already verified; a direct procedure is cheaper than a rebuild. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The outcome phrased as a single testable sentence | | | | Yes | Statements with a verification flag and their source | | | | Yes | Borrowed claims with the evidence that would support them | | | | No | Hard limits the rebuild must respect | Procedure 1. State the goal as a single testable sentence; reject goals that cannot be phrased as an outcome. 2. List every foundation the plan currently rests on, separating verified facts from borrowed assumptions. 3. For each fact, record how it was verified; entries without verification are reclassified as assumptions. 4. For each assumption, record what evidence would confirm it and mark it kept only when that evidence exists or the plan explicitly tolerates its failure. 5. Derive requirements from the facts alone; every requirement must trace to at least one fact. 6. Rebuild the plan upward: foundations first, then requirements, then steps, then schedule estimates. 7. Record the kept and dropped assumption verdicts next to the plan so a reviewer can audit the derivation. 8. Re-run the rebuild whenever a foundation changes; a plan is only as current as its facts. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Steps derived from foundations and requirements | | | | Verified facts the plan rests on, with their sources | | | | Kept or dropped verdicts with the deciding evidence | | | | Entries reclassified from facts to assumptions | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Analogy smuggling | A last-time practice recorded as a fact | Reclassify it as an assumption and give it a verdict | | Untestable goal | The goal is phrased as an activity, not an outcome | Rephrase as a single testable sentence | | Verdict theater | Assumptions marked kept with no supporting evidence | Require the evidence or an explicit tolerance for failure | | Rebuild fan-out | Everything is rebuilt from scratch | Rebuild only what the changed foundations touch | | Stale rebuild | Foundations changed after the plan was written | Re-run the rebuild on every foundation change | Security and Authority Boundary Rebuilding a plan from first principles grants no authority to bypass review or existing controls. Dropping an assumption is an analytical verdict, not a decision: changes to scope, budget, or commitments still require the normal approval boundaries. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s article on Aristotle, the classical source of the first-principles method (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle). 2. Wikipedia’s article on first principles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_principle). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Game-Theoretic Strategy Reasoning
description: Model multi-agent interactions as games with explicit payoff matrices, identify equilibria and dominant strategies, and choose actions under strategic interdependence with stated assumptions about opponent rationality.
body: Game-Theoretic Strategy Reasoning Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description When outcomes depend on what other deciding agents do, choosing the best action requires modeling their incentives, not just your own. This skill covers representing an interaction as a game (players, strategies, payoffs), finding dominant strategies and Nash equilibria, and deciding what to do when opponents are not perfectly rational. The model is a decision aid; real counterparties deviate from equilibrium. When to Use Use when two or more adaptive parties make interdependent choices: negotiation, competitive positioning, mechanism evaluation, adversarial planning. Do not apply to a counterpart that is a fixed procedure with no strategy of its own — a plain optimization problem needs no game theory. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Deciding parties, each with a strategy set | | | | Yes | Utility for every strategy profile (per player) | | | | No | (default), , or | Procedure 1. Enumerate players and their discrete strategy sets; merge continuous choices into named options. 2. Build the payoff matrix, sourcing each utility from evidence, not intuition, and record uncertainty. 3. Check each player for dominant strategies; a dominant strategy overrides equilibrium search for that player. 4. Find pure-strategy Nash equilibria: profiles where every strategy is a best response to the others. 5. If none exist, compute mixed-strategy equilibria and treat them as long-run frequencies, not one-shot advice. 6. Sanity-check against the rationality assumption: ask what a boundedly rational or spiteful opponent would do, and pick the action that survives both models. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Pure and mixed equilibria with payoffs | | | | Chosen strategy with rationale | | | | Worst-case loss if opponents deviate from the model | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Equilibrium assumed to be behavior | Real actors err, bluff, and act spitefully | Check recommendations under bounded rationality too | | Guessed payoffs | Utilities invented without evidence | Record payoff sources and uncertainty per cell | | Wrong game class | Repeated or signaling structure flattened to one-shot | State the game horizon and information structure | | Mixed equilibrium misread | Frequencies treated as a single-action recipe | Present mixed equilibria as long-run rates only | | Ignored collusion space | Games with more than two players admit coalitions | Extend the model or restrict the claim | Security and Authority Boundary Strategic reasoning about other parties must stay within the task's authority. It must not be used to manipulate, deceive, or socially engineer real people, and adversarial modeling of a user is out of scope for an assistant agent. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Nashpy library for computing equilibria of two-player games (https://pypi.org/project/nashpy/). 2. The Nash equilibrium reference article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nash_equilibrium). title: Least-to-Most Prompting
description: Decompose a complex problem into a sequence of simpler sub-problems and solve them in order, feeding each solution as context for the next. Achieves generalisation on problems that defeat standard Chain-of-Thought.
body: Least-to-Most Prompting Description Least-to-Most Prompting (Zhou et al., 2022) solves complex tasks by first asking the model to break the problem into an ordered list of sub-problems (easiest first), then solving each one sequentially, appending each answer to the context before tackling the next. The key insight: if the model can solve every sub-problem, composing the answers gives the final solution. This overcomes CoT failures where the model attempts to solve everything at once and loses track of intermediate steps. On SCAN compositionality tasks, Least-to-Most achieved 99.7% accuracy versus CoT's 16%. It also significantly outperforms CoT on DROP and math word problems with multiple constraints. When to Use - Multi-constraint math or logic problems where intermediate state matters. - Compositional generalisation tasks (new combinations of known sub-tasks). - Agent planning where each step's output becomes the next step's input. - Don't use for simple single-step tasks; the decomposition overhead is wasteful. title: Meta-Prompting
description: Use a meta-model (or meta-prompt) to dynamically generate, select, or refine prompts for a task-specific model. Enables automated prompt engineering and zero-shot task specialisation at runtime.
body: Meta-Prompting Description Meta-Prompting (Zhang et al., 2024) operates at the prompt-construction level rather than the answer level. A meta-model receives a task description and generates the optimal prompt (or a set of candidate prompts) for a task model to execute. This creates a two-level hierarchy: 1. Meta-level: "Given this task, what is the best prompt to give a model to solve it?" 2. Task-level: The generated prompt is executed by the task model. In production, meta-prompting is used in AutoGen's system message generation, Semantic Kernel's planner, and DSPy's optimizer. When to Use - You have a diverse set of task types and can't hand-craft prompts for each. - You want automatic prompt adaptation to user intent at runtime. - Building multi-agent systems where agent prompts should specialise per task. - Don't use when task distribution is narrow and fixed prompts are optimal. title: Pareto Analysis
description: Rank causes or contributors by their share of an effect, find the few inputs that produce most of the outcome, and act on that measured concentration.
body: Pareto Analysis Category: Reasoning | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most effects are concentrated: a minority of causes produces the majority of results. Pareto analysis measures that concentration instead of assuming it — ranking contributors by measured share, identifying the set that crosses a stated threshold, and directing effort where leverage is real. The skill is about the measurement, not the folklore: not every distribution is 80/20, and the split must be computed, not quoted. When to Use Use when effort must be allocated across many candidate causes — defect sources, error classes, cost drivers, usage patterns — and the budget cannot cover everything. Do not cite the 80/20 ratio as a finding; measure the actual concentration and report the real split. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Measured contribution per cause | | | | No | Cumulative share defining the vital few; default 0.8 | | | | No | Display names per cause | Procedure 1. Measure contributions on a single, stated scale; shares computed across mixed units are meaningless. 2. Sort causes by contribution, descending, and compute each one as a share of the total. 3. Accumulate shares in rank order and identify the smallest set that crosses the threshold. 4. Report the actual split — how many causes reach what cumulative share — instead of the assumed 80/20. 5. Check the tail: the long tail still matters when it aggregates, and concentration at the top does not make the rest zero. 6. Re-measure after acting on the vital few; the distribution shifts once the top contributors are addressed. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Causes in descending contribution order | | | | Smallest set crossing the cumulative threshold | | | | Actual cause-count to cumulative-share split measured | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed split | The 80/20 ratio is quoted rather than measured | Compute and report the actual split | | Mixed scales | Shares computed across incommensurable units | Measure on one stated scale | | Static ranking | An old distribution guides new effort | Re-measure after each intervention | | Tail neglect | The aggregated tail is dismissed as zero | Report tail totals alongside the vital few | | Single-cause rounding | Near-equal causes split arbitrarily | Note ranks that are statistically indistinguishable | Security and Authority Boundary Pareto rankings over incident, access, or failure data can reveal which components of a system are most fragile. Treat the ranking itself as sensitive when the underlying data is, and share it on a need-to-know basis. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of the Pareto principle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paretoprinciple). 2. Wikipedia's overview of the Pareto chart used for this analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paretochart). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Planning Decomposition
description: Break a complex agent goal into an ordered sequence of actionable sub-tasks, each with clear inputs, outputs, and success criteria. The cognitive foundation for plan-and-execute, LangGraph pipelines, and CrewAI task breakdown.
body: Planning Decomposition Description Planning Decomposition is the cognitive skill of converting a high-level objective into an explicit, ordered plan of sub-tasks that an agent (or multi-agent system) can execute sequentially or in parallel. It is the reasoning backbone behind: - LangGraph state graphs where each node is a decomposed task - CrewAI task sequences with explicit agent assignments - AutoGen conversation-driven planning where a Planner agent decomposes before Executors act - BabyAGI task-creation loops Planning Decomposition differs from Goal Decomposition (which operates at the intent/objective level) by producing actionable, executable steps with tool bindings, not just sub-goals. When to Use - The agent goal requires more than 3 sequential tool calls. - Sub-tasks can be independently validated (each has a clear done condition). - Different sub-tasks may be parallelisable across sub-agents. - Don't use for single-shot tasks; the planning overhead is not justified. title: Planning
description: Generate a typed, ordered plan from a goal — each step has an action, expected outcome, and a contingency, ready for an executor agent to consume.
body: Planning Description Turns a fuzzy human goal into a structured, executable plan: a typed list of steps where each step has an action, an expected outcome the executor can verify, and a contingency for when the action fails. The plan is the contract between the planner and the executor — typed, validated, and replannable. When to Use - Long-horizon agent tasks (deploy a service, write a research report, run a data pipeline). - You want plans that are inspectable and editable by humans before execution. - You need a clear seam between planning and acting (Plan-and-Execute, HTN, ReWOO). title: Prompt Engineering
description: Design, structure, test, and refine prompts so language models receive clear objectives, constraints, context, output contracts, and evaluation criteria.
body: Prompt Engineering Description Prompt Engineering is the disciplined design and refinement of model instructions. A production prompt should make the task objective explicit, constrain important behavior, provide the context the model needs, and define an output contract that downstream code can validate. When to Use - A model must follow a repeatable task contract. - Output quality depends on explicit context or constraints. - A workflow needs structured output that can be validated automatically. - You need to compare prompt variants using a repeatable evaluation set. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Objective the model must complete | | | | Relevant facts, examples, or retrieved material | | | | Explicit behavioral or formatting constraints | | | | Expected machine-readable output contract | | → | | Complete model instruction | Minimal Runnable Pattern Core Practices 1. State the objective before implementation details. 2. Separate trusted context from instructions. 3. Make constraints explicit rather than relying on implied behavior. 4. Define structured outputs with a schema when software consumes the result. 5. Use representative evaluation cases before accepting a prompt change. 6. Keep prompts versioned when prompt behavior is part of a production contract. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Ambiguous output | Objective or schema is underspecified | Add explicit output requirements | | Instruction conflict | Multiple requirements have unclear precedence | Define precedence and constraints explicitly | | Prompt regression | Changes are not evaluated consistently | Maintain a deterministic evaluation set | | Context overload | Too much irrelevant context | Retrieve or summarize only task-relevant context | Related Skills - Meta-Prompting — dynamically generates or refines prompts - Step-Back Prompting — adds abstraction before solving a task - Goal Decomposition — clarifies objectives before prompt construction - ReAct Pattern — combines reasoning, action, and observation in a tool loop Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2025-03 | v1 | Canonical prompt engineering skill source restored as an explicit graph node | | 2026-09 | v1 | Added production-oriented output contract and evaluation guidance |

title: Reasoning Under Uncertainty
description: Reason and make decisions when information is incomplete, ambiguous, or contradictory. Combines confidence calibration, hedged reasoning, and explicit uncertainty representation to produce reliable agent decisions under incomplete knowledge.
body: Reasoning Under Uncertainty Description Reasoning Under Uncertainty (RuU) is a structured reasoning procedure for an agent to: 1. Explicitly represent uncertainty — "I am 70% confident this is correct" 2. Hedge conclusions appropriately — distinguish facts from inferences from guesses 3. Request clarification or additional evidence when uncertainty is too high to proceed 4. Commit to a best-estimate decision even under incomplete information when action is required This is distinct from Uncertainty Quantification (which measures statistical uncertainty in model outputs) — RuU is the reasoning approach an agent uses when facing incomplete knowledge. Used in: Anthropic's extended thinking (uncertainty-driven budget allocation), GPT-4's calibrated confidence expressions, LangChain's agent fallback chains, and medical/legal reasoning agents where hedged outputs are required. When to Use - The agent must act despite missing information (incomplete evidence). - Downstream systems need to know confidence level (for human review routing). - Multiple contradictory sources require explicit confidence weighting. - Don't use for tasks with deterministic answers; hedge signals waste tokens. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Question or decision to reason about | | | | Available evidence items | | | | Minimum confidence to proceed (default 0.7) | | → | | Best-estimate answer with hedges | | → | | 0.0–1.0 confidence score | | → | | What additional evidence would improve confidence | | → | | proceed / clarify / escalate | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Overconfidence (confidence=1.0 always) | Model calibration issue | Require explicit evidence citation for confidence | | Refusal to act below threshold | Threshold too high | Tune threshold per risk tolerance | | Confidence not propagated downstream | No structured output | Use JSON schema with field | Production Applications - G02 Research Agent: Classify research findings by evidence strength before synthesis - G01 Coding Agent: Hedge before modifying unfamiliar codebases; request context when uncertain - G04 RAG Assistant: Score retrieved chunks by relevance confidence before including Related Skills - Self-Consistency — uses voting to reduce uncertainty in answers - Hypothesis Generation — generates candidate explanations for uncertain situations - Reflection Pattern — re-evaluates low-confidence outputs - RAG Retrieval — retrieves evidence to reduce uncertainty Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2025-06 | v1 | Initial skill file | | 2026-06 | v2 | Full runnable example, structured output, action routing |

title: Resource Allocation
description: Assign scarce resources — budget, capacity, attention — across competing demands by stating the objective, constraints, and the cost of what is left unfunded.
body: Resource Allocation Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Resource allocation is deciding what does not get done. This skill structures that decision: state the objective explicitly, inventory demands with their expected returns and constraints, solve or approximate the assignment, and surface the marginal cost — what the objective loses at the boundary — so trade-offs are argued in the open rather than settled by whoever pushes hardest. When to Use Use when demands exceed capacity — team time across projects, compute across workloads, budget across candidates — and an explicit assignment is more defensible than implicit juggling. Do not allocate without recording what was left unfunded; an allocation with no visible remainder hides its own cost. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Available amounts per constrained resource | | | | Yes | Candidate demands with expected return and resource needs | | | | Yes | Maximize total return, minimize shortfall, or meet a stated target | Procedure 1. State the objective and constraints as explicit expressions before looking at demands. 2. Inventory demands with their resource needs and expected returns, including uncertainty on both. 3. Rank demands by return per unit of the scarcest resource and test a greedy assignment as a baseline. 4. Where demands interact — dependencies, mutual exclusion, diminishing returns — solve with the interaction represented or state the approximation. 5. Record what the allocation left unfunded and the estimated cost of the top unfunded item. 6. State marginal values: what one more unit of each resource would be worth under this allocation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Allocated amounts per demand | | | | Demands left unmet with their estimated cost | | | | Marginal value of one more unit per resource | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Implicit allocation | Resources shift toward whoever argues loudest | State the objective and solve explicitly | | Hidden remainder | The unfunded list is never recorded | Report what was left unfunded and its cost | | Point estimates | Returns are treated as certain | Carry uncertainty and re-rank under adverse draws | | Objective drift | The objective changes to fit a preferred answer | Fix the objective before demands are argued | | Static plan | The allocation is never revisited as returns are realized | Re-allocate at stated checkpoints | Security and Authority Boundary Allocation decisions encode priorities and can reveal strategic direction — reserved capacity, defense budgets, sensitive workloads. Treat allocation tables as sensitive when the demands are, and apply the same access control as the underlying plans. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of resource allocation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resourceallocation). 2. Wikipedia's overview of the knapsack problem, the canonical constrained-assignment model (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapsackproblem). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Self-Consistency
description: Sample N independent reasoning chains for the same question and majority-vote the final answer. Trades cost for accuracy — robust on math and logic, surprisingly cheap with smaller-than-frontier models.
body: Self-Consistency Description Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) augments Chain of Thought by sampling N independent reasoning chains at temperature > 0, parsing each one's final answer, and majority-voting. Wrong reasoning chains tend to scatter across many wrong answers; correct reasoning converges. So the modal answer is usually the right one. It's the simplest "test-time compute" trick that exists, and it works. On GSM8K-style arithmetic, self-consistency typically lifts accuracy by 5–15 points over single-shot CoT at the cost of ~N× tokens. When to Use - The task has a single, parseable final answer (math, logic, multiple-choice, classification). - You can afford N× cost (typically 5). - You don't have access to a reasoning-tuned model that already does this implicitly. - Don't use when the answer is open-ended text — voting is meaningless on prose. title: Sensitivity Analysis
description: Measure how much each input drives a model or decision output, varying inputs over stated ranges and ranking their influence before trusting the result.
body: Sensitivity Analysis Category: Reasoning | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Any computed recommendation rests on inputs with different leverage. Sensitivity analysis varies each input across a stated range, observes the output response, and ranks which inputs actually drive the conclusion — turning a raw model output into a statement of the form: the conclusion holds unless a named assumption moves by more than a stated amount. When to Use Use before committing to a decision, forecast, or model-based recommendation when inputs are uncertain and someone needs to know which uncertainty matters. Do not report a single-number output without its dominant sensitivities; a point estimate with unranked assumptions is not a decision aid. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Function or process mapping inputs to output | | | | Yes | Tested low and high bounds per input | | | | No | Monte Carlo draws when joint effects are tested | Procedure 1. Freeze the output metric before varying anything; sensitivity to an undefined metric is meaningless. 2. Vary one input at a time across its stated range with others held at nominal values, recording the output response. 3. Rank inputs by output swing and identify which ones cross decision thresholds. 4. Where inputs interact, sample combinations with a Monte Carlo design and report joint effects, not just single-input swings. 5. Report the ranges tested; a sensitivity claim outside the tested range is an extrapolation. 6. State the consequence: which input, moved how far, reverses the conclusion. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Inputs ranked by influence on the output | | | | Input values at which the decision flips | | | | Tested ranges, design, and sampled effects | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unranked assumptions | All inputs presented as equally uncertain | Rank by measured output swing | | Hidden interactions | Single-input swings miss joint effects | Sample combinations where inputs interact | | Range omission | Sensitivity claimed outside tested ranges | Always report the tested bounds | | Nominal anchoring | Results conditional on one nominal point | Test alternative nominal values for stability | | Threshold silence | Nobody knows which change flips the decision | Report decision thresholds explicitly | Security and Authority Boundary Sensitivity analysis can expose which parameters a system is most vulnerable to — including security-relevant ones. Treat high-leverage parameter lists as sensitive when the underlying model is, and do not publish attack-surface rankings for systems that are not yours. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The SALib sensitivity analysis library documentation (https://salib.readthedocs.io/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of sensitivity analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensitivity_analysis). title: Step-Back Prompting
description: Prompt the LLM to first answer a high-level abstraction (the 'step-back' question) before solving the original task. Improves performance on multi-step reasoning by grounding the answer in principles before details.
body: Step-Back Prompting Description Step-Back Prompting (Zheng et al., 2023) instructs the model to first retrieve a high-level principle or concept relevant to the question before attempting a solution. The two-step structure is: 1. Step-back question: "What is the general principle or concept behind this problem?" 2. Grounded answer: Use the retrieved principle as context for the original answer. On MMLU (physics, chemistry) and TimeQA benchmarks, Step-Back Prompting improved accuracy by 7-27% over direct prompting and 1-11% over Chain-of-Thought. When to Use - Multi-hop questions requiring domain knowledge before specific calculation. - Research agents that need to ground answers in principles before synthesis. - RAG pipelines where the retrieval query benefits from abstraction before specifics. - Don't use for simple factual lookups or purely procedural tasks with no principles.
