title: Task Decomposition
description: Split a complex task into a structured, ordered list of subtasks small enough that a single LLM call (or tool call) reliably solves each one.
body: Task Decomposition Description Decomposition is the first move of any non-trivial agent task: break the user's goal into 3–10 atomic subtasks the executor can dispatch independently. Distinct from Planning — decomposition produces what to do, planning adds order, deps, constraints. Done well, decomposition shrinks the per-call solution space, lets you parallelise independent work, and gives you a clean unit to retry / verify / cache. Done badly, you get vague subtasks ("research the topic") that don't actually reduce difficulty. When to Use - The user request is too large to answer in one model call. - You want to run subtasks in parallel. - You need an audit trail of "what the agent decided to do" before it does it. - For trivial tasks (single API call, single lookup), skip — decomposition adds latency and tokens for no gain. title: Cache Management
description: Operate a bounded cache with explicit admission, TTL expiry, deterministic LRU eviction, and a measured hit rate so memory stays capped and staleness stays bounded by policy.
body: Cache Management Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A cache becomes a correctness risk the moment it has no policy: unbounded growth exhausts memory, and stale entries serve wrong answers with no bound. This skill defines an explicit cache contract — capacity, TTL, eviction order, and a measured hit rate — so behavior is predictable and observable. It covers in-process caches; distributed cache coherence is out of scope. When to Use Use when an agent or service keeps derived or fetched values in memory and either the memory footprint or the staleness window must stay bounded. Do not use for long-lived stores of record; use the memory and retrieval skills for durable state. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Maximum number of live entries | | | | Yes | Expiry window applied to every entry | | | | No | Injectable clock value for deterministic tests | | | | No | Callback invoked with each evicted key | Procedure 1. Declare capacity and TTL before the first write; never admit an entry without both bounds set. 2. On write, store the value with its absolute expiry timestamp and move the key to the most-recently-used position. 3. Evict least-recently-used entries whenever the live count exceeds capacity; eviction order must be deterministic. 4. On read, treat an expired entry as a miss, delete it, and count it as a miss; never serve a value past its expiry. 5. Count hits and misses on every access so the hit rate is measured, not assumed. 6. Re-measure the hit rate after any capacity or TTL change; an unmeasured cache is a liability, not an optimization. 7. Expose the live size, the measured hit rate, and the eviction count for monitoring. 8. Fail closed on unbounded configurations: a cache without capacity or TTL is rejected, not silently tolerated. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The stored value, or a miss indicator when absent or expired | | | | Accesses served from the cache within expiry | | | | Accesses not served, including expiry misses | | | | Measured hits divided by total accesses over the window | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unbounded growth | Capacity was never set | Reject cache creation without a capacity bound | | Stale serve | Expiry checked lazily or not at all | Check expiry on every read and delete expired entries | | Eviction thrash | Capacity sits below the working set | Measure the hit rate and resize on evidence | | Silent cache | No hit or miss counters exist | Count every access and expose the measured rate | | Clock coupling | Tests read the wall clock directly | Inject the clock so expiry behavior is deterministic | Security and Authority Boundary Operating a cache grants no authority over the source of truth. Cached values are read-only projections; writes flow to the underlying store through its normal controls. Entries holding sensitive data inherit the source’s retention rules: TTL and eviction must not become a way to keep data past its declared lifetime. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s survey of cache replacement policies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachereplacementpolicies). 2. Python’s collections module documentation covering OrderedDict (https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Context Compaction
description: Compress long agent context while preserving active task state, user constraints, tool dependencies, and evidence required for correct continuation.
body: Context Compaction Description Reduce an agent's active context when it approaches a configured budget while preserving the information required to continue correctly. Compaction must preserve active objectives, constraints, decisions, unresolved work, tool dependencies, authoritative evidence, and user-provided requirements while discarding redundant or safely recoverable history. When to Use - Long-running agent sessions approach context limits. - Tool-heavy workflows accumulate large outputs. - Repeated context windows cause cost or latency pressure. - An agent must continue work after a context boundary without restarting. Inputs / Outputs | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Conversation state, active task, completed actions, pending actions, evidence, dependencies, and context budget. | | Outputs | Compact continuation state plus a deterministic record of what was retained, discarded, or made recoverable. | | Invariant | The compacted state must not claim completion for unfinished work. | Procedure 1. Detect context pressure before the hard limit. 2. Identify active objective, constraints, current state, dependencies, evidence, and pending actions. 3. Preserve user requirements and facts needed to verify continuation. 4. Collapse redundant tool output and stale narration. 5. Prevent self-referential summaries from re-expanding the context. 6. Validate the compacted state against the active task before resuming. 7. If critical state cannot be preserved, stop and recover from an authoritative checkpoint instead of guessing. Runnable Example Failure Modes - Repeated compaction with no net reduction. - Loss of active task or user constraints. - Dropped tool dependency causing incorrect continuation. - Summary claims a step is complete when it is only planned. - Full transcript repeatedly re-sent to the compression model, creating unnecessary cost. - Compaction failure silently continues with an over-budget context. Recovery Boundary Compaction is a state-preservation operation, not a license to infer missing facts. Missing critical state must produce BLOCKED or trigger an authoritative recovery mechanism. Evidence Public 2026 agent issues document repeated compaction failures, context bloat, lost checkpoints, and substantial token/cost waste in long-running agent workflows. These are direct demand signals for reliable context-management behavior. Related - short-term-memory.md - working-memory.md - long-term-memory.md - state-machine.md - retry-backoff.md

title: Memory Conflict Resolution
description: Detect and resolve contradictions between stored memories and new observations using recency, provenance, and confidence evidence, with explicit resolution records instead of silent overwrites.
body: Memory Conflict Resolution Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Long-lived agents accumulate memories that later observations contradict: a user corrects a stored preference, a price changes, a source updates. This skill covers detecting the conflict, weighing evidence (recency, source authority, confidence), choosing a resolution policy, and recording what was superseded so the decision is auditable. Conflict resolution is not fact-checking — it decides which memory the agent will act on, not what is cosmically true. When to Use Use when a new observation or instruction disagrees with a stored memory that downstream behavior depends on. Do not use it to silently overwrite history; the losing value must remain recoverable. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Stored memory entry with provenance | | | | Yes | New observation with provenance | | | | No | , , , or | Procedure 1. Detect the conflict: same subject key, incompatible predicates or values. 2. Gather provenance for both sides: source, timestamp, confidence, and how each was obtained. 3. Select the policy the domain warrants (recency for volatile facts, authority for canonical ones, confidence when sources differ in quality, ask when stakes are high). 4. Resolve by superseding, not deleting: write the winner forward and tombstone the loser with a pointer to the resolution record. 5. Record the decision: both values, the policy, the winner, and the timestamp. 6. Propagate: invalidate derived artifacts (summaries, cached plans) that embedded the losing value. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The memory the agent will act on | | | | Policy, inputs, and outcome for audit | | | | Tombstoned entries kept for recovery | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Recency clobbers authority | A newer noisy observation beats an authoritative one | Use or policy for canonical facts | | Conflict missed | Subject keys normalized differently ( vs ) | Normalize subject keys before comparison | | Flapping | Two sources alternate winning on every observation | Add hysteresis or an explicit merge step | | Lost history | Overwrite without tombstone | Supersede and keep the resolution record | | Stale derivatives | Cached summaries still embed the old value | Propagate invalidation to derived artifacts | Security and Authority Boundary Memories hold user data. Resolution records must contain only what audit needs; do not leak memory values into shared logs beyond the task's purpose, and never resolve conflicts in a way that hides a user's explicit instruction. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Automerge CRDT library for conflict-aware document merging (https://github.com/automerge/automerge). 2. The Yjs conflict-free replicated data types library (https://github.com/yjs/yjs). title: Memory Consolidation
description: Periodically compress episodic memories into durable semantic facts, keeping the compression lossy-but-recorded rather than silent or lossless-but-unreadable.
body: Memory Consolidation Category: Memory | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Raw episodic history grows faster than it can be recalled: every interaction leaves traces, most of which never matter again. Consolidation turns that pile into structure — recurring observations become semantic facts, stable patterns become procedural rules, and the source episodes are cited rather than deleted. The skill covers deciding what to consolidate, what the compressed form loses, and how to audit the compression. When to Use Use when long-running agents accumulate episodic records across sessions and retrieval quality degrades — noisy recall, repeated re-derivation of the same facts. Do not consolidate silently: a compressed memory with no trace of what was compressed or lost cannot be audited or undone. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw episodic records with timestamps and provenance | | | | Yes | What counts as recurring and when consolidation triggers | | | | No | Semantic, procedural, or profile store for the result | Procedure 1. Group episodes by subject and time window before extracting anything; consolidation on ungrouped history invents patterns. 2. Extract candidate generalizations only where recurrence is measured — occurrence counts, not impressions. 3. Promote a candidate to a semantic fact with its support: which episodes, how many, over what period. 4. Cite the source episodes in the consolidated record so the compression can be audited. 5. Record what the compression lost — dropped exceptions, outlier episodes — rather than presenting the fact as lossless. 6. Keep the source episodes available for a stated re-derivation window before any cleanup. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Consolidated semantic facts with support citations | | | | What the compression dropped per fact | | | | Recurring patterns below the promotion threshold | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Pattern invention | A single episode becomes a generalization | Require measured recurrence | | Silent loss | Exceptions are dropped without record | Record what each compression dropped | | Provenance cut | Consolidated facts cite nothing | Keep source episode references in every fact | | Over-consolidation | Distinct behaviors are merged into one rule | Group by subject before extracting | | No re-derivation | Sources are deleted before any audit | Keep sources for a stated window | Security and Authority Boundary Consolidation concentrates sensitive details into durable claims about people and systems — a summarized profile is more shareable and more permanent than its source episodes. Apply profile-level access controls and honor deletion requests against consolidated facts, not only raw episodes. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of semantic memory as the durable-fact store destination (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semanticmemory). title: Memory Indexing
description: Index stored memories for retrieval — keyword, inverted, and vector structures — with stated ranking, measured recall, and maintenance against index drift.
body: Memory Indexing Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An agent's memory is only as good as its retrieval, and retrieval is only as fast as its index. This skill covers choosing and building the right structure for the query mix — exact keyword lookups, full-text search, similarity search — measuring recall against the corpus, and maintaining the index as memories are written, updated, and expired rather than letting it drift from the store. When to Use Use when the memory store grows beyond a scan-all lookup and queries must select a bounded subset — long-term memory, knowledge bases, session archives. Do not trust an index without measuring it; a silently degraded index returns plausible-but-wrong memories. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Stored memory records with fields | | | | Yes | Expected query types and frequency | | | | No | Latency and memory limits for the index | Procedure 1. Characterize the query mix before choosing the structure — exact lookups need inverted indexes, fuzzy recall needs vector or trigram structures. 2. Build the index on the corpus fields queries actually filter on, not every field available. 3. Measure recall against a labeled query set: what the index returns versus what a full scan would return. 4. Keep the index updated in the same transaction as the store, or run a stated reconciliation sweep for the gap. 5. Record index metadata — build time, size, last reconciliation — so drift is observable. 6. Rebuild from the corpus when drift exceeds a stated bound instead of patching forward. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The built index with its structure and fields | | | | Measured recall against the labeled query set | | | | Index size, build time, and last reconciliation | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent drift | The index diverges from the store | Reconcile on a schedule and measure the gap | | Unmeasured recall | Nobody knows what retrieval misses | Measure recall against a labeled query set | | Wrong structure | Vector search for exact lookups or scans for fuzzy recall | Match the index to the query mix | | Unbounded growth | Deleted and expired entries linger in the index | Remove index entries in the same transaction as deletes | | Hidden ranking | Result order is unexplained | State the ranking signal per query type | Security and Authority Boundary Indexes leak corpus content in their structures — term lists, embeddings, and summaries are readable from the index itself. Apply the same access control to the index as to the records, and never build shared indexes across principals with different visibility. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The SQLite FTS5 full-text search extension documentation (https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of full-text search structures (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-text_search). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Memory Injection

title: Memory TTL
description: Attach explicit time-to-live policies to stored memories so entries expire by design, with expiry sweeps and refresh rules instead of unbounded accumulation.
body: Memory TTL Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Memory without expiry becomes a landfill of stale facts: yesterday's price, last month's availability, a user status that quietly stopped being true. This skill attaches a time-to-live to each stored memory at write time, sweeps expired entries on a schedule, and defines when a TTL refreshes — so the agent recalls recent truth and forgets expired claims by design rather than by accident. When to Use Use when memory entries have a natural freshness horizon — prices, availability, user status, cache-like facts — where an old value is worse than no value. Do not give long-lived identity facts a short TTL; expiring stable knowledge wastes retrieval and erodes trust in the memory layer. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The memory being written | | | | Yes | Time-to-live applied at write time | | | | No | Access pattern that extends or resets the TTL | Procedure 1. Set the TTL at write time from the fact class, not as an afterthought — statuses decay faster than identity facts. 2. Store the expiry timestamp explicitly with the entry rather than computing it lazily at read time. 3. Sweep expired entries on a fixed schedule instead of relying on reads to trigger deletion. 4. Define the refresh rule explicitly: a read refreshes, an update resets, or the TTL is fixed regardless of access. 5. Keep expired entries observable — log sweep counts and categories rather than silently deleting. 6. Audit classes that never expire and justify each one; permanent entries are the exception, not the default. title: Progressive Skill Loading
description: Load skills into an agent context in escalating tiers - registry metadata first, the selected skill body second, and escalation only on measured need - so a large skill library costs a bounded, predictable token budget instead of loading every skill body up front.
body: Progressive Skill Loading Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Progressive skill loading keeps the context cost of a skill library proportional to what the current task actually uses. Skills enter the context window in escalating tiers: cheap registry metadata is loaded first; the full body of a selected skill is loaded only when the task requires it; and loading additional skill bodies happens only when measured evidence shows the smaller tiers are insufficient. This skill is intended for agent runtimes that consume large skill libraries. It does not replace retrieval, selection, or context compaction; it bounds the token cost of the skill layer itself. When to Use Use when an agent consumes a library of many skills and the skill layer's token cost is large or unmeasured. Do not use this to defer loading when the required skill is already known and affordable; load it directly. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Available skills with metadata-tier and full-body token costs | | | | Yes | Context budget reserved for the skill layer this turn | | | | Yes | Current task and required capabilities | | | | No | Skills already selected by an upstream selection boundary | | | | No | Tier order, escalation thresholds, and load caps | Loading Procedure 1. Load the metadata tier for catalog skills within the reserved budget, cheapest first. 2. Record the measured token cost of the metadata tier against the reserved budget. 3. Resolve the required skill through the normal selection boundary. 4. Load the selected skill's full body and re-measure the remaining budget. 5. Escalate to loading additional skill bodies only when the loaded tiers demonstrably cannot satisfy the task. 6. Prefer unloading or compacting unused skill bodies over exceeding the budget. 7. Record which tiers were loaded, their measured cost, and every escalation decision. 8. Fail closed when the budget cannot cover even the required skill body; report instead of silently truncating. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Which skills are loaded at which tier and at what token cost | | | | Measured skill-layer cost for the turn | | | | Escalations performed, with the measured trigger | | | | Skills demoted or evicted from context | | | | , , or | Decision Contract A valid loading decision must answer all of these questions: - What is the measured token cost of the metadata tier? - Which skill bodies are loaded, and why is each one loaded? - What measured evidence triggered any escalation? - What was evicted or compacted to stay within budget? - What happens when the budget cannot cover the required body? A skill must not be fully loaded merely because it might be relevant later. Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent full-load | Runtime loads every body at startup | Enforce tier order with measured costs | | Budget overflow | Bodies loaded without re-measuring | Re-measure after every tier escalation | | Starved metadata tier | Budget too small for even the metadata tier | Enlarge the budget or shrink the catalog; fail closed | | Stale cost estimates | Token costs changed after skill edits | Re-measure costs on version change | | Wrong-skill escalation | Body loaded on guessed relevance | Escalate only on selection-boundary decisions | | Hidden truncation | Body cut mid-way without notice | Treat truncation as OVER-BUDGET, not OK | | Cache incoherence | Loaded tier state diverges from the registry | Reload from the registry as source of truth | Security and Authority Boundary Loading a skill body into context does not grant execution authority. A loaded skill still executes only within its declared permissions and the runtime's approval controls. Skill bodies from untrusted sources must pass the security audit boundary before being loaded at all. Evidence This skill is motivated by dated public ecosystem evidence: 1. Public discussion of skill visibility in agent coding tools reports that carrying roughly 30-40 skills can consume on the order of 800-1,200 tokens per turn and requests explicit visibility tiers (https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/75376). 2. Microsoft Agent Framework documentation directs skills to stay under 5,000 tokens and describes progressive disclosure of skill content (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/agents/skills). 3. A 2026 agent-skills lifecycle survey describes token-budget-aware skill loading as a recurring lifecycle concern (https://redreamality.com/blog/agent-skills-2026-survey-lifecycle-map/). Honest boundary: these signals establish that skill-layer token cost is a real, measured concern in agent runtimes; they are not adoption data, and the specific numbers are runtime-dependent examples, not universal constants. The demand evidence is recorded in . title: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
description: Augment an LLM call with the top-k most relevant chunks from a private corpus, retrieved by embedding similarity. The standard recipe for grounding answers, citing sources, and shrinking hallucinations on a known knowledge base.
body: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) Description RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) is the dominant pattern for grounding LLMs on private or fast-moving data: at query time, embed the question, fetch the top-k most similar chunks from a vector store, stuff them into the prompt as context, and let the LLM answer with citations. It's cheaper than fine-tuning, easy to update (just re-embed), and the citations make hallucinations auditable. This skill is the minimal end-to-end recipe — chunk → embed → store → retrieve → prompt — with the knobs that actually matter (chunk size, top-k, similarity threshold, citation format) and the failure modes you will absolutely hit in production. When to Use - The answer must come from a specific corpus (your docs, your tickets, your codebase) and the model alone doesn't know it. - The corpus is larger than the context window, or queries touch a small unpredictable subset. - You need citations / provenance — RAG returns the exact chunks used. - Don't use when: the corpus fits in the context (just stuff it), the answer requires multi-hop reasoning across the whole corpus (use a graph-RAG / agentic retrieval pattern instead), or the corpus is the open web (use Web Search). Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | User query in natural language | | | | Pre-chunked documents with + | | | | Number of chunks to retrieve (default 4) | | | | Cosine threshold; chunks below are dropped (default 0.25) | | → | | Grounded answer with inline citations | | → | | Chunks actually used (subset of top-k after threshold) | | → | | Top similarity score; useful for cascade gating | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Wrong chunk retrieved (low recall) | Chunks too large, query specific to a sub-paragraph | Smaller chunks (200–500 tokens) with overlap, or hierarchical indexing | | Right chunk retrieved, ignored by LLM | Buried in the middle of a large context | Use top-k≤6, put question last ("lost in the middle"), reduce noise | | Hallucinated citation | Model invented an id that wasn't in context | Validate cited ids against ; on mismatch, mark answer untrusted | | "I don't know" when answer IS in corpus | too high or chunk too long | Lower threshold; switch to hybrid (BM25 + dense); add a re-ranker | | Stale answers | Corpus re-embedded on a slow schedule | Stream updates; use upsert with and prefer fresher | | Cost spikes on long contexts | Large k × large chunks | Re-rank with a cross-encoder, then keep only the top 2-3 | Variants | Variant | When | |---|---| | Naïve RAG (above) | Default, well-trodden, works for FAQ/support/docs | | Hybrid retrieval | Add BM25/keyword score and fuse — fixes "exact-match" queries embeddings miss | | Re-ranking RAG | Retrieve k=20, re-rank with a cross-encoder, keep top 4 — best precision | | Multi-query RAG | Have the LLM rewrite the question into N variants, union the hits | | Graph-RAG / Agentic RAG | Multi-hop questions; the agent decides what to retrieve next | | Long-context RAG | Skip retrieval, stuff the corpus, rely on a 1M-token model — wasteful but simple | Frameworks & Models | Framework | Notes | |---|---| | Direct API (above) | Maximum control; ~80 lines | | LangChain | Pre-baked chains; verbose but feature-complete | | LlamaIndex | Best DX for multi-source, hybrid, hierarchical | | Haystack | Strong on enterprise pipelines + production deploy | | pgvector / Qdrant / Pinecone | Pick based on ops; title: Retention Policy
description: Define and enforce how long each class of stored memory is kept — legal floors, purpose limits, and deletion mechanics — before accumulation becomes liability.
body: Retention Policy Category: Memory | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every stored record is a liability as well as an asset: it ages, it contradicts newer facts, and it answers requests you did not invite. A retention policy decides, per class of memory, how long it is kept, why, and what happens at the boundary. This skill structures that policy — classes, floors, ceilings, deletion mechanics — and keeps the decision explicit instead of the default of keeping everything until something breaks. When to Use Use when an agent persists memory across sessions and operates under privacy obligations, data agreements, or plain hygiene requirements. Do not apply a single blanket retention to all classes; volatile facts, stable preferences, and legally required records decay on different clocks. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Memory categories with their purpose | | | | No | Legal or contractual floors and ceilings per class | | | | No | Delete, anonymize, or archive at expiry | Procedure 1. Classify stored memory by purpose — operational, preference, legal, diagnostic — because retention hangs on purpose, not on storage technology. 2. For each class, state the ceiling (how long it may be kept) and any floor (how long it must be kept), with the obligation cited. 3. Choose the expiry mechanic per class — hard delete, anonymize, archive — and note that archive is not deletion. 4. Wire expiry into the write path: every record carries its class and expiry, so enforcement is mechanical rather than a periodic cleanup project. 5. Audit enforcement: sample records past expiry and verify the policy ran. 6. Handle deletion requests end-to-end — active store, indexes, backups, and derived artifacts — and record what was out of reach. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-class floors, ceilings, and mechanics | | | | Expiry execution status per class | | | | Out-of-reach stores and policy violations found | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Blanket retention | One duration is applied to every class | Classify by purpose and set per-class rules | | Missing floors | Legally required records are deleted early | Cite obligations and enforce floors | | Archive-as-delete | Records are moved somewhere and called gone | State the mechanic honestly | | Backup blind spot | Deletion never reaches backups or exports | Record what was out of reach | | No enforcement audit | A policy exists but never runs | Sample past-expiry records and verify | Security and Authority Boundary Retention is the primary lever that limits exposure of personal data: shorter ceilings, purpose-bound classes, and honest mechanics reduce both breach impact and compliance failure. This skill is not legal advice; retention obligations vary by jurisdiction and must be confirmed with counsel where they apply. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of data retention (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dataretention). 2. Wikipedia's overview of ISO 8601 date and duration notation used in retention rules (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO8601). title: Short-Term Memory
description: The bounded conversational scratchpad — recent turns + tool outputs the model can see this turn. Trims under a token budget so the agent never crashes on context overflow.
body: Short-Term Memory Description Short-term memory (STM) is the rolling context window the agent shows the model on every turn: the last N user/assistant messages, plus any tool outputs and a small set of pinned system facts. It's the simplest, most-deployed memory pattern — and the one that breaks first when it isn't bounded by a real token budget. A correct STM does three things every turn: (1) compute current token count, (2) drop oldest non-pinned messages until under budget, (3) optionally summarise the dropped chunk so the model still has a thread of the past. This skill is what the rest of Long-Term Memory, Episodic Memory, and Memory Injection build on top of. When to Use - Always in any chat or agent loop — even one-turn agents need a bounded STM for tool outputs. - When sessions are long enough that the raw history will exceed your model's context (~128k for current frontier). - Pair with Memory Injection when you also want long-term, cross-session recall. title: Vector Store Retrieval
description: Look up the top-k items in a vector store by cosine similarity to a query embedding. The retrieval primitive that powers RAG, semantic search, deduplication, recommendation, and clustering.
body: Vector Store Retrieval Description A vector store is a (id, vector, metadata, payload) collection plus a similarity-search index. Vector store retrieval is the act of embedding a query into the same space and returning the top-k items by cosine similarity (or dot-product, or L2). It's the lookup primitive underneath RAG, semantic dedup, recommendation, and "find me similar tickets" features. This skill covers the retrieval-side contract and shows the same in-memory implementation hardened with normalisation, optional metadata filtering, and a clean swap-point for production stores (pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate). When to Use - You have an indexed corpus of vectors and a stream of query embeddings. - You want semantic matches, not lexical (BM25 doesn't match "renew" → "extend"). - The corpus is too large to scan linearly per query (>~10k items) — production needs an ANN index, not Python loops. - Don't use when an exact lexical match suffices (use grep/BM25), or the entire corpus fits in the context window. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Unit-normalised dense vector | | | | Items to return (default 5) | | | | Metadata predicates ANDed together | | | | Drop hits below this similarity (default 0.0) | | → | | Sorted by similarity, descending | | → | | Cosine similarity in [-1, 1] | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Top-1 is irrelevant but high score | Embedding model conflates topic with intent | Switch model, or add a re-ranker (cross-encoder) | | Recent items never surface | Index isn't being updated | on every write; never rebuild from scratch | | Latency spikes at >100k items | Linear scan in Python | Move to ANN index (HNSW, IVF) — pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone | | Wrong distance metric | Mixed cosine/L2 between index and query | Normalise on write AND on query; document the metric | | Stale duplicates | Two different ids for the same content | Hash text → id (SHA-1 first 12 chars); upsert by hash | | Filter excludes everything | Over-strict metadata predicates | Apply filter loosely first; title: Working Memory
description: Maintain bounded active task state, intermediate results, errors, and checkpoints during a multi-step agent workflow.
body: Description Maintain bounded active task state, intermediate results, errors, and checkpoints during a multi-step agent workflow. When to Use Use when memory state must persist across steps or sessions and the workflow can define ownership, provenance, retention, and verification rules. Inputs / Outputs / Failure Modes | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | goal, current state, completed steps, tool results, errors, and checkpoint policy. | | Outputs | validated working state, checkpoint, next action, and failure context. | | Failure modes | Stale memory, unsupported inference, conflicting records, unauthorized retention, context growth, or acceptance without revalidation. | Procedure 1. Define the memory scope, owner, retention rule, and acceptance criteria. 2. Validate incoming memory candidates and preserve their provenance. 3. Apply explicit freshness, confidence, conflict, and size bounds. 4. Retrieve only the memory relevant to the current task. 5. Revalidate memory before treating it as authoritative when material. 6. Record updates, conflicts, and unresolved uncertainty. Runnable Example Failure Modes - Memory is stale or its provenance cannot be established. - A model-generated inference is stored as an explicit user fact. - Conflicting records are silently merged. - Retention exceeds the declared scope or authorization. - Memory growth exhausts context or storage budgets. - A stored procedure or fact is used without required revalidation. Safety Boundary Treat memory as state, not truth. Preserve provenance and scope. Do not store sensitive or personal information unless explicitly authorized by the governing application policy, and honor correction or deletion requirements. title: Archive Extraction
description: Extract files from zip, tar, and compressed archives safely, with path-traversal defense, decompression-bomb limits, and integrity verification before any extracted byte is used.
body: Archive Extraction Category: Action Execution | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Extracting an archive means executing a promise made by untrusted bytes: a manifest of names, sizes, and attributes that the extractor must not believe. This skill covers detecting the real format, bounding the total decompressed size, rejecting traversal paths, and extracting into a staging area so nothing extracted is used before validation completes. When to Use Use when ingesting bundles, backups, datasets, or dependency archives into a working environment. Do not extract untrusted archives into privileged paths, and do not treat extension names as format evidence. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The archive file on disk | | | | Yes | Staging directory for extraction | | | | No | Decompression-bomb ceiling (default 1 GiB) | Procedure 1. Detect the format from magic bytes (PK\x03\x04, ustar, gzip, xz), never from the file extension. 2. Read the entry manifest; reject the archive if declared total size exceeds the ceiling. 3. Validate every entry name: reject absolute paths, segments, and non-materializable entries such as device nodes. 4. Verify checksums when the archive provides them (CRC, or sidecar signature files). 5. Extract into the staging directory with permissions normalized; do not execute or import anything during extraction. 6. Move validated files into the destination only after every entry passed. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Validated paths now in the destination | | | | Rejected entries with reasons | | | | Format, counts, sizes, checksum results | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Zip bomb | Compressed ratio and total size unchecked | Enforce on declared sizes | | Path traversal | Entry names contain or absolute paths | Validate every entry name before writing | | Extension spoofing | A gzip stream named fed to the wrong parser | Detect format from magic bytes | | Partial success | Extraction stopped mid-archive but reported done | Extract to staging; report skipped entries | | Overwritten files | Destination already contained same-named files | Stage first, then move with explicit overwrite policy | Security and Authority Boundary Archives are untrusted input with code-execution risk: entries can be executable or symlinks pointing outside the staging tree. Extract with least privilege, never auto-run extracted code, and treat any archive from an unknown source as hostile until validated. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The patool portable archive utility (https://pypi.org/project/patool/). 2. The Python standard library tarfile documentation, including its extraction-safety notes (https://docs.python.org/3/library/tarfile.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Shell Command — the execution layer that performs the extraction steps. - Batch Processing — the pattern for handling many extracted entries uniformly. title: Batch Processing
description: Execute many homogeneous operations as a bounded batch — chunking, per-item status, partial-failure handling, and resumable checkpoints — instead of a fragile loop.
body: Batch Processing Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Bulk work fails in ways single operations do not: item four thousand of ten thousand errors, the connection drops at sixty percent, and a naive loop either stops the world or loses track of what happened. This skill structures bulk execution as bounded chunks with per-item status, so any run can resume from where it stopped and report exactly which items succeeded, failed, or were skipped. When to Use Use when the same operation applies to many items — bulk API calls, mass file transforms, database migrations — and partial failure is expected rather than exceptional. Do not run unbounded batches: without chunking and checkpoints, a bulk run is a single point of failure for the whole set. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The full item set to process | | | | Yes | The operation applied to each item | | | | No | Batch size and checkpoint interval | Procedure 1. Persist the item manifest before starting so progress survives interruption and is auditable afterwards. 2. Chunk the work: process bounded batches, not the full set in one unbounded pass. 3. Record per-item status — pending, succeeded, failed, skipped — with the error attached at failure time. 4. On interruption, resume from the last checkpoint by reading the manifest, not by re-deriving what was done. 5. Apply a failure budget: stop the batch when the failure rate crosses a stated bound instead of processing the full set into a known-bad state. 6. Reconcile at the end: counts of succeeded, failed, and skipped must sum to the manifest size. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-item status for the full set | | | | Counts by status plus timing per chunk | | | | Checkpoint state for resuming an interrupted run | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | All-or-nothing stop | One failure halts the whole set | Record per-item status and continue within the failure budget | | Lost progress | An interrupted run restarts from zero | Checkpoint against a persisted manifest | | Unbounded chunks | The full set is processed in one pass | Chunk into bounded batches | | Silent skips | Skipped items are never reported | Count and list skips in the summary | | Count mismatch | Statuses do not sum to the manifest | Reconcile at run end | Security and Authority Boundary Batch operations concentrate access — bulk reads and writes move data at a scale that interactive use never touches. Scope credentials to the batch job, log the manifest rather than the payloads, and do not let bulk jobs bypass per-item authorization checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Apache Kafka documentation on producer batching and consumer group mechanics (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of stream processing, where bounded chunks are the unit of work (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_processing). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Compensating Actions
description: Design undo for side effects that cannot be transactional — reverse operations, saga compensation in reverse order, and recorded forward-recovery paths for each step.
body: Compensating Actions Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some operations cannot be wrapped in a transaction: money moves between systems, messages leave, external state changes. When one step in a chain fails, earlier effects must be reversed — and that reversal needs to be designed, not improvised. This skill maps each step of a multi-system workflow to its compensating action and records what happens when compensation itself fails. When to Use Use when a workflow spans multiple systems without a shared transaction — order plus payment plus shipping, provision plus notify — and partial failure must leave a coherent state. Do not assume every step can be undone; some can only be acknowledged and corrected, and that difference belongs in the design. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Ordered steps with their side effects | | | | Yes | Reverse action per step, or explicit not-compensable | | | | No | Forward-recovery and manual-intervention rules | Procedure 1. List the workflow steps with their side effects before writing any of them; compensation design needs the full picture. 2. For each step, define its compensating action — the reverse operation, an acknowledge-and-correct path, or explicit not-compensable. 3. Define failure handling as a saga: on failure at a given step, run compensations for all earlier steps in reverse order. 4. Record semantic invariants — what the compensations must restore in meaning, not just mechanics — and check them after recovery. 5. Plan for compensation failure: retry the compensation, then fall back to a recorded manual-intervention path. 6. Log forward progress for steps that cannot be reversed, so operators see what was done rather than guessing. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-step reverse actions and their order | | | | What the recovery must restore | | | | Compensations attempted, with outcomes | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Improvised undo | Reversal is invented during the incident | Design compensations before the chain runs | | Uncompensable silence | Irreversible steps are not marked | Mark not-compensable steps explicitly | | Compensation failure | Undo itself fails with no fallback | Retry, then route to a recorded manual path | | Lost invariants | Recovery restores mechanics but not meaning | Check semantic invariants after recovery | | Phantom success | A step is reported done but never landed | Verify each compensation effect instead of assuming | Security and Authority Boundary Compensating actions carry the same authority as the actions they reverse — a refund moves money, an unprovision removes access. Scope compensation credentials narrowly, log every compensation in an operator-visible record, and treat unexpected compensation triggers as an audit event. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The saga pattern description for distributed transactions (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of compensating transactions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compensating_transaction). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. body: HTTP Request Description An outbound HTTP call is the most common side-effect an agent performs. When to Use - The agent needs to call any HTTP endpoint — REST, JSON-RPC, webhook, anything. - You want uniform retry / timeout / logging behaviour across all calls. - Even when a "client library" exists — wrap its failures in this contract for consistent agent ergonomics. - Don't reimplement when calling a major SaaS provider's SDK that already handles retries (Stripe, Anthropic, OpenAI). title: Idempotent Retries
description: Make retries safe by designing operations to be idempotent — client-generated keys, state checks before effect, and receiver-side dedupe — before any retry loop runs.
body: Idempotent Retries Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A retry that re-applies a side effect is worse than the original failure: duplicate charges, double sends, repeated writes. This skill makes an operation idempotent before retrying it — the caller attaches a stable operation key, the receiver dedupes, and the effect happens once regardless of how many attempts the network takes. When to Use Use for any operation with side effects that might be retried — payments, emails, writes, external state changes — especially across network boundaries where timeouts make outcomes ambiguous. Do not retry a non-idempotent operation; make it idempotent first or refuse the retry. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The side-effecting operation to make retryable | | | | Yes | Client-generated stable operation key | | | | No | Receiver state for dedupe, when modeling the remote side | Procedure 1. Generate the operation key once per logical operation, before the first attempt, and reuse it on every retry. 2. Design the receiver to dedupe on the key: return the original result for a repeated key instead of re-applying the effect. 3. Check current state before applying the effect — the operation may already have succeeded on a previous attempt. 4. Retry only on retryable failures — timeouts and transient errors — with exponential backoff and a stated attempt cap. 5. Treat ambiguous outcomes, such as a timeout after send, as pending rather than failed: resolve by querying the receiver with the key before retrying. 6. Record the operation key in the audit trail so duplicates are explainable after the fact. title: Quota Management
description: Track and enforce consumption limits — API calls, model tokens, spend, rate windows — with explicit budgets, remaining-capacity reporting, and early refusal at the boundary.
body: Quota Management Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Quotas turn a request to use resources responsibly into a number. This skill tracks consumption against an explicit budget per resource and window, reports remaining capacity before an operation starts, and refuses work at the boundary instead of discovering the limit inside an error response. The failure mode it exists to prevent is the silent approach to exhaustion, where an agent runs out mid-task. When to Use Use when operations consume a metered resource — third-party API calls, model tokens, spend against a budget, writes per window — and running out mid-task is worse than declining work. Do not rely on provider error responses as the quota signal; by the time the provider refuses, the workflow is already interrupted. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Limit per resource per window | | | | Yes | Consumption so far in the current window | | | | Yes | The operation with its estimated resource cost | Procedure 1. Declare the budget per resource per window at configuration time, with the window boundary explicit. 2. Track consumption at the point of use, attributing it to the operation that spent it. 3. Before starting an operation, check remaining capacity against its estimated cost and decline early when insufficient. 4. Refuse at the boundary with a stated reason — which quota, how much remains, when the window resets — instead of attempting and failing. 5. Report remaining capacity to the caller and the plan layer so scheduling can route around exhausted quotas. 6. Reconcile tracked usage against provider-reported usage on a schedule; drift means the tracker is wrong. title: Scheduled Execution
description: Run work at explicit times or intervals — cron-style schedules, ISO 8601 recurrences, and named time zones — with missed-run handling stated instead of improvised.
body: Scheduled Execution Category: Action Execution | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A request to run something every night hides a stack of decisions: which time zone, what happens to a run missed during downtime, and whether overlapping runs are allowed. This skill turns schedule intent into an explicit schedule — recurrence expression, time zone, catch-up policy, concurrency rule — and makes missed-run behavior a stated choice rather than an accident. When to Use Use for recurring agent or system work — periodic syncs, reports, maintenance, retention sweeps — that must happen at known times without a human pressing go. Do not deploy a schedule without deciding missed-run behavior; a scheduler that silently skips or silently piles up is one incident away from discovery. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The work to run | | | | Yes | Cron expression or ISO 8601 recurrence | | | | Yes | The zone the schedule is anchored to | | | | No | Missed-run and overlap handling | Procedure 1. Express the recurrence in an explicit, reviewable form — a cron expression or ISO 8601 rule — not as an opaque delay constant. 2. Anchor the schedule to a named time zone; unanchored times drift with daylight-saving shifts and server moves. 3. Decide the missed-run policy — run once on catch-up, skip, or run every missed slot — and state it next to the schedule. 4. Decide the overlap policy: cancel the previous run, allow concurrent runs, or skip if the previous run is still going. 5. Record each run with its scheduled time, actual start, and outcome so schedule health is observable. 6. Test at the boundaries — month ends, daylight-saving transitions, leap days — because that is where schedule defects live. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Recurrence, zone, and policies for the task | | | | Per-run record with scheduled and actual times | | | | Missed, skipped, and overlapping run counts | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating times | No zone means the meaning changes with the server | Anchor to a named time zone | | Silent skips | Missed runs during downtime are never addressed | State the missed-run policy | | Overlap pile-ups | Long runs spawn concurrent copies | Decide the overlap policy explicitly | | DST surprises | Off-by-one hours around transitions | Test daylight-saving boundaries | | Invisible health | Nobody knows how often runs were missed | Record per-run scheduled and actual times | Security and Authority Boundary Scheduled work runs unattended with whatever credentials the scheduler holds. Scope those credentials to the task, prefer short-lived credentials, avoid schedules that trigger privileged actions without limits, and alert on schedule changes — a moved job is a common persistence trick. title: Webhook Handling
description: Verify webhook deliveries with an HMAC signature over raw request bytes, reject replays outside a bounded window, and dispatch events idempotently so duplicate deliveries cause no double effects.
body: Webhook Handling Category: Action Execution | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Webhooks are the entry point for external systems to trigger effects, which makes them a double risk: an unverified sender can forge events, and a redelivered event can double-charge or double-create. This skill defines the handling contract: verify a signature computed over the raw request bytes, bound the replay window, and dispatch idempotently by event identity. It covers verification and dispatch; handler business logic stays in its own skills. When to Use Use when a service accepts event callbacks from an external platform and a forged or duplicated delivery would cause a wrong effect. Do not use for outgoing API calls or polling; the request and API-call skills fit those boundaries. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The exact request bytes the signature was computed over | | | | Yes | Received signature from the delivery headers | | | | Yes | Shared key used to compute the expected signature | | | | Yes | Maximum tolerated age of a delivery in seconds | | | | Yes | Durable record of already-dispatched event identities | Procedure 1. Read the raw request bytes before any parsing; re-serialization changes the bytes the signature covers. 2. Compute the expected HMAC over the raw bytes and compare with a constant-time comparison; reject on mismatch. 3. Check the delivery timestamp against the replay window before any handler runs. 4. Derive a stable event identity and check it against the seen set; duplicates are acknowledged, not dispatched. 5. Dispatch to the handler registry only after verification and identity checks pass, in that order. 6. Record the event identity durably in the same step that applies the effect, so a crash cannot split them. 7. Acknowledge the delivery only after the handler reports success; failed handlers return a retryable error to the sender. 8. Alert on verification failures at a threshold; repeated failures are an attack signal, not noise. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | ACCEPTED, DUPLICATE, STALE, or REJECTED with the failing check | | | | Whether a handler ran for this delivery | | | | The stable identity used for deduplication | | | | The check that failed, when the delivery was rejected | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Verification bypass | The signature is compared after JSON parsing | Verify over the raw bytes with a constant-time compare | | Replay attack | The delivery timestamp is unchecked | Bound the replay window and check it before dispatch | | Double dispatch | The seen set is updated after the effect | Record the event identity atomically with the effect | | Key leakage | The signing key sits in code or logs | Hold keys in declared secret storage and never log them | | Silent drop | Verification failures are logged nowhere | Alert on verification failures at a threshold | Security and Authority Boundary Verifying a webhook signature grants no authority beyond the sender’s declared events. The signing key is a credential: it lives in the runtime’s declared secret storage, is never embedded in code or logs, and rotates on the platform’s schedule. Verified events still pass through the handler’s own permission checks before any effect. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. GitHub’s guide to validating webhook deliveries (https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/using-webhooks/validating-webhook-deliveries). 2. Python’s hmac module documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Code Fuzzing
description: Feed generated, malformed, and adversarial inputs to a target until it fails, then minimize the failure into a reproducible defect report using coverage feedback.
body: Code Fuzzing Category: Code | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Fuzzing is automated guessing about where code breaks. Instead of hand-picking edge cases, a fuzzer generates many inputs — mutated, malformed, structure-aware — and keeps the ones that reach new code or new failures. This skill covers running a fuzzer with feedback, triaging what it finds, and minimizing a failing input into a defect report a maintainer can reproduce. When to Use Use on parsers, decoders, and anything that consumes untrusted input, where the input surface is too large for hand-written cases and crashes or memory corruption are real risks. Do not fuzz as a one-off: coverage-guided fuzzing finds defects with sustained runtime and a corpus that grows, not with a single short run. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The function or binary under test | | | | Yes | Entry point that feeds generated inputs to the target | | | | No | Seed inputs to start from | | | | No | Time or iteration limit | Procedure 1. Write a harness that calls the target with a generated input and turns any crash, hang, or assertion violation into a recorded failure — the harness is the contract. 2. Seed the corpus with realistic and boundary inputs so the fuzzer starts near interesting code. 3. Run coverage-guided generation: keep inputs that reach new paths and mutate them further. 4. Record every unique failure with its input, stack trace, and the coverage state that produced it. 5. Minimize each failing input — strip bytes and simplify structure — while confirming the failure persists. 6. Deduplicate by root cause rather than by input: a hundred crashes from one null dereference are one defect report. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Unique failures with inputs and traces | | | | Reduced reproducer per failure | | | | Coverage, executions, and time budget spent | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Harness blind spots | Failures the harness never observes | Write the harness against the crash contract, then review it | | Empty seeds | Fuzzing starts from nothing and stalls | Seed with realistic and boundary inputs | | Crash-only triage | Hangs and assertion violations go unreported | Record timeouts and invariants, not only crashes | | Unminimized reports | Maintainers receive giant inputs | Minimize while the failure persists | | Root-cause pileup | One defect is filed many times | Deduplicate failures by cause | Security and Authority Boundary Fuzzing cuts both ways: the same harness that finds defects in your code can be pointed at systems you do not own. Run fuzzers only against targets you own or are authorized to test, and treat findings in third-party code as responsible-disclosure material. title: Code Review
description: Review a code change for correctness, security, maintainability, tests, and repository conventions; return evidence-backed findings with severity and file/line anchors. Activate when the task is to review, critique, or assess source code quality—not when the task is only to explain review theory without inspecting code.
body: Code Review Description Code review inspects a concrete code change (diff, PR, or file set) and reports evidence-backed findings: what is wrong or risky, why, where (file/line), and how severe it is. It is not a vague opinion and not a rewrite of the code unless the task explicitly asks for fixes. Activate this skill when the user asks to review, critique, assess, or find issues in source code. Prefer this skill over web search or RAG when the subject is the code itself. When to Use - A pull request, diff, or set of source files must be reviewed for correctness, security, or maintainability. - The task names acceptance criteria, coding standards, or test expectations to check against. - The user wants a structured findings list before merge or ship. Do not use when: - The user only wants an explanation of how code review works, with no code to inspect (answer conceptually; do not pretend to review). - The task is pure code generation with no review request (use Code Generation). - The need is open-web research (use Web Search) or private-corpus Q&A (use RAG). title: Database Migration Writing
description: Write versioned, reversible schema migrations that ship application code and schema changes together, with explicit up and down paths, preflight checks, and lock-time budgeting.
body: Database Migration Writing Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A schema migration is a deployment, not a script: it changes the shape every live query depends on while the system runs. This skill covers writing migrations that go additive-first, carry a real rollback path, preflight their base version, and order operations so hot tables are not locked longer than the change is worth. When to Use Use for any change to a live database schema: new tables, columns, indexes, constraints, or type changes. Do not mix one-off data surgery into a versioned migration; separate scripts keep both reviewable. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Desired schema delta, declaratively stated | | | | Yes | Schema version the migration applies on top of | | | | No | Dialect-specific lock and syntax rules | Procedure 1. State the change additively where possible: new nullable columns and new tables before renames, type changes, and drops. 2. Write the down migration and verify it actually reverses the up path on a copy, data included. 3. Preflight: assert the database's schema version equals ; refuse to run otherwise. 4. Order operations by lock cost: build indexes concurrently, backfill in batches, drop only after the code no longer reads the old shape. 5. Round-trip test up, down, up on a production-shaped copy. 6. Record the new version and the lock-time estimate in the migration's header. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Versioned up/down files with preflight guards | | | | Steps and expected data state after down | | | | Expected blocking operations and durations | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Destructive step before backfill | Column dropped or retyped while still read | Add new shape, migrate code, then drop | | Down migration is a stub | Rollback written but never tested on data | Round-trip up/down/up on a copy | | Long lock on a hot table | Blocking index build or type change | Concurrent builds, batched backfills | | Version drift | Migration applied on an unexpected base | Preflight the schema version | | Schema and data changes entangled | One migration does both | Split into schema migrations and data scripts | Security and Authority Boundary Migrations execute with elevated database rights. Grant the minimum per step, never embed credentials or secrets in migration files, and treat down migrations with the same review standard as up migrations because they can destroy data. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Alembic database migration tool (https://pypi.org/project/alembic/). 2. The Flyway database migration project (https://github.com/flyway/flyway). title: Error Handling Design
description: Design the failure path as deliberately as the happy path — typed error classes, explicit boundaries, and recovery decisions made where the context lives.
body: Error Handling Design Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most systems get their error handling designed by accident: catch blocks appear where crashes were once observed, each with its own policy. This skill designs the failure path deliberately — classify errors by what recovery is possible, translate them at boundaries, and decide retry, fallback, or fail-fast where the context to decide actually lives. When to Use Use when designing or reviewing any module that can fail meaningfully — network calls, parsers, transactions, agents — especially where multiple layers could each independently retry or swallow errors. Do not catch broadly and continue; a swallowed error is a delayed failure with a lost cause. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The failing operations to design for | | | | Yes | Layer or system boundaries where errors translate | | | | Yes | Recovery rule per error class | Procedure 1. Enumerate the error classes per operation — transient, permanent, resource, integrity — before writing any handler; recovery decisions follow the class. 2. Fail fast on integrity and configuration errors; retrying a deterministic failure multiplies cost without changing the result. 3. Retry only transient errors, with backoff and a stated cap, and treat ambiguous outcomes as pending rather than failed. 4. Translate errors at boundaries: map internal classes to a documented contract with status, cause, and correlation id. 5. Attach context at the raise site — what operation, on what input class, at what stage — rather than reconstructing it later from strings. 6. Handle or propagate, and record which one happened where; an empty return after a caught error hides the failure from its caller. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Error classes, meanings, and boundary translations | | | | Recovery decisions per class with justification | | | | Correlation ids linking cause to observed failure | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Swallowed errors | Catch-all blocks continue with broken state | Handle or propagate; do not silently continue | | Retry everything | Deterministic failures retry to the cap | Classify before deciding recovery | | Lost cause chains | Context is stripped at the first boundary | Translate with cause and correlation id | | Empty returns after errors | Callers see empty results and no reason | Return the error or a documented default, with a record of which | | Boundary policy conflict | Two layers both retry, multiplying attempts | Decide retry ownership once per chain | Security and Authority Boundary Error messages are a disclosure channel: stack traces, query fragments, and file paths leak internals to callers and logs. Sanitize at trust boundaries, log the detail internally, and do not echo raw framework or driver errors to untrusted callers. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of exception handling (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exception_handling). 2. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model applications, whose failure-mode guidance this skill operationalizes (https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/). title: IDE Integration
description: Integrate AI coding agents with an IDE through explicit context, code intelligence, diagnostics, edits, tests, and controlled IDE actions while preserving least privilege and verifiable state.
body: IDE Integration Description Connect an AI coding agent to an IDE or IDE-like development surface so the agent can use editor-native context and feedback without treating the IDE as an unbounded control plane. A useful integration exposes only the operations the agent needs: repository/context inspection, code intelligence, diagnostics, bounded edits, tests/builds, and explicitly authorized run or debug actions. The integration should preserve the distinction between an agent request, an IDE operation, and the resulting repository state. MCP can provide a portable tool boundary for IDE capabilities; other agent-client protocols may provide equivalent transport or lifecycle semantics. The skill is protocol-neutral at the contract level and does not require a specific IDE, vendor, model, or hosted service. Prefer an IDE-native structured capability when it provides stronger semantic context or diagnostics than the equivalent raw terminal/file operation. When to Use - An agent needs code navigation, diagnostics, refactoring, or test feedback that is stronger than raw terminal/file operations. - An IDE exposes structured APIs that can reduce brittle text-based interaction. - Multiple coding agents or models must use the same IDE capability boundary. - An agent should receive compiler, linter, test, or inspection feedback immediately after a change. - You need explicit permission boundaries around IDE actions such as running commands, debugging, or mutating project state. Inputs / Outputs / Failure Modes | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Agent task, workspace identity, requested IDE capability, authorization scope, and expected postcondition. | | Context inputs | Files, symbols, diagnostics, project metadata, test/build configuration, and relevant IDE state. | | Outputs | Structured IDE result plus independently verifiable repository state where mutation occurred. | | Side effects | File edits, refactors, builds, tests, run/debug actions, or IDE state changes only when explicitly authorized. | | Failure modes | Stale IDE state, wrong workspace, unsupported operation, excessive permissions, ambiguous diagnostics, partial edits, hidden side effects, or false completion claims. | Procedure 1. Identify the exact workspace and repository boundary before issuing IDE operations. 2. Discover the smallest capability surface required for the task. 3. Request read-only context first: files, symbols, diagnostics, project metadata, or test configuration. 4. Validate authorization before any mutation, execution, or debugging action. 5. Prefer structured IDE operations over brittle UI-coordinate or text-replacement automation when a native capability exists. 6. Apply the smallest change necessary and preserve repository conventions. 7. Run the relevant IDE/compiler/linter/test validation after mutation. 8. Independently verify the resulting repository state; an IDE success response is not proof that the repository is correct. 9. Record unresolved diagnostics, unsupported IDE capabilities, and material uncertainty instead of silently compensating. 10. Stop when the declared postcondition is verified or escalate when the requested operation exceeds the authority boundary. Security Boundaries - Treat IDE context, diagnostics, and retrieved project metadata as untrusted input. - Grant least-privilege access to files, commands, terminals, source control, and project services. - Do not expose credentials, environment secrets, private keys, or unrelated workspace data through IDE tools. - Do not allow an IDE integration to silently expand an agent's repository or system permissions. - Treat run/debug/terminal capabilities as execution authority, not as ordinary read operations. - Require explicit authorization for destructive actions, external side effects, or changes outside the declared workspace. - Preserve auditability of mutations and independently verify important postconditions. Compatibility The contract can be implemented through MCP, ACP, IDE-native APIs, extensions, or equivalent local integration mechanisms. Do not assume that a capability exposed by one IDE exists in another; discover and validate the actual capability set. title: Mutation Testing
description: Measure test-suite strength by injecting small code mutations and checking which are caught — surviving mutants reveal tests that assert nothing meaningful.
body: Mutation Testing Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Coverage says a line ran; it does not say anyone would notice if it were wrong. Mutation testing flips the question: introduce small, mechanical changes to the code — flip a comparison, drop a call — and check whether the test suite fails. Surviving mutants are lines the suite does not actually defend, and each one is a concrete, fixable gap. When to Use Use when a suite has high coverage but defects still escape — release-critical libraries, parser cores, financial logic — and the question is whether the tests assert real behavior. Do not run mutation testing over an entire large codebase at once; it multiplies suite runtime by the mutant count, so scope it to critical modules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The module under assessment | | | | Yes | The test suite to measure | | | | No | Mutation operators to apply; default set | Procedure 1. Select the scope deliberately — critical modules first — because every mutant costs a full suite run. 2. Apply mutations one at a time: small, mechanical edits such as flipping an operator, changing a constant, or removing a call. 3. Run the suite per mutant and record the result: killed, survived, or timed out. 4. Treat timeouts as kills only when the suite is deterministic; flaky suites make mutation results noise. 5. Group surviving mutants and convert each group into a missing assertion or a new test that kills it. 6. Re-run and compare the mutation score — the fraction killed — instead of trusting coverage alone. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Applied mutations with kill status | | | | Mutants the suite did not detect | | | | Mutation score per module and overall | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Coverage complacency | High coverage hides unasserted behavior | Measure mutation score on critical modules | | Flaky suite noise | Timeouts and reruns corrupt kill counts | Stabilize the suite before mutating | | Whole-codebase runs | Mutation cost explodes with suite time | Scope to critical modules | | Survivor neglect | Survivors are recorded but never fixed | Convert each survivor into a new assertion | | Equivalent mutants | Untestable-by-design mutants counted as gaps | Review and exclude provably equivalent mutants | Security and Authority Boundary Mutation testing modifies code in working directories and can, with careless tooling, leak mutants into builds. Run it in an isolated checkout, never commit mutated files, and gate CI on the original source with mutants applied only in ephemeral workspaces. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The mutmut mutation testing tool documentation (https://mutmut.readthedocs.io/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of mutation testing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutation_testing).
