title: Property Based Testing
description: Test executable invariants over generated inputs instead of fixed examples, then shrink failing cases toward minimal counterexamples that reproduce the defect with the least context.
body: Property Based Testing Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Example-based tests check the cases someone thought of; property-based tests state invariants and let a generator search the input domain for violations. When a generated case fails, shrinking reduces it toward the smallest reproducer, which becomes the bug report and a permanent regression test. This skill covers that loop — declare invariants, generate, shrink, repair — as a reviewable engineering procedure. When to Use Use when a function or service has a checkable invariant over a wide input space and hand-written examples cover only a thin slice of it. Do not use for exact-output specifications or UI flows; deterministic example tests fit those better. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Predicates that must hold for every generated input | | | | Yes | Input-domain definitions including edge cases | | | | No | Maximum shrinking steps per counterexample | | | | No | Deterministic seed for reproducible runs | Procedure 1. State each invariant as a predicate over generated inputs; an invariant that cannot be phrased as a predicate is a smell. 2. Define the input domain explicitly, including boundaries: empty, zero, negative, and maximum-shaped cases. 3. Run generated cases against each invariant and collect every failing input. 4. Shrink each failing input toward a minimal reproducer; the shrunk case is what gets reported. 5. Pin the shrunk counterexample as a permanent deterministic example test. 6. Repair the defect, re-run the full property, and only then remove any temporary filters. 7. Rotate seeds on a schedule; a fixed seed set forever is just a slow example suite. 8. Record which invariants ran; an unexercised invariant is untested behavior. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Generated inputs that violated an invariant | | | | Minimal reproducers suitable for regression tests | | | | Pass or fail state per declared invariant | | | | Number of generated cases executed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Weak invariant | The property restates the implementation | Derive invariants from the specification, not the code | | No shrinking | The first random failure is reported as-is | Shrink toward minimal inputs before reporting | | Shrunk-case loss | The counterexample is never pinned | Add the shrunk case as a deterministic regression test | | Fixed-seed blindness | The same seed runs forever | Rotate seeds while keeping failures reproducible | | Generator gaps | The domain excludes edge values | Include empty, zero, negative, and maximum cases | Security and Authority Boundary Property-based testing grants no authority to run generated inputs against production systems. Generators produce untrusted data: targets under test must be sandboxed, and shrinking must never reduce toward inputs that trigger real side effects. title: Static Analysis
description: Find defects without executing code — dataflow, taint paths, and lint rules — triaging true positives from noise with a stated, documented rule inventory.
body: Static Analysis Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Static analysis reads code the way a reviewer with infinite patience would: every path, every assignment, every tainted flow from input to dangerous sink. Its problem is signal — tools over-report, and untriaged findings train teams to ignore them. This skill covers configuring analyzers, triaging output honestly, and maintaining a rule inventory that documents why each rule earns its noise. When to Use Use as a continuous gate on changed code and as a periodic deep pass — taint analysis on untrusted-input paths, security rules on everything that handles data. Do not run analyzers in default configuration over legacy code and report thousands of findings at once; that output gets archived rather than acted on. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The codebase or module to analyze | | | | Yes | Rule set and severity thresholds in force | | | | No | Previously triaged and waived findings | Procedure 1. Configure a profile for the codebase: enabled rules, severities, and the reasoning that each noisy rule is worth its cost. 2. Analyze the whole program where the tool supports it — cross-function taint paths die at file scope. 3. Triage every finding against the baseline: confirm, waive with a reason, or fix now; never leave untriaged findings in the gate. 4. Distinguish findings by kind — real defect, style preference, false positive — and adjust rules to shrink the third category. 5. Feed confirmed security findings to the defect queue with the taint path attached, not just the line number. 6. Re-baseline after fixes: the baseline records what was consciously accepted, not what was ignored. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Confirmed defects with locations and paths | | | | Accepted findings with reasons and expiry | | | | Counts by severity, rule, and status over time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Alert fatigue | Untriaged findings train ignore-first behavior | Triage everything and waive with reasons | | Default profiles | Stock rules mismatch the codebase | Configure and document the rule profile | | File-scope blindness | Cross-file taint paths are missed | Use whole-program analysis where available | | Frozen baselines | Waivers never expire or get revisited | Put expiry dates on waivers | | Findings without paths | A line number with no dataflow context | Attach the taint or value-flow path to each finding | Security and Authority Boundary Static analysis is itself a security control, and its output is sensitive: a triaged findings list is a map of known weaknesses. Restrict access to findings, share waivers with the team that owns the code, and do not publish detailed weakness inventories for unfixed systems. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Bandit security linter documentation for Python (https://bandit.readthedocs.io/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of static program analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staticprogramanalysis). title: Structured Logging
description: Emit logs as structured events — timestamp, level, ids, and measured fields — with stable schemas, correlation ids, and redaction rules instead of free-text lines.
body: Structured Logging Category: Code | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A log line that only a human can parse is a cost center: it cannot be filtered, alerted on, or audited at scale. Structured logging emits events — a stable name, a level, a timestamp, and measured fields — with correlation ids that tie each event to the request or agent step that produced it, and redaction rules that keep sensitive values out of records by design. When to Use Use whenever more than one system or more than one day separates writing from reading — services, pipelines, agent frameworks — where logs must be filtered by field rather than grepped by hope. Do not log raw payloads as fields; structure exists partly to make redaction enforceable. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The operations to instrument | | | | Yes | Field names and types per event | | | | No | Fields to drop or mask at emit time | Procedure 1. Define the event vocabulary first — a stable event name per operation, with a documented field schema per event. 2. Include correlation ids in every event: request id, run id, step id, so a chain is reconstructable across systems. 3. Emit at the level that matches the reader: debug for development detail, info for operations, warning for degraded-but-serving, error for failures with an owner. 4. Redact by schema rather than by review: sensitive fields are masked or dropped at emit time, before any sink sees them. 5. Measure rather than narrate: durations, counts, and statuses as typed fields, with free text as a supplement rather than the record. 6. Log an error once with full context at the handling site, not re-logged at every layer of propagation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Structured records with schema-conformant fields | | | | Event-to-field contracts | | | | Sink routing and retention per level | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Free-text only | Records cannot be filtered or alerted on | Emit schema-conformant fields | | Context stripping | Events lack the ids to reassemble a chain | Correlate every event to request and run | | Redaction by review | Sensitive values reach sinks before anyone looks | Mask or drop by schema at emit time | | Level inflation | Everything is an error and nothing is actionable | Map levels to reader decisions | | Duplicate error logging | The same failure is logged at every layer | Log once with full context at the handling site | Security and Authority Boundary Logs are among the most commonly exfiltrated artifacts: they outlive sessions, replicate to multiple sinks, and reach wide audiences. Enforce schema-level redaction, treat log systems as production data stores, and audit what event fields can carry before adding them. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of log files and their role in operational systems (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log_file). 2. The JSON Lines format documentation for newline-delimited structured records (https://jsonlines.org/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Audience Analysis
description: Profile who will receive a message — their prior knowledge, stakes, and constraints — before deciding what to say and in what form to say it.
body: Audience Analysis Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Most failed communication was written before anyone asked who would read it. This skill front-loads that question: name the audience precisely, establish what they already know and what is at stake for them, and let those facts decide depth, order, and channel. The profile constrains the wording, not the truth — it changes how something is said, never whether the substance gets stated. When to Use Use before sending anything consequential to a group you cannot see — documentation, announcements, incident notices, decision requests. Do not use the profile to stereotype individuals or to substitute imagined preferences for the purpose of the message; a profile guides wording, it does not license telling people only what they want to hear. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | What the audience should know or do afterward | | | | Yes | Roles, prior knowledge, stakes, and constraints of the readers | | | | No | Where the message will arrive, with format constraints | Procedure 1. Name the audience precisely: "all users" is not an audience, while "first-time administrators configuring single sign-on" is. 2. Establish the baseline: what the reader already knows, so the message starts where they are rather than where the author wishes they were. 3. Establish the stakes: what changes for the reader if they act, and what changes if they do not. 4. Decide depth per segment — background, working detail, or decision summary — because one message cannot be all three at once. 5. Choose the channel and format each segment actually reads, and record constraints such as length limits or review requirements. 6. Revisit the profile when feedback arrives, because audiences drift and a stale profile misroutes everything built on it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Segments with baseline knowledge, stakes, and constraints | | | | Per-segment decisions on depth, order, and channel | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed knowledge | Readers lack context the author took for granted | Start from the actual baseline of the audience | | Self-reference | Message organized around the author instead of the reader | Reorder sections around reader stakes | | Averaged audience | One compromise message serves no segment | Split by segment and depth | | Stale profiles | The audience changed since the last analysis | Revalidate against observed feedback | | Missing stakes | Readers cannot tell why it matters to them | State consequences for the reader early | Security and Authority Boundary Audience analysis is a distribution decision, and distribution is a boundary: the segments a message will reach must feed directly into what it may contain, and no segment broader than the intended trust level of the content may be added as a recipient. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of audience analysis (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audience_analysis). 2. The PlainLanguage.gov guidelines on writing for the audience (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/). title: Feedback Delivery
description: Deliver critique so the recipient can act on it — observed behavior, concrete impact, and a specific request, separated from judgment of the person.
body: Feedback Delivery Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Feedback fails in two directions: it is so soft the recipient misses the point, or so blunt the recipient defends instead of acting. This skill holds the message to three separable parts — what was observed, what it caused, and what change is requested — and refuses to mix them with verdicts about the person. The test of good feedback is not how it feels in the moment; it is whether the next artifact observably changes. When to Use Use when reviewing work product — code, writing, analysis, performance — in written reviews or in conversation. Do not use feedback structure to smuggle in verdicts about people, and do not deliver critique when either party is depleted; timing is part of the message. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The specific behavior or artifact observed | | | | Yes | The concrete effect of that behavior | | | | Yes | The specific, checkable change proposed | Procedure 1. Ground in observation: quote the artifact or name the behavior before interpreting it. 2. State impact concretely: what follows from the behavior, for whom, measurably where possible. 3. Make the request specific and checkable — name a change a future reader could verify happened. 4. Keep person and artifact separate: critique the work, never the character or motives of the worker. 5. Check receipt: ask what the recipient heard, and correct drift before it hardens into grievance. 6. Close the loop: record what was agreed, and revisit it after the next instance of the same work. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Observation, impact, and request stated separately | | | | What the recipient heard and committed to | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Verdict without evidence | A judgment with no citable observation | Quote the artifact before interpreting | | Vague requests | A change request nobody could verify | Ask for something a future reader can check | | Character leakage | Critique slides from the work to the person | Critique the artifact, never the person | | Sandwich dilution | Praise wrapped around critique disguises the point | Deliver recognition and critique separately | | Drive-by timing | Delivered when the recipient cannot absorb it | Pick a moment both parties can engage | Security and Authority Boundary Review feedback can surface sensitive detail: findings about security flaws belong in channels scoped to the trust of the recipient, with exploitable specifics kept out of open threads until a fix or a disclosure decision is made. title: Incident Communication
description: Write timely, structured incident updates — severity, impact, and a committed next-update time — so stakeholders stay informed while responders keep working.
body: Incident Communication Category: Communication | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An incident produces two obligations at once: fix the thing, and tell the truth about it at a pace people can rely on. This skill separates narration from response — a designated owner handles the updates while responders respond — and gives each message a fixed shape: observed impact, current status, and when the next message lands. The cadence promise is the core mechanism: a stakeholder who knows the next update arrives in thirty minutes reads silence as work, not as abandonment. When to Use Use whenever an incident is visible to anyone beyond the responders — customers, leadership, partner teams — and from the first acknowledgement, not from the moment of diagnosis. Do not let updates displace response work, and do not publish causal claims before evidence supports them; a stated unknown ages better than a wrong early diagnosis. title: Meeting Notes
description: Turn live meeting transcripts into structured notes with attributed decisions, owner-assigned action items, and open questions so follow-up work is trackable instead of relying on memory.
body: Meeting Notes Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Meeting value leaks through unrecorded decisions and ownerless actions. This skill defines a note contract for live meetings: capture decisions with attribution and verbatim wording where it matters, convert actions into owner-task-date triplets, and keep open questions visible with a follow-up owner. The notes are the record; the transcript is only the input. When to Use Use when a live or asynchronous meeting produces decisions or actions that anyone must act on later. Do not use for verbatim transcripts or archival records; capture and summarization skills fit those goals. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamped contributions keyed by speaker | | | | Yes | Names and roles used for attribution | | | | No | Line prefix that marks action items | | | | No | Expected date format for action deadlines | Procedure 1. Record every participant and role before discussion starts; unattributable statements are flagged, not guessed. 2. Capture decisions with their speaker, the exact phrasing, and the point in the agenda where they were made. 3. Extract actions as owner, task, and due date; a missing owner is recorded as UNASSIGNED, never silently filled. 4. Keep open questions in their own list with a named follow-up owner and a next checkpoint. 5. Quote verbatim where wording matters; paraphrase only when the meaning is unambiguous. 6. Publish the structured notes in the same channel as the meeting so latecomers see the same record. 7. Reconcile actions against the previous meeting’s notes; uncompleted actions carry forward visibly. 8. Retain the notes under the organization’s retention policy; notes are records, not scratch space. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Attributed decision entries with verbatim wording | | | | Owner-task-date triplets including UNASSIGNED flags | | | | Unresolved items with follow-up owners | | | | Actions reopened from the previous notes | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Ghost actions | A task is recorded without an owner | Record UNASSIGNED and surface it at review | | Decision drift | A paraphrase replaces the agreed wording | Quote verbatim where the wording matters | | Lost question | An open issue drops out of the notes | Keep a dedicated open-questions list | | Attribution guess | The speaker is inferred from context | Attribute only from known participants, or flag | | Phantom closure | Actions are never revisited | Reconcile against the previous notes every meeting | Security and Authority Boundary Taking notes grants no authority to speak for participants. Attributed statements must match what the participant actually said, and notes shared beyond the meeting must respect the organization’s information-handling rules. Commitments belong to whoever made them; personal observations belong to their author. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Negotiation
description: Prepare and conduct negotiations by mapping the interests behind stated positions, quantifying reservation values and alternatives, and trading on differences to reach agreements that hold.
body: Negotiation Category: Communication | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Negotiation is reaching agreement when parties' interests partly conflict. The reliable core is preparation: separating positions from interests, knowing your reservation value and best alternative to a negotiated agreement (BATNA), and identifying differences that can be traded instead of split. This skill covers that preparation and the conduct of exchanges that produce precise, verifiable terms — without fabricating leverage or inventing concessions. When to Use Use when terms must be agreed with a party that has its own interests: scope and price discussions, vendor terms, resource allocation between teams. Do not use it to manipulate or deceive a counterpart; commitments made must be within your actual mandate. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Ranked underlying interests, not opening positions | | | | Yes | Hard limits: budget, deadline, authority scope | | | | No | Known interests and pressures of the other side | | | | No | What happens if no agreement is reached (BATNA) | Procedure 1. Convert each stated position into the interest behind it; list them in priority order. 2. Quantify the reservation value: the worst acceptable outcome, derived from constraints and BATNA, not from hope. 3. Inventory tradable differences: things cheap for you and valuable to them, and vice versa. 4. Propose packages across several issues rather than conceding issue by issue. 5. Test every emerging agreement against both sides' alternatives; an agreement worse than a party's BATNA will not hold. 6. Close with precise terms: who, what, when, and how verification happens. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Precise, verifiable commitments | | | | What was offered and traded, with rationale | | | | Whether the reservation value was breached | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Single-issue tunnel vision | Everything reduced to price or one headline term | Negotiate packages across multiple issues | | Fabricated leverage | Bluffs collapse and destroy trust when called | Represent only real alternatives and constraints | | Unverifiable agreement | Terms too vague to check delivery | Close with measurable terms and verification steps | | Ignored stakeholders | The counterparty's principal is not at the table | Confirm who can actually commit | | Sunk-cost drift | Conceding past the reservation value to save the deal | Recheck the reservation value before each concession | Security and Authority Boundary An agent negotiates only within an explicit mandate from its principal. Never commit beyond that scope, never share confidential information beyond what the mandate permits, and surface the walk-away recommendation instead of agreeing to terms outside the reservation envelope. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Program on Negotiation at Harvard Law School (https://www.pon.harvard.edu/). 2. The negotiation reference article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negotiation). title: Plain Language Writing
description: Rewrite technical statements so a busy reader needs no extra context — short sentences, concrete nouns, active verbs, and no jargon left undefined.
body: Plain Language Writing Category: Communication | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Plain language is not simplified thinking; it is text that survives first contact with a reader who has no reason to reread it. This skill works mostly by subtraction: state the point in one sentence, prefer words the reader already owns, split sentences that carry more than one idea, and cut hedges until a claim stands alone. Terms of art survive only when they are load-bearing, and then they are defined on first use. When to Use Use for mixed or non-specialist audiences — documentation, summaries, status updates, user-facing messages — wherever the reader cannot be assumed to share the vocabulary of the author. Do not strip precision that the audience needs; plain language is calibrated to its readers, and for a specialist audience the shared vocabulary is part of the clarity, not an obstacle to it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The passage to rewrite | | | | Yes | Who will read it and what they already know | | | | Yes | The single takeaway or action the reader should leave with | Procedure 1. Write the point in one sentence before touching the draft; if that sentence does not exist, the passage has no spine yet. 2. Replace each term of art with plain wording, or keep it and define it on first use when the term is load-bearing. 3. Split any sentence that carries more than one idea, and put the actor before the verb in each half. 4. Cut throat-clearing openings and stacked hedges; say the claim once and let it stand. 5. Pair every number with a reference point, because bare figures force the reader to supply the missing scale. 6. Reread as the target reader, and delete anything that survives only to comfort the author. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The plain-language version of the passage | | | | Kept terms of art, each with its plain definition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Simplified into vagueness | Plain wording dropped load-bearing precision | Keep the technical term and define it inline | | Audience mismatch | Text calibrated to the wrong prior knowledge | Fix the audience statement before rewriting | | Hedge fog | Qualifiers stacked until nothing is asserted | State the claim once, plainly | | Sentence sprawl | One sentence carrying three ideas | Split at idea boundaries | | Naked numbers | Figures with no comparison given | Attach a reference point to every number | Security and Authority Boundary Plain text travels: writing for a broad audience multiplies the chance a passage is quoted out of context, so a rewrite must not widen disclosure — anything sensitive stays in documents scoped to the audience that may see it, and the plain version inherits the classification of its source. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The PlainLanguage.gov guidelines (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of plain language (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plain_language). title: Translation
description: Translate text between languages with an LLM while preserving meaning, tone, and inline placeholders (URLs, code, ICU variables).
body: Translation Description Converts text from a source language to a target language without losing meaning, register, or any inline tokens that must survive the round-trip (URLs, code, JSX variables, ICU placeholders like ). Modern frontier LLMs typically beat both Google Translate and DeepL on context-rich content; they trail dedicated MT systems on extremely short or terminology-heavy snippets. When to Use - Localizing UI strings, docs, user-generated content. - Translating with explicit tone instructions ("formal Arabic", "casual European Portuguese"). - Translating content that contains code, URLs, or ICU placeholders that a generic MT would mangle. - When you need glossary enforcement (always translate "Skills Tree" as "Skills Tree", never "شجرة المهارات"). title: API Pagination
description: Walk paged API result sets to completion — cursor or page parameters, per-request limits, and a terminal condition — without missing or double-processing records.
body: API Pagination Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A paged response is a promise that the full list exists and a refusal to hand it over at once. This skill treats the pager as an explicit state machine: the request carries the continuation token, the response carries the next one, and iteration stops only when the API says it is finished. Rate limits are part of the traversal, not an error condition — a pager that ignores them will be right about the data and wrong about the budget. When to Use Use whenever an API returns lists with a cursor, page token, or offset parameter — directories, event logs, resource listings — and the task needs the complete set. Do not fetch all pages when the task only needs a bounded prefix; a search that stops at the first match should not traverse the whole corpus. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The paged API operation to traverse | | | | Yes | Records requested per page, within the API maximum | | | | Yes | What to do with each record as pages arrive | | | | No | The request budget the traversal must respect | Procedure 1. Read the API contract for its pagination style — cursor, offset, or page token — before writing any loop. 2. Issue the first request with the largest page size the API allows, because fewer round trips is fewer chances to rate-limit. 3. Hand each record to the collector as its page arrives, rather than accumulating every page in memory. 4. Persist the continuation token between requests, and treat an absent or null token as the terminal condition — never a missing key. 5. Respect the rate limit: back off when the API says so, and prefer the retry-after guidance over a fixed sleep when it is offered. 6. Record the traversal outcome — pages fetched, records seen, terminal reason — so an incomplete walk is detectable after the fact. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Each record delivered as its page arrives | | | | Page count, record count, and terminal condition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Dropped records | A null next-token value misread as an error | Treat the documented null token as the sole terminal condition | | Double processing | A retried page appended twice | Make the collector idempotent or track the last token processed | | Memory blowout | Every page held until the end | Collect per page; never retain the full traversal | | Rate-limit storms | Consecutive throttled responses during the walk | Back off on the first signal, not the third | | Silent truncation | A walk stopped early and nobody noticed | Report pages, records, and stop reason at the end | Security and Authority Boundary Continuation tokens are credentials for data position: they can leak record ranges and query context when logged or shared, so treat them as sensitive in logs, and scope every traversal to the caller whose credentials opened it — a walk must never resume under a different principal. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Stripe API documentation on pagination (https://docs.stripe.com/api/pagination). 2. Wikipedia's overview of rate limiting (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_limiting). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: API Version Pinning
description: Pin every external API to a specific, recorded version — and upgrade as a deliberate, tested change — so upstream evolution never rewrites behavior silently.
body: API Version Pinning Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An unpinned API call is a bet on someone else's release calendar. This skill removes the bet: each external dependency is pinned to a concrete version in configuration, the pin is visible in code review, and upgrades happen as deliberate changes with a diff, a changelog read, and a test pass. Pinning goes further than a version number where the provider allows it — dated pins and versioned endpoints record the wire behavior the tests actually exercised. When to Use Use for every external API integration that reaches production, and pin in configuration rather than in a dependency default. Do not pin so hard that upgrades never happen; an integration left on an unsupported version is a slower, quieter failure mode. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The external API or SDK being integrated | | | | Yes | The concrete version recorded in configuration | | | | Yes | How and when deliberate upgrades are scheduled | Procedure 1. Record the pin in configuration, not in a lockfile default or a floating latest, so it appears in review and in audits. 2. Read the provider versioning model — dated pins, endpoint versions, deprecation windows — and record the model beside the pin. 3. Subscribe to change: watch the changelog or deprecation feed for the pinned version, and treat deprecation notices as scheduled work. 4. Upgrade deliberately: new pin, changelog diff read, integration tests run, and the change shipped as its own reviewable commit. 5. Roll back the pin, not the code, when an upgrade misbehaves — the pin is the smallest reversible unit. 6. Audit pins periodically: a pin on an unsupported version is a defect even while everything still works. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Dependency to recorded version, with pinning model | | | | Deliberate upgrades with date, diff, and test evidence | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating latest | The SDK default changes behavior on its own | Pin every integration in reviewed configuration | | Missed deprecation | A deprecation window closed unwatched | Watch the changelog feed for the pinned version | | Surprise upgrades | A dependency bump upgraded the wire behavior | Upgrade the pin in its own reviewed change | | Unauditable pins | Nobody can list what versions run in production | Keep pins in config and audit them periodically | | Unreviewable rollback | A bad upgrade reverted by editing code | Move the pin back, the smallest reversible unit | Security and Authority Boundary Version pins interact with trust: upgrading an API client changes what is sent and to whom, so pin changes deserve security review like any dependency change, and a pin must never be loosened to make an unrelated integration problem go away. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Stripe documentation on API versioning and upgrades (https://docs.stripe.com/upgrades). 2. The twelve-factor app guidance on configuration (https://12factor.net/config). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Function / Tool Calling
description: Let the model emit a structured request to call one of your functions, with type-checked arguments — the foundation of every tool-using agent.
body: Function / Tool Calling Description The model is told what your functions do via a JSON-Schema spec. When the user's request matches a function, the model emits instead of free text. Your code parses the arguments, runs the function, and feeds the result back so the model can keep going. This is the primitive that turns an LLM into an agent. Every higher-level pattern — ReAct, tool-use loops, multi-step plans — is built on it. When to Use - Anywhere the model must act on the world — query a DB, hit an API, run a calculation. - When you need typed arguments the model can't fudge. - When you want a clean audit trail (every action is a parsed call). - Don't use when the answer is purely text generation — you'll spend tokens on a schema for nothing. title: Streaming Tool Output
description: Consume tool output as it arrives — newline-delimited chunks, incremental parsers, bounded buffers — so long-running results become usable before they finish.
body: Streaming Tool Output Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some tool calls are streams pretending to be calls: search results that arrive page by page, logs that emit lines for minutes, models that produce tokens before the sentence is done. This skill treats the output as a sequence with a protocol — a delimiter or an event frame — and consumes it incrementally: parse what has arrived, hold a bounded remainder for the incomplete tail, and surface progress to whoever is waiting. The alternative is buffering everything, which turns a long result into a long silence followed by a large object. When to Use Use for long-running or high-volume tool output — event streams, incremental search, anything that delivers value before completion. Do not add streaming machinery to short, fast calls; a buffered read of a small response is simpler and equally correct. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The tool output arriving incrementally | | | | Yes | The boundary that separates records, newline by default | | | | Yes | What to run on each complete record as it parses | | | | No | Maximum bytes held for an incomplete tail | Procedure 1. Fix the protocol first: know what delimits a record — a newline, a frame header, a terminator — before reading a byte. 2. Read incrementally and split on the delimiter, keeping the incomplete tail in a buffer rather than discarding it. 3. Dispatch each complete record to the handler immediately, so downstream work overlaps with the remaining stream. 4. Bound the buffer: a tail that grows past its limit is a protocol violation, and streaming must fail loudly, not allocate quietly. 5. Surface progress — records seen, bytes read — so a slow stream is observable while it runs. 6. Handle terminal conditions distinctly: end-of-stream, error frame, and cancellation are different events and must close differently. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Complete records yielded as they parse | | | | Records and bytes consumed so far | | | | Terminal state of the stream when it ends | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Split records | A record divided across chunk boundaries | Buffer the incomplete tail and split on the delimiter | | Unbounded buffering | A stream with no delimiters fills memory | Enforce a buffer limit and fail loudly on overflow | | Lost tails | Final unterminated record dropped at close | Yield the remainder when the stream ends | | Blocked consumers | Slow handler stalls the entire stream | Dispatch records and let the consumer set pace | | Ambiguous closes | Error, cancel, and completion all look alike | Close with an explicit terminal reason per stream | Security and Authority Boundary Streamed output bypasses the size checks that whole responses get: incremental data must still be validated per record at the boundary, and progress events must not leak record contents into logs where whole payloads would never be allowed. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The JSON Lines format specification site (https://jsonlines.org/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of stream processing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_processing). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Tool Output Validation
description: Check tool outputs against a declared schema before they enter the reasoning stream, so a malformed result fails loudly at the boundary instead of downstream.
body: Tool Output Validation Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tool result is untrusted input with a confident tone: it arrives as a string, a dict, or a truncated fragment, and whatever shape it claims is a claim. This skill moves the checking to the boundary: each expected output is declared as a schema, each result is validated on arrival, and a failure is reported as a structured error with the offending path — not smuggled into the conversation for the caller to misread. Validation failures are normal control flow, not exceptions to silence. When to Use Use whenever a tool result feeds decisions — structured data, numeric values, identifiers — and especially when results come from external services outside your control. Do not validate ad hoc fields nobody consumes; a schema that checks everything protects nothing in particular and costs every call. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The raw output returned by the tool | | | | Yes | The declared shape the result must satisfy | | | | No | Reject, repair, or re-request when validation fails | Procedure 1. Declare the schema for what the result must contain — required fields, types, and bounds — before calling the tool. 2. Validate on arrival: check presence first, then types, then value constraints such as ranges or enum membership. 3. Collect every violation with its path rather than failing on the first, so one pass describes the whole gap. 4. Route failures by policy: reject the result, attempt a bounded repair, or re-request once with a corrected call. 5. Never stringify a failed result into the reasoning stream; a rejected result enters as an error record with its path and reason. 6. Keep the schema under version control beside the tool integration, and bump it when the upstream contract changes. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The checked result, ready for downstream reasoning | | | | Per-path failures with type, constraint, and observed value | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent coercion | A wrong-typed value cast into the stream | Reject on type mismatch; never coerce silently | | Partial acceptance | Some fields validated, others assumed | Validate the declared contract completely or not at all | | Schema drift | Upstream changed shape and the schema did not | Version the schema; test against real samples | | Error laundering | Failures stringified as if they were data | Failures enter as structured error records | | Over-validation | Unused fields strictly checked, blocking good data | Schema exactly what consumers read, nothing more | Security and Authority Boundary Validation is a security boundary, not just a correctness one: bounds and enum checks constrain what malformed or hostile payloads can inject into downstream logic, so schemas on tool outputs must be treated with the same review rigor as schemas on user input. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The JSON Schema specification site (https://json-schema.org/). 2. The pandera data validation framework documentation (https://pandera.readthedocs.io/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Tool Result Caching
description: Reuse identical tool calls that already succeeded — keyed by operation and arguments — so repeat work costs a lookup instead of another remote round trip.
body: Tool Result Caching Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every tool call that returns the same answer for the same arguments is a cache wearing a network costume. This skill makes that explicit: a deterministic operation gets a cache key built from its identity and its arguments, responses are stored with a time-to-live and a staleness policy, and a hit must be marked as cached so downstream consumers know what they are reading. The discipline is deciding which calls are cacheable — deterministic and side-effect-free — before caching anything. When to Use Use for deterministic, read-only calls whose arguments repeat across a session or pipeline — enrichment lookups, reference data fetches, idempotent reads. Do not cache calls whose results depend on hidden state, side effects, wall-clock time, or caller identity, and do not let a cache silently answer after the underlying data contract changes underneath it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The tool operation being cached | | | | Yes | The call arguments that form part of the cache key | | | | Yes | How long a cached response may be served | | | | No | What happens on expiry — refetch, or serve-stale-while-refreshing | Procedure 1. Confirm the operation is deterministic and side-effect-free; anything with hidden state is disqualified before a key is built. 2. Build the cache key from the operation identity and the full, normalized argument set, so two calls that differ only in formatting still share an entry. 3. Store the response with its time-to-live and the timestamp of the fetch, not the timestamp of the read. 4. On a hit, return the cached value marked as cached, with its original fetch time, so consumers can reason about staleness. 5. On expiry, refetch — or serve stale while refreshing when the policy allows — and record the miss rate per operation. 6. Invalidate by key when the underlying data is known to change, and treat a change in the data contract as a full invalidation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The deterministic key for the operation and arguments | | | | The stored response with fetch timestamp and provenance | | | | Hit rate, miss rate, and staleness served per operation | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Stale answers | The underlying source changed within the TTL | Keep TTLs short for volatile data and invalidate on known writes | | Key collisions | Different calls normalized into one key | Include the full argument set and operation in the key | | Side-effect caching | A non-deterministic call got cached | Cache only deterministic, read-only operations | | Silent provenance | Consumers cannot tell a hit from a fetch | Mark every served value as cached with its fetch time | | Unbounded growth | Entries accumulate without eviction | Bound the cache and evict on a replacement policy | Security and Authority Boundary A cache is a copy of data outside its origin's access control: cache stores inherit the sensitivity of what they hold, so entries holding user-scoped or restricted data must be keyed to the caller's scope and evicted on scope change, never shared across principals. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of caching in computing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache%28computing%29). 2. Wikipedia's overview of cache replacement policies (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cachereplacement_policies). title: Tool Schema Design
description: Design LLM tool schemas with disciplined names, bounded parameters, enumerated options, and structured errors so model calls stay valid, predictable, and cheap to validate.
body: Tool Schema Design Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tool schema is the contract between a model and an execution surface, and most tool failures are schema failures: vague names, unbounded numbers, free text where an enum fits, and error shapes nobody planned. This skill defines the design contract: name tools after their effects, bound every parameter, prefer closed value sets, reject unknown keys, and return structured errors the caller can branch on. When to Use Use when defining or revising an LLM-callable tool so that model errors become invalid calls instead of wrong effects. Do not use for human-facing CLI design or internal library APIs; those audiences read documentation instead of schemas. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The distinct effects the surface must expose | | | | Yes | Per-parameter limits including minimum and maximum | | | | No | Closed value sets per parameter | | | | No | Structured error codes the surface can return | Procedure 1. Name each tool after the effect it performs, verb first; a schema named after its data invites misuse. 2. Give every parameter a type, a description, and where possible a bound; unbounded parameters are rejections in waiting. 3. Prefer closed enums over free text wherever the value space is known. 4. Mark required parameters explicitly and document what omitting an optional one means. 5. Reject unknown keys; permissive parsing lets hallucinated parameters reach execution. 6. Return errors as structured payloads with a stable code, a human-readable message, and a retryability flag. 7. Validate calls against the schema before execution; a call that fails validation never reaches the effect. 8. Version the schema; breaking changes take a new tool name, not a silent redefinition. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The tool definition including parameter bounds and enums | | | | Structured rejections naming the parameter and rule | | | | The stable error vocabulary callers branch on | | | | The schema version callers pin against | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Vague naming | A tool is named after its data instead of its effect | Name tools verb-first after what they do | | Unbounded input | A numeric parameter has no limits | Declare minimum and maximum bounds | | Enum omission | Free text sits where a closed set exists | Enumerate the value space | | Permissive parsing | Unknown keys are silently ignored | Reject undeclared keys at validation | | Shapeless errors | Errors come back as prose | Return a code, a message, and a retryability flag | Security and Authority Boundary Designing a tool schema grants no execution authority. Schemas bound what a call may contain, not what it may do: the execution surface still enforces its own permission checks, rate limits, and audit logging. Error messages must never echo credentials or internal paths. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The JSON Schema step-by-step getting-started guide (https://json-schema.org/learn/getting-started-step-by-step). 2. Python’s json module documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: WebSocket Communication
description: Establish and maintain WebSocket sessions with framing-correct message handling, heartbeat keepalives, reconnect with bounded backoff, and explicit close-code interpretation.
body: WebSocket Communication Category: Tool Use | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description The WebSocket protocol upgrades an HTTP connection into a long-lived, bidirectional message channel. Unlike a single HTTP call, a session lives for minutes or hours, so the real engineering is in staying healthy: heartbeats, bounded reconnect backoff, close-code interpretation, and queues that do not grow without limit. When to Use Use when the remote endpoint provides a WebSocket API and the workload is genuinely streaming or bidirectional: live feeds, telemetry, interactive tool protocols. Prefer ordinary HTTP for one-shot request/response; a session adds failure modes, not value. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | endpoint (never over untrusted networks) | | | | Yes | Callbacks per message type | | | | No | Ping cadence in seconds (default 30) | Procedure 1. Open the handshake and validate the negotiated subprotocol against the one you expect. 2. Route incoming frames through handlers; answer server pings automatically. 3. Send heartbeats on the configured cadence and treat a missed pong as a dead session, not a busy one. 4. On abnormal close, reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter; cap the delay and the total retry budget. 5. Interpret close codes precisely: 1000 is a normal close with no retry, 1006 is abnormal (no close frame), 1011 is a server error that may not be retryable. 6. Bound both send and receive queues; drop or fail explicitly rather than buffering without limit. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | , , with last close code | | | | Messages sent with server acknowledgment, where the protocol provides one | | | | Final close code, reason, and reconnect attempts | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent half-open session | Connection died without a close frame | Heartbeat pings; dead sessions detected in one interval | | Reconnect storm | All clients retry in lockstep | Jittered backoff with a cap | | Close code misread | 1006/1011 treated as clean close | Map close codes explicitly and record them | | Unbounded queueing | Slow consumer during a fast stream | Bound queues; apply explicit overflow policy | | Order assumptions across reconnects | Reconnect creates a new session | Use sequence numbers or re-sync state after reconnect | Security and Authority Boundary Use everywhere outside localhost; is plaintext. Validate the Origin on the server side, treat every inbound frame as untrusted input, and never reconnect with credentials that the endpoint should no longer hold. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The websockets Python library (https://pypi.org/project/websockets/). 2. RFC 6455, The WebSocket Protocol (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Audio Diarization
description: Segment an audio stream into who-spoke-when turns from frame-level acoustic evidence with deterministic boundary rules so speaker attribution yields explicit, testable segments.
body: Audio Diarization Category: Multimodal | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Speaker attribution is only as trustworthy as its segment boundaries. This skill builds diarization as a rule-bound pipeline: acoustic frames carry a speaker label, consecutive same-label frames merge into turns, and every turn records its speaker, start, and end. The merge rules are deterministic so the same frame sequence always produces the same turn list. Acoustic labeling itself is delegated to a classifier; this skill governs the segmentation contract. When to Use Use when a transcript or analysis needs per-speaker attribution — meeting minutes, call analytics, or speaker-indexed search — and the output must be a reviewable turn list rather than a black-box label. Do not use for raw transcription without speakers; apply the audio transcription skill instead, and diarize its alignment if per-speaker turns are needed. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Acoustic frames with inferred speaker labels, time-ordered | | | | No | Shortest turn duration kept; shorter turns are dropped | | | | No | Label treated as no-speaker; frames with it are not merged | Procedure 1. Require frames to be sorted by start time before merging; unsorted input is rejected. 2. Merge a frame into the previous turn only when speaker labels match and boundaries are contiguous. 3. Start a new turn on any label change, gap, or boundary discontinuity; never merge across gaps. 4. Apply the minimum-turn rule after merging, dropping turns shorter than the declared floor. 5. Record each turn as (speaker, start, end) with an identifier stable across runs. 6. Expose a coverage metric: total speech time minus turn gaps, so silent regions are visible. 7. Treat classifier labels as evidence, not truth: keep the label confidence alongside each turn when available. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Ordered, non-overlapping speaker turns | | | | Fraction of the stream covered by turns | | | | Turns removed by the minimum-turn rule | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Over-merge | Gap ignored between same-speaker frames | Merge only on contiguous boundaries | | Under-merge | Rounding splits contiguous frames | Compare with tolerance and normalize timestamps first | | Unstable labels | Classifier flickers between speakers | Smooth labels before merging and record confidence | | Unsorted input | Frames arrive out of order | Validate sort order up front and reject violations | | Silent regions hidden | Gaps never reported | Compute and expose coverage alongside turns | Security and Authority Boundary Diarization output identifies who spoke when; treat it as personal data. It grants no authority to act on speakers and must respect the retention and consent rules of the source audio in every downstream store. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s survey of speaker diarisation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_diarisation). 2. Python’s wave module documentation for reading PCM audio fragments (https://docs.python.org/3/library/wave.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Audio Mixing
description: Blend multiple PCM audio tracks under explicit gain envelopes with sample-accurate summation, hard clipping bounds, and a measured output peak so a mix is reproducible and cannot silently exceed the output range.
body: Audio Mixing Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Mixing becomes destructive the moment gain is improvised: summed samples clip, quiet tracks get buried, and the result varies run to run. This skill treats a mix as an explicit contract — per-track gains, optional timed envelopes, a declared clip limit, and a measured peak — so the output is byte-reproducible from its inputs. It operates on in-memory PCM sample lists; codec-level or streaming mixdowns are out of scope. When to Use Use when combining two or more recorded or synthesized mono PCM tracks into one output track where loudness behavior and clipping must be decided by policy rather than by accident. Do not use for real-time streaming mixdowns or codec-domain processing; apply this contract after decoding, on sample data. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Two or more mono sample lists at identical length basis | | | | Yes | One fixed gain multiplier per track, declared before summation | | | | Yes | Hard output bound, e.g. 32767 for 16-bit audio | | | | No | Timed gain points applied per track before summation | Procedure 1. Declare every track gain and the clip limit before the first sample is summed; mixing with undeclared gains is rejected. 2. Verify all tracks share a sample rate and channel layout; resample or reject before mixing, never inside it. 3. Apply each track’s gain (and optional timed envelope) sample by sample, in a fixed track order. 4. Sum tracks sample-accurately in integer domain so the result is identical across runs and platforms. 5. Clip each summed sample to the declared limit and count clipped samples as a quality signal. 6. Measure the output peak after mixing; an unmeasured mix cannot be compared or improved. 7. Record the gain set, envelope, clip count, and peak alongside the output so the mix is reproducible. 8. Re-mix rather than normalize after the fact when the clip count is nonzero; clipping already destroyed information. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The clipped, summed output track | | | | Largest absolute sample value in the output | | | | Number of samples bounded by the clip limit | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Clipping distortion | Summed samples exceed the output range | Declare a clip limit up front and count clipped samples | | Buried quiet tracks | Gains improvised per mix | Fix the gain set before summation and record it with the output | | Rate mismatch | Tracks mixed at different sample rates | Verify a shared rate before mixing; resample or reject | | Non-reproducible mix | Float ordering and undeclared gains vary | Sum in a fixed track order with declared gains | | Unmeasured output | Peak level never computed | Measure and record peak and clip count with every mix | Security and Authority Boundary Mixing grants no authority over source recordings. Source material keeps its license and consent state; a mix does not launder restricted audio into usable output. Output loudness is a technical measurement, not a safety claim. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of audio mixing practice (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audiomixing(recorded_music)). 2. Python’s wave module documentation for reading and writing PCM files (https://docs.python.org/3/library/wave.html). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Image Resizing
description: Compute contain and cover resize boxes with integer arithmetic, explicit rounding, and declared upscale policy so scaled pixel targets are deterministic across runtimes.
body: Image Resizing Category: Multimodal | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description “Scale to fit” hides two different contracts: contain fits the whole image inside a box with letterboxing, cover fills the box and crops the overflow. This skill computes both as pure integer math with declared rounding and upscale rules, so every runtime derives the same target box from the same inputs. Resampling filters and color management are out of scope; this is the geometry contract that runs before them. When to Use Use when a fixed display box must receive images of arbitrary aspect ratio and the output box — letterboxed, cropped, or bounded — must be computed exactly. Do not use for art-directed aspect changes; creative crop choices belong to image editing, not to mechanical geometry. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Source image width in pixels | | | | Yes | Source image height in pixels | | | | Yes | Target bounding box | | | | Yes | Fit inside the box, or fill it and crop | Procedure 1. Reject non-positive dimensions or box before computing. 2. Compute contain as the minimum scale that fits both sides, never exceeding the box on either axis. 3. Compute cover as the maximum scale that fills both sides, at least as large as the box on either axis. 4. Floor results to integer pixels with one documented rounding rule applied to both axes. 5. Apply the upscale policy: contain never exceeds the source size unless enlargement is declared; cover enlarges only as required to fill. 6. Return the box with the effective scale and the crop offsets for cover, so the caller can apply them mechanically. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The resized output dimensions | | | | Effective scale factor applied | | | | Cover-strategy center-crop offsets | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Strategy confusion | Cover applied where contain was intended | Require the strategy argument and document the difference | | Aspect drift | Independent per-axis rounding | Scale from one factor and floor both axes once | | Unexpected upscale | Small sources enlarged by contain math | Cap scale at 1.0 unless enlargement is declared | | Crop misalignment | Center offsets computed on the box, not the scaled size | Derive offsets from scaled dimensions minus the box | | Zero-dimension output | Flooring small boxes to zero | Clamp outputs to at least one pixel | Security and Authority Boundary Resizing grants no authority over source media and removes no protection: an access-controlled image stays access-controlled at every derived size, and metadata stripping is a separate decision that must be made explicitly. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of image scaling algorithms (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Image_scaling). 2. Pillow’s documentation for resize and thumbnail geometry (https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/). title: Image Super-Resolution
description: Upscale low-resolution images with model-based super-resolution while bounding hallucinated detail, preserving identity-critical features, and labeling the synthesized output as reconstruction.
body: Image Super-Resolution Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Super-resolution uses a learned model to upscale an image beyond its pixel count. The model invents plausible high-frequency detail; it does not recover what was truly there. This skill covers applying SR appropriately, inspecting the output for hallucinated structure, and keeping the output labeled as a reconstruction — never as recovered evidence. When to Use Use for restoring legacy assets, enlarging crops for human viewing, and cleaning up downscaled media where plausibility is the goal. Do not use SR output for identification, forensics, medical reading, or any decision where invented detail could be mistaken for captured fact. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Low-resolution source image | | | | No | Target upscale (x2 default; x4 for very low sources) | | | | No | , , or to select the model variant | Procedure 1. Confirm the use case permits synthesized detail; refuse evidentiary use up front. 2. Select the model variant matching the content type; text and faces need the strictest handling. 3. Run SR at a power-of-two scale; larger factors by chained passes, not one extreme pass. 4. Inspect the output for hallucination signatures: invented text glyphs, warped faces, repeated window or brick patterns. 5. Keep the original untouched alongside the output; never overwrite the source. 6. Record in metadata that the image is model-upscaled, with model and scale named. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The synthesized high-resolution reconstruction | | | | Sharpness gain, artifact inspection summary | | | | Regions where invented structure is suspected | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Invented text or faces | Model fills in what it expects to see | Flag text/face tiles as high risk; human review | | Identity drift | Upscaled face is a different, plausible person | Refuse identification use; compare against original | | Over-sharpening artifacts | Halos at strong edges | Use conservative scale; inspect edges | | Output treated as evidence | Reconstruction believed to be capture | Label outputs and keep the original | | Noise upscaling | Sensor noise enlarged into texture | Denoise before SR, not after | Security and Authority Boundary Super-resolution output is synthesized imagery. It must be labeled as such, must not feed identification or forensic pipelines, and must not be presented in a way that implies detail the sensor never captured. title: Perceptual Image Hashing
description: Compute average-hash fingerprints from downsampled grayscale data and compare them by Hamming distance so near-duplicate images are detected without byte equality.
body: Perceptual Image Hashing Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Byte hashes cannot recognize the same picture after a resize or re-encode. A perceptual hash captures visual structure: downsample to a fixed grid, threshold each cell against the grid mean, and pack the bits into a fixed-width fingerprint. Two images then compare by Hamming distance, and a declared threshold turns that distance into a duplicate decision. Face or semantic similarity is out of scope; this is structural near-duplicate detection. When to Use Use when a corpus must be deduplicated against resizes, crops, and re-encodes, and the decision must be explainable as a measured distance against a declared threshold. Do not use for semantic matching — different scenes with similar histograms compare equal; use classification or embedding retrieval for meaning-level search. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Downsampled grayscale values in row-major order | | | | Yes | Hamming distance at which two hashes count as duplicates | | | | No | Bits per hash; derived from grid length when omitted | Procedure 1. Downsample every image to the same fixed grayscale grid before hashing; grid mismatch makes hashes incomparable. 2. Compute the grid mean and threshold every cell to one bit, using a strict greater-than comparison. 3. Pack the bits in row-major order into a fixed-width integer fingerprint. 4. Compare fingerprints by Hamming distance — popcount of the XOR — never by string similarity. 5. Apply the declared duplicate threshold and record the distance, not just the verdict. 6. Treat dark, flat, or synthetic grids as unhashable noise: their bits carry no structure and produce false matches. 7. Never edit images to force a match; if distances sit at the threshold, collect more evidence instead. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The perceptual fingerprint of the grid | | | | Hamming distance between two hashes | | | | Threshold-applied verdict, recorded with its distance | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False positives | Flat or low-contrast images hash to noise | Flag degenerate grids and exclude them from matching | | Grid mismatch | Images hashed at different resolutions | Downsample everything to one fixed grid first | | Threshold guessing | Cutoff tuned on unlabeled data | Calibrate the threshold on labeled pairs and record it | | Bit-order drift | Cells packed in inconsistent order | Pack row-major in one documented order everywhere | | Semantic overreach | Different scenes counted as duplicates | Keep the decision structural and confirm borderline pairs | Security and Authority Boundary Perceptual hashes are derived features of their source images; they inherit every access restriction of the source. A hash that survives deletion of the original can still identify it, so retention policy must cover hashes too. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia’s overview of perceptual hashing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perceptual_hashing). 2. Python’s statistics module documentation for mean computation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html). title: Subtitle Generation
description: Build well-formed WebVTT subtitle cues from timestamped transcript segments with monotonic ordering, overlap detection, and exact timestamp formatting so captions render correctly and validate mechanically.
body: Subtitle Generation Category: Multimodal | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A caption file is a format contract: cue timestamps must be ordered, non-overlapping, and formatted to the millisecond, or players drop or smear cues. This skill turns timestamped segments into a validated WebVTT payload — exact formatting, overlap detection, and a deterministic builder that never emits an invalid cue. Content quality of the translation itself is out of scope; this is the timing-and-format contract. When to Use Use when transcript segments with start and end times must become a caption track that players and validators accept as-is. Do not use to align audio to text from scratch; alignment belongs to transcription tooling, and this skill consumes its timestamped output. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Timestamped transcript segments in seconds | | | | No | Longest single cue allowed before splitting | | | | No | Per-cue character cap applied by re-segmentation | Procedure 1. Format every timestamp as HH:MM:SS.mmm computed from seconds with integer millisecond rounding. 2. Reject any segment whose end precedes or equals its start; malformed timing never reaches the output. 3. Detect overlaps between consecutive cues and fail closed instead of silently emitting both. 4. Split cues exceeding the duration or character caps before formatting, in reading order. 5. Emit cues in a fixed order: header once, then timing line, text, blank separator per cue. 6. Round-trip the payload: re-parse the emitted cues and assert the turn count and ordering match the input. 7. Keep the builder deterministic — identical segments produce byte-identical output. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The complete WebVTT payload with header and cues | | | | Number of cues emitted | | | | Input segments rejected for timing or overlap reasons | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Overlapping cues | Segments overlap after alignment | Detect overlaps and fail closed or split on evidence | | Smearing timestamps | Floating-point drift in formatting | Round to integer milliseconds from seconds | | Zero-length cue | End time not after start | Reject malformed segments before emission | | Player rejection | Missing blank line between cues | Emit the separator line after every cue | | Silent split drift | Long cues exceed player caps | Apply duration and character caps deterministically | Security and Authority Boundary Caption generation processes potentially private spoken content. The payload inherits the source recording’s disclosure state; rendering or publishing captions grants no new authority over the underlying media. title: Thumbnail Generation
description: Derive bounded thumbnail dimensions from source width and height using integer-only aspect-ratio arithmetic so preview sizes are exact, reproducible, and free of rounding drift.
body: Thumbnail Generation Category: Multimodal | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A thumbnail pipeline needs one deterministic answer per input: given a source size and a bound, what target box does every runtime agree on? This skill defines that answer with integer math — scale by the limiting side, floor to whole pixels, never upscale past the bound — so galleries and indexes render identical sizes everywhere. Pixel resampling quality is out of scope; this is the sizing contract. When to Use Use when generating preview images for galleries, feeds, or search results where the target box must be computed, not guessed, and must match across implementations. Do not use for art-directed crops; creative sizing belongs to image editing, not to this mechanical contract. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Source image width in pixels | | | | Yes | Source image height in pixels | | | | Yes | Largest permitted thumbnail dimension | | | | No | Whether already-small sources may be enlarged; default false | Procedure 1. Reject non-positive width, height, or maxside before any math runs. 2. Compute the scale as the minimum of maxside/width, maxside/height, and 1 when upscaling is disabled. 3. Apply the scale to both dimensions and floor to whole pixels, flooring identically in every implementation. 4. Clamp each result to at least one pixel so degenerate inputs never yield an empty box. 5. Return the box together with the computed scale so callers can verify the bound was respected. 6. Keep the operation pure: same inputs, same box, no environment state. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The integer thumbnail dimensions | | | | The limiting scale factor applied | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Aspect distortion | One dimension rounded independently of the ratio | Scale both dimensions by the same limiting factor | | Upscaled previews | Small sources enlarged and blurred | Cap the scale at 1.0 unless upscaling is explicitly enabled | | Zero-size box | Degenerate source or flooring to zero | Clamp each dimension to at least one pixel | | Cross-runtime drift | Float rounding differs by platform | Floor with integer truncation in a fixed order | | Unbounded thumbnails | maxside not validated | Reject non-positive bounds before computing | Security and Authority Boundary Thumbnails inherit the access state of their source image.
