title: Web Scraping
description: Fetch a URL and extract its main readable content + metadata. Pairs with web-search to follow promising hits, with HTML→Markdown conversion + boilerplate stripping so the output is LLM-friendly.
body: Web Scraping Description Web scraping pulls a URL and returns its main readable content as clean text or Markdown — stripped of nav, ads, footer, JS warnings, cookie banners. It's the second half of agentic browsing: web search picks the URL, scrape gets the actual answer. Naive floods the LLM with chrome and JavaScript stubs. This skill uses (state of the art readability extraction) with a fallback, follows redirects, sets a real User-Agent, respects timeouts, and returns metadata (title, author, publishedat) so downstream RAG can cite it. When to Use - You have a URL (from search, the user, or a previous answer) and need its content. - The page is server-rendered HTML — most news, docs, blogs, GitHub, MDN, Wikipedia. - The site permits scraping (check ; respect rate limits). - Don't use for SPAs that render client-side (use a headless browser like Playwright instead), API-providing sites (use the API), or paywalled content. title: Web Search
description: Query a search API (Tavily, Serper, Bing, Brave, Exa) and return ranked URLs + snippets. The agent's bridge to fresh, open-web information when its training cutoff or private corpus isn't enough.
body: Web Search Description Web search is the agent's escape hatch from the training cutoff: when it doesn't know, it searches. The contract is simple — query string in, ranked list of out — but the choice of provider, query rewriting, and result re-ranking dictate whether the agent finds the answer or makes one up. This skill wraps a single provider (Tavily by default — small, agent-tuned, returns clean snippets) behind a stable interface, then adds query rewriting, caching, and a host-allowlist guard. You can swap providers without touching the consumer. When to Use - The question is about fresh events, prices, releases, news, or anything past the model's cutoff. - The corpus is the open web, not a private collection (use RAG for the latter). - You need citations with publication dates — search APIs return both. - Don't use when the question is purely conceptual (the model already knows), or when the answer must come from your own data. title: Data Lineage
description: Record where each dataset came from and what it fed — inputs, transformations, outputs — so any result can be traced to its sources and any change traced forward.
body: Data Lineage Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A number without ancestry is a rumor with formatting. This skill records ancestry as a first-class artifact: every dataset declares its inputs, the transformation and code version that produced it, and the outputs that depend on it. Lineage answers two questions the moment they are asked — where did this come from, and what breaks if this changes — and a lineage graph that cannot answer both is decoration, not documentation. When to Use Use for datasets that feed decisions, reports, or models — anywhere a wrong number needs to be traced to its source or an upstream change needs its blast radius known. Do not hand-maintain lineage for throwaway exploratory scratch data; capture it where outputs persist and matter, and let the pipeline write the graph. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dataset whose ancestry is being recorded | | | | Yes | Upstream datasets and their versions | | | | Yes | The code, version, and parameters that produced the dataset | Procedure 1. Record inputs precisely: which upstream datasets, at which versions or snapshots, fed the transformation. 2. Record the transformation itself — code version, parameters, and environment — enough to reproduce the output. 3. Write lineage at run time from the pipeline itself, not by hand afterward; hand-maintained lineage is yesterday's graph. 4. Register outputs symmetrically: a dataset knows what it fed, so impact analysis can walk forward as easily as backward. 5. Attach the lineage record to the data — a table property, a manifest, a catalog entry — not to a wiki page. 6. On any upstream change, consult the forward graph before it merges: blast radius is a lineage query, not a guess. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Inputs, transform, and outputs for the dataset | | | | Downstream datasets affected by a change to this one | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Hand-drawn graphs | Lineage edited by hand and drifting from reality | Capture lineage at run time from the pipeline | | Version-blind inputs | Upstream named but not pinned to a snapshot | Record input versions or snapshots, not just names | | Half-lineage | Origins recorded but dependents unknown | Register outputs symmetrically for forward walks | | Orphan manifests | Lineage stored far from the data it describes | Attach lineage to the dataset, not the wiki | | Unqueried impact | Upstream changes merged without blast-radius checks | Make forward impact a pre-merge step | Security and Authority Boundary Lineage is a map of how sensitive data moves: a complete graph shows exactly where restricted columns flow, so lineage stores must enforce the same access scope as the data they describe, and impact queries must not leak the existence or shape of restricted datasets to callers who cannot read them. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OpenLineage open standard for lineage (https://openlineage.io/). 2. title: Data Profiling
description: Measure a dataset before using it — row counts, distributions, null rates, cardinalities — so assumptions about the data are recorded facts instead of hopes.
body: Data Profiling Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Every analysis rests on beliefs about its data: that ids are unique, that the date column is a date, that the two category columns relate the way they did last quarter. Profiling replaces those beliefs with measurements: counts, distinct values, null rates, ranges, and distribution shapes, recorded per column and compared over time. The profile is not the analysis — it is the ground the analysis stands on, and a profile that changed since last week is often the whole explanation for a number that stopped making sense. When to Use Use when a dataset is new to you, before publication or reporting on it, and periodically on datasets assumed stable. Do not profile a known-stable, schema-verified table on every read; repeated profiling of unchanged data is cost without information. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The data being profiled | | | | Yes | Counts, null rates, distinct values, ranges to measure | | | | No | A prior profile to diff against | Procedure 1. Profile structure first: column names, types, row count, and how those differ from any recorded schema. 2. Measure completeness per column — null rates and default values — and distinctness: cardinality and top values. 3. Profile ranges and distributions for numeric and temporal columns, recording min, max, and shape, not just the mean. 4. Diff against the baseline profile and flag every metric that moved beyond its historical band. 5. Record the profile with the dataset version and date, so future comparisons have something concrete to diff. 6. Turn anomalies into constraints: a property that surprised you is a rule for the validation boundary. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-column measurements with dataset version and date | | | | Movements against the prior profile, empty when none | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Assumed schemas | Analysis built on a shape nobody verified | Profile structure before any measurement | | Mean-blindness | Averages hiding bimodal or skewed reality | Record distribution shape, not just the mean | | Unrecorded profiles | Measurements made once and lost | Persist profiles with dataset version and date | | Unbounded profiling | Whole-table scans repeated on every read | Profile new or changed data; sample what is stable | | Anomaly blindness | A moved metric nobody diffs against history | Always diff against the prior profile | Security and Authority Boundary Profiles are exfiltration-shaped: cardinalities, top values, and ranges of sensitive columns can disclose individual records, so profiling outputs on restricted data inherit its access scope and profiling jobs must not write measurements to stores more public than the data itself could reach. title: Data Validation
description: Check datasets against declared constraints — schema, types, ranges, and cross-field rules — before they enter analysis or models, failing loudly at the boundary.
body: Data Validation Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Data arrives wrong more often than it arrives late: nulls where keys live, strings where numbers were promised, duplicate rows quietly doubling a metric. This skill moves checking to the boundary: constraints are declared alongside the pipeline, every batch is validated on arrival, and a violation stops the data instead of following it downstream. The essential move is declaring expectations explicitly — an undeclared constraint cannot be checked, and an unchecked constraint eventually becomes a wrong number someone acted on. When to Use Use at every ingestion boundary — files, API feeds, database extracts — and before anything feeds reporting, training, or user-visible output. Do not validate beyond what consumers depend on; a constraint nobody relies on still costs every batch and fails runs for no operational reason. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The batch or table arriving at the boundary | | | | Yes | Declared types, required fields, and nullability | | | | Yes | Value rules — ranges, enums, uniqueness, cross-field logic | Procedure 1. Declare the schema first — column names, types, nullability — and version it beside the pipeline that enforces it. 2. Add value constraints that consumers actually rely on: ranges, enum membership, uniqueness of keys, referential joins. 3. Run validation on arrival, per batch, and collect all violations rather than stopping at the first. 4. Route failures by severity: hard violations quarantine the batch, soft ones are logged with counts and rates. 5. Report violation statistics as data — failure rates by rule over time — so drift is visible before it becomes an outage. 6. Change the schema deliberately: a constraint change ships as a reviewed edit with a migration, not as a hotfix to silence a failing rule. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The batch that passed, cleared for downstream use | | | | Per-record rule failures with the offending values | | | | Rule-level pass and failure counts for the batch | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Silent coercion | A wrong-typed column parsed into plausible nonsense | Type-check at the boundary; never rely on parse leniency | | Null smuggling | Missing keys flow into aggregates as zeros or blanks | Declare nullability; fail on missing required fields | | Duplicate keys | The same record counted twice in a metric | Uniqueness-check primary keys per batch | | Rule sprawl | Constraints accumulated that nobody depends on | Retire constraints no consumer relies on | | Failure fatigue | Frequent red pipelines ignored as background noise | Severity-route; only hard violations block | Security and Authority Boundary Validation reports quote offending values: constraint failures on sensitive columns must surface the shape of the violation without reproducing the raw value in logs, and validation stages should inherit the access scope of the data they check. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The pandera data validation framework documentation (https://pandera.readthedocs.io/). 2. title: Embedding Generation
description: Turn text (or images, audio) into dense unit-normalised vectors with a hosted embedding model. Batch the API calls, cache by content hash, and handle the per-token / per-input limits explicitly.
body: Embedding Generation Description Embedding generation converts arbitrary inputs (most commonly text) into fixed-dimensional dense vectors that encode semantic similarity: similar inputs land near each other in vector space. The vectors are produced by a frozen pre-trained model and consumed by retrieval, clustering, classification, and recommendation systems. This skill covers the production-grade contract: deterministic batching to maximise throughput, content-hash caching so you don't re-embed unchanged inputs, dimension reduction (via Matryoshka truncation when supported), and the silent-failure modes — wrong tokenizer, mixing dimensions, missing normalisation — that bite teams six months in. When to Use - You need a vector representation that downstream code (vector store, classifier, ranker) can consume. - The input is text (most common), or images/audio with a multimodal embedding model. - You're embedding once and querying many times → cache by content hash; embeddings are deterministic for fixed model+content. - Don't use when a sparse keyword index (BM25, tf-idf) is sufficient or when you need a probability distribution rather than a similarity vector. title: Incremental Processing
description: Process new data as it arrives instead of reprocessing the whole corpus — checkpoints, watermarks, and late-arrival handling — so cost stays flat as history grows.
body: Incremental Processing Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A pipeline that recomputes everything on every run is a pipeline with a half-life: the corpus grows, the run lengthens, and the day arrives where the run no longer fits between the arrivals. This skill switches the unit of work from the dataset to the delta: the process tracks what it has already consumed, takes only the new records past that mark, and handles the stragglers — late, out-of-order, or corrected records — by explicit rule rather than by accident. When to Use Use when data arrives continuously or the corpus is large enough that full recomputation no longer fits its window — event streams, append-only logs, growing tables. Do not add incremental machinery to small, fully recomputable datasets; a full pass over a small table is simpler, idempotent by construction, and easier to reason about. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The arriving data with an ordering or event time | | | | Yes | The consumed position the run resumes from | | | | Yes | Window wait, watermark, or drop for late arrivals | Procedure 1. Pick the position marker — an offset, a timestamp, or a sequence column — that strictly advances as new data arrives. 2. Persist a checkpoint after each processed unit, and make downstream updates idempotent so a replay from the checkpoint is safe. 3. Process only records past the checkpoint, committing the new checkpoint only after the unit is durably processed. 4. Handle late arrivals by rule: bounded wait behind a watermark, correction events, or explicit drop — never by silent overwrite. 5. Measure lag — arrival time to processed time — and alarm when the checkpoint stops advancing, because a stalled marker is the failure mode. 6. Periodically reconcile the incremental result against a full recomputation, so drift between the two is caught at a known cost. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Records consumed since the previous checkpoint | | | | The new resume position, durable after commit | | | | Arrival-to-processed delay and stall detection | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Checkpoint stalls | The marker stops advancing and data piles up | Alarm on lag and on checkpoint age | | Replay damage | Reprocessing a unit double-counts downstream | Make downstream updates idempotent per event | | Late-arrival chaos | Out-of-order records dropped or duplicated silently | Apply an explicit watermark and late policy | | Full-scan relapse | The incremental path quietly recomputing everything | Track processed volume per run | | Unverified drift | Incremental result slowly diverges from truth | Reconcile periodically against a full recomputation | Security and Authority Boundary Incremental state is attack surface: checkpoints record positions and the process holds partial aggregates, so both must inherit the access scope of the source data, and late-arrival or correction paths — which can rewrite aggregates — deserve the same authorization checks as the primary path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Apache Kafka documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of stream processing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_processing). title: Missing Data Imputation
description: Profile per-column missingness, choose an explicit imputation strategy per column, fit fill values on training rows only, and record an imputation mask so later analyses can audit the change.
body: Missing Data Imputation Category: Data | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description How values are missing carries as much signal as the values themselves, and a single global fill rule such as zero-for-everything destroys that signal. This skill defines the disciplined loop: profile per-column missingness, pick a strategy per column, fit fill values on training rows only, and record an imputation mask so every filled cell stays identifiable for later audit. When to Use Use when training or reporting data has missing cells and the fill rule affects the result. Do not use for already-masked experimental data where missingness is part of the design; that case is analysis configuration, not imputation. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Records with absent cells represented as null | | | | Yes | Columns to profile and fill | | | | Yes | Per-column strategy such as median, mode, constant, or none | | | | No | Row subset used to fit fill values, defaulting to training rows | Procedure 1. Profile every column: missing count, missing rate, and the pattern of co-missingness across rows. 2. Classify each column’s missingness mechanism before choosing a strategy; uniform filling across mechanisms is a smell. 3. Choose a strategy per column and record why it was chosen. 4. Fit fill values on the declared fit scope only; never let test or future rows influence a fill value. 5. Apply fills to a copy; the original rows stay untouched for audit. 6. Record an imputation mask alongside the filled data so every filled cell is identifiable later. 7. Re-profile after filling and compare distributions; a fill that moves a distribution needs a second look. 8. Document the mask’s retention period; the mask is analytical metadata, not a permanent record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Copies with missing cells filled per strategy | | | | Row-column positions that were filled | | | | Per-column missingness before and after filling | | | | Fitted fill values with their fit scope | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Global fill | One rule is applied to every column | Choose a strategy per column and record why | | Test leakage | Fill values are fitted on all rows | Fit on training rows only | | Mask loss | Filled data ships without its mask | Ship the mask beside the filled data | | Distribution shift | The fill moves the column’s shape | Re-profile after filling and compare | | In-place overwrite | Original rows are mutated | Fill copies and keep the originals untouched | Security and Authority Boundary Imputing values grants no authority to invent records. Filled cells are estimates and must remain identifiable as such through the mask. Data subject to privacy or retention limits keeps those limits through the whole loop: profiling, filling, and the mask inherit them. title: Character Design
description: Build fictional characters as explicit profiles — voice, motivation, capability, limits — with mechanically checkable arc beats so characters stay consistent and their growth is deliberate.
body: Character Design Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A character is a contract with the reader: the way they speak, what they want, what they cannot do. Breaking that contract by convenience is how stories lose trust. This skill defines a character as a structured profile — identity, motivation, capabilities with explicit limits, and voice rules — plus a beat sheet for their arc, so consistency is checkable against a record instead of remembered vibes. When to Use Use when introducing a recurring character into any narrative work — prose, games, scripts — whose behavior must stay consistent across scenes and writers. Do not use for background figures who appear once; a full profile for a walk-on role is overhead. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Identity, motivation, capabilities, and limits | | | | Yes | Planned arc beats in story order | | | | No | Beat types the arc must contain | Procedure 1. Write the profile before the character acts: motivation, capability set with explicit limits, and voice rules with examples. 2. State what the character cannot do; limits are what make capability meaningful. 3. Plan the arc as an ordered beat list and check it contains the required beat types before writing. 4. Check every written scene against the profile; out-of-character action requires either a new beat that earns it or a profile revision. 5. Keep the profile versioned with the work so any scene can be traced to the character state it assumed. 6. Give each distinct character a distinguishable voice rule set; interchangeable voices are a design failure. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The recorded character profile | | | | Required arc beats not yet planned | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Out-of-character action | Scene convenience overrides the profile | Check scenes against the profile or revise it deliberately | | Missing arc stages | Key beats skipped in planning | Check required beats before writing the arc | | Interchangeable voices | All characters speak alike | Write and test a distinct voice rule per character | | Capability inflation | Limits quietly dropped under plot pressure | Restate limits in the profile and enforce them | | Stale profiles | Character grows but the record does not | Version the profile with each earned change | Security and Authority Boundary Characters borrowed from real people or cultures carry real obligations. Design with researched respect, avoid caricature, and keep provenance notes so borrowed elements are used with attribution and consent where applicable. title: Dialogue Writing
description: Write character dialogue with explicit speaker turns, subtext layers, and mechanical exchange checks so conversations stay consistent, purposeful, and attributable line by line.
body: Dialogue Writing Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Dialogue has mechanics and meaning: every line belongs to a speaker, turns should not blur into monologue by accident, and what a character says should rarely be exactly what they mean. This skill treats dialogue as structured data — (speaker, text) turns with optional subtext — plus checks for alternation, tagging, and emptiness, so the craft decisions sit on a verifiable exchange structure. When to Use Use when writing scenes of two or more voices where speaker attribution and turn structure must stay clean — prose, scripts, or interactive fiction. Do not use for interior monologue; unattributed thought is not dialogue and follows different rules. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Dialogue turns in order with explicit speakers | | | | No | Intended unstated meaning per line | | | | No | Per-speaker voice constraints | Procedure 1. Write every line as an explicit (speaker, text) turn; unattributed lines are a structural defect, not a style. 2. Run the exchange checks before polishing prose: same-speaker runs must be intentional, empty lines removed. 3. Give each line a purpose — information, pressure, or relationship change — and cut lines with none. 4. Set the subtext deliberately; when text equals meaning, that sameness should be the decision, not the default. 5. Read voices against their speaker rules; a line that fits no voice is a draft error. 6. Keep the exchange table with the draft so revisions do not silently drop speakers or turns. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The checked, ordered exchange | | | | Structural problems found by the checks | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Speaker blur | Turns run together without clear attribution | Tag every line and run the alternation check | | Talking heads | Exchange carries no scene purpose | Give each line information, pressure, or change | | Flat text | Characters say exactly what they mean | Set subtext deliberately per line | | Voice bleed | All characters speak with one voice | Write per-speaker voice rules and check against them | | Unversioned drafts | Revisions drop turns silently | Keep the exchange table with the draft | Security and Authority Boundary Dialogue written in real people’s voices — impressions of living individuals — carries defamation and dignity risks. Fictional voices should stay fictional, and borrowed real-world dialect deserves researched respect. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. body: Name Generation Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Naming by staring at a blank page produces the first defensible option; naming by generation produces the space of options and then chooses. This skill defines name generation as a constrained search: a morpheme inventory, a construction pattern, a banned list, and collision checks against existing names — producing a reproducible candidate set instead of a lucky guess. When to Use Use when a product, character, place, or brand needs a name and the process should explore the option space deliberately rather than seize the first idea. Do not use where naming is externally fixed by standards, clients, or convention; constrained search cannot substitute for a mandated name. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Declared morpheme inventories for construction | | | | Yes | Shape rule a candidate must satisfy | | | | Yes | Substrings and collisions excluded from results | Procedure 1. Declare the inventories and construction rules before generating; free-form generation cannot be reproduced or audited. 2. Generate the full candidate set from the inventories under the construction rules. 3. Filter by the declared pattern so shape violations never reach review. 4. Apply the banned list and collision checks against existing names before presenting candidates. 5. Present candidates with their construction provenance — which morphemes and rules produced them. 6. Record the chosen name with the generator settings so the decision is reproducible later. title: Plot Structure
description: Organize a story into declared structural acts with positioned beats so pacing, reversals, and climaxes land where the chosen form requires and deviations are deliberate.
body: Plot Structure Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Structure is the load-bearing frame a story hangs from: acts, beats, and their positions. Without declared positions, a “slow second act” is a feeling; with them, it is a measurable gap between the inciting event and the midpoint. This skill defines plot structure as a table — beats named, positioned on a 0–100 scale, and assigned to declared acts — so the shape is visible and every deviation is a decision. When to Use Use when planning or diagnosing a story’s shape — novels, screenplays, episodes — before or during drafting, or when a draft feels structurally off. Do not use to impose structure on completed work by force; if a story resists the chosen form, change forms deliberately rather than mangle the story. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Story beats with positions on a 0–100 scale | | | | Yes | Declared act boundaries on the same scale | | | | No | Beats the chosen form mandates | Procedure 1. Choose the structural form first and declare its act boundaries on a normalized 0–100 scale. 2. Position each beat on the same scale; relative position is the contract, not chapter count. 3. Check that every beat falls inside exactly one act; boundary orphans indicate scale drift. 4. Check the form’s required beats are present and positioned within their expected ranges. 5. Report structural gaps — long stretches with no beat — as measurable intervals, not impressions. 6. Revise positions on evidence when pacing is off; the table is the plan of record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Beats mapped to their acts | | | | Beats outside every declared act | | | | Unusually long beat-free intervals | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Act drift | Beats straddle declared boundaries | Normalize positions to one scale and reassign | | Missing mandatory beats | The chosen form’s obligations unmet | Check required beats against the declared form | | Unmeasured pacing | “Slow” sections felt but not located | Report beat-free intervals as numbers | | Form mismatch | Story forced into an unsuitable structure | Choose the form from the story, not habit | | Stale plan | Draft diverges from the structural table | Keep the table current or admit it is abandoned | Security and Authority Boundary Structure tools shape creative output but claim no ownership; a structural template is scaffolding, and the finished work inherits only the licenses of its actual sources. title: Poetry Forms
description: Write within fixed poetic forms by checking their mechanical constraints — syllable counts, line counts, rhyme schemes — so form compliance is verified rather than asserted.
body: Poetry Forms Category: Creative | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A fixed form is a contract in counts: five and seven for the haiku, fourteen lines with a rhyme scheme for the sonnet. Meeting the contract by assertion is how “approximate haiku” happens. This skill treats form compliance as checkable arithmetic — per-line syllable counts against declared targets, line count against the form, rhyme pattern against the scheme — with the checks running before the poem is presented as done. When to Use Use when writing in a fixed form, when an exercise or publication requires exact form compliance, or when teaching forms where the mechanics matter. Do not use for free verse; imposing fixed-form checks on open forms misreads the contract. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The poem’s lines in order | | | | Yes | Declared constraints: syllables, line count, rhyme scheme | Procedure 1. Declare the form’s numeric contract up front — syllable targets per line, line count, rhyme scheme. 2. Count syllables per line with a stated counting convention, and record the count next to each line. 3. Check line count against the form before deeper checks; wrong length is the first failure. 4. Map rhyme classes per line and compare the resulting pattern against the declared scheme. 5. Report every deviation with the offending line rather than a bare failure flag. 6. Revise the line, not the check; weakening the contract to pass is self-deception. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Syllable count per line, in order | | | | Lines violating the declared form | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Approximate form | Counts asserted without checking | Run the arithmetic and record per-line counts | | Heuristic overtrust | Vowel-run counter treated as ground truth | Flag heuristic counts for human review on hard cases | | Contract weakening | Targets edited to fit the draft | Revise the line, not the declared form | | Scheme drift | Rhyme pattern left unchecked | Map the realized scheme against the declared one | | Form confusion | Free verse judged by fixed-form rules | Match the checks to the declared form | Security and Authority Boundary Form constraints govern counts and sound, not appropriation. Diction borrowed from living traditions carries the same research and respect obligations as any cultural material, regardless of syllable totals. Wikipedia’s overview of the sonnet form (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet). title: Worldbuilding
description: Construct fictional settings as an explicit fact ledger with category constraints and mechanical consistency checks so a story world stays coherent as it grows.
body: Worldbuilding Category: Creative | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A fictional world breaks the moment its facts disagree: the bridge was built two centuries after the plague it preceded. This skill treats worldbuilding as a ledger — every established fact recorded once, with dates, places, and in-world sources — plus mechanical checks that new material does not contradict the record. The ledger is the artifact; prose merely cites it. When to Use Use when creating or extending a fictional setting — for novels, games, or campaigns — that will outlive a single writing session and must remain internally consistent. Do not use for improvisational settings that exist for one scene; a ledger for throwaway fiction is overhead, not value. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The established fact ledger with dates and sources | | | | Yes | New material proposed for the ledger | | | | No | Category rules, e.g. event ordering or population bounds | Procedure 1. Record every accepted fact exactly once with its in-world date, location, and the source that established it. 2. Check every draft fact against the ledger before it is accepted; contradictions are reported with both records. 3. Encode ordering constraints between dated events so chronology is checked mechanically, not by memory. 4. Prefer reconciling a contradiction over retconning silently; when a retcon is chosen, record it as a new ledger entry. 5. Keep the ledger versioned with the work so any chapter can be traced to the world state it was written against. 6. Leave gaps explicitly marked as unknown; unrecorded is not the same as unrestricted. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The updated fact ledger | | | | Draft facts that conflict with the ledger | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Chronology drift | Dates held in memory across chapters | Record every dated fact in the ledger and check drafts | | Silent retcons | Old facts rewritten without a record | Log every retcon as its own ledger entry | | Fact duplication | One event recorded with two dates | Key facts by a single canonical name | | Unbounded invention | New material contradicts category rules | Check drafts against recorded constraints | | False gaps | Unknown mistaken for unrecorded | Mark unknowns explicitly in the ledger | Security and Authority Boundary Fictional worlds can contain real patterns worth protecting: place names, cultures, and communities borrowed from reality deserve respectful, researched use, and the ledger documents provenance so inherited material is cited, not erased. title: Agent Skill Security Audit
description: Audit an agent skill and its bundled resources before installation or execution, checking declared behavior, permissions, credential access, network egress, obfuscation, and sandbox requirements.
body: Agent Skill Security Audit Description An agent skill is executable trust-boundary content when it contains instructions, scripts, hooks, references, or tool permissions. Audit the complete skill package before installation or execution rather than trusting its description or publisher metadata. The audit is primarily static and compares declared behavior with the actual SKILL.md instructions and every bundled executable/resource file. Check for unexpected permission grants, credential reads, network egress, obfuscated content, hidden behavior, unsafe hooks, and mismatch between advertised and observable behavior. Dynamic analysis is optional and must run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic or no credentials, bounded resources, controlled network access, and explicit teardown. An audit result is evidence for a trust decision; it is not a guarantee that a skill is benign. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | skillroot | path | yes | Root directory containing the skill manifest and bundled resources | | declaredpermissions | list | no | Permissions/tools explicitly declared by the skill or host metadata | | runtimepolicy | object | no | Sandbox, filesystem, network, credential, and execution constraints | | auditmode | enum | yes | static or sandboxed | Output is a structured audit record containing findings, evidence locations, severity, confidence, declared-vs-observed deltas, sandbox requirements, and a disposition such as allow, review, or deny. Audit Procedure 1. Parse frontmatter and record declared name, purpose, permissions, compatibility, and provenance. 2. Inventory SKILL.md, scripts, hooks, binaries, configuration, references, and generated files under the skill root. 3. Compare advertised behavior with actual instructions and executable content. 4. Identify credential and sensitive-file access, including environment variables, SSH material, cloud credentials, token stores, and unrelated user data. 5. Identify network destinations and egress mechanisms. Treat undeclared network access as a finding requiring review. 6. Inspect for shell/process execution, package installation, dynamic code loading, obfuscation, encoded payloads, persistence, or attempts to hide behavior from the user. 7. Compare declared tool permissions with the minimum permissions required by observed behavior. 8. Record exact evidence locations and never treat absence of a detected pattern as proof of safety. 9. If dynamic analysis is required, run only in an isolated sandbox with synthetic credentials, bounded resources, controlled egress, and no access to the auditor real environment. 10. Produce a fail-closed disposition when high-confidence critical behavior is incompatible with the declared purpose or execution policy. Runnable Example This example is a bounded static signal detector, not a malware detector. Production audits need language-aware analysis, archive/binary handling, symlink controls, policy evaluation, and reproducible evidence capture. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Trusting metadata | Description differs from bundled behavior | Audit executable/resource contents and record declared-vs-observed deltas | | Credential exposure | Skill reads real secrets or credential stores | Deny or isolate access; use synthetic credentials for dynamic testing | | Hidden egress | Network access is not declared or constrained | Default to no network and allow only policy-approved destinations | | Permission overreach | Skill requests tools broader than its purpose | Apply least privilege and require explicit review for elevated permissions | | Obfuscation | Encoded/dynamic content hides behavior | Flag for manual/static analysis and preserve exact evidence location | | Sandbox escape | Dynamic test reaches the host | Use a maintained isolated runtime with resource, filesystem, and network controls | | False negative | Static checks miss behavior | Treat audit output as evidence, not a safety guarantee; use layered controls | | False positive | Benign implementation matches a heuristic | Record confidence and require contextual review rather than automatic condemnation | Design Rules 1. Treat every third-party skill package as untrusted input until its behavior is reviewed. 2. Audit the complete package, not only SKILL.md frontmatter. 3. Preserve provenance and exact evidence locations for every finding. 4. Compare declared permissions and behavior against the least-privilege execution policy. 5. Default dynamic analysis to synthetic/no credentials, bounded resources, and restricted network access. 6. Never claim that a static scan proves a skill is safe. 7. Keep audit evidence separate from authorization; a passing audit does not itself grant permission to execute a skill. 8. Prefer deterministic checks for path, permission, secret, network, and package-integrity findings where practical. References - OWASP Secure Agent Playbook issue #21: https://github.com/OWASP/secure-agent-playbook/issues/21 - 2026 research on detecting malicious agent skills: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06547 - Skills Tree Sandboxed Execution: sandboxed-execution.md - Skills Tree Secret Scanning: secret-scanning.md Evidence status: the cited sources support the audit problem and defensive methodology. This skill does not claim complete malware detection, compliance certification, or universal safety. title: Approval Before Destructive Tools
description: Require explicit human or automated approval before any agent executes an irreversible tool action.
body: Approval Before Destructive Tools Category: security | Level: intermediate | Stability: stable | Version: v2 Description Destructive tools — database deletes, file overwrites, API calls that send emails or charge customers, infrastructure changes — must never execute based solely on LLM intent. An approval gate enforces a mandatory review step: the agent proposes the action, execution is interrupted, a human or automated policy approves or rejects, and only then does the tool run. This prevents hallucination-driven data loss. Inputs - : proposed tool name and arguments from the agent - : function or human reviewer deciding approve/reject - : LangGraph , OpenAI guardrail, or custom middleware - : append-only log recording every decision Outputs - Approved: tool executes, result returned to agent - Rejected: agent receives structured rejection with reason, can propose alternative Example Failure Modes | Cause | Symptom | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Destructive tool not in blocklist | Auto-executed without approval | Maintain allowlist of safe tools, block everything else by default | | Approver rubber-stamps requests | No real oversight | Require approver to confirm by typing action name, not just clicking OK | | Agent bypasses middleware | Approval skipped | Enforce at infrastructure level, not only application code | Prompt Patterns Basic: Chain-of-Thought: Constrained Output: Model Comparison | Capability | GPT-4o | Claude 3.7 Sonnet | Gemini 2.0 Flash | |---|---|---|---| | Risk classification accuracy | ✅ High | ✅ Very High | ⚠️ Moderate | | Policy design quality | ✅ Good | ✅ Strong | ⚠️ Generic | | Allowlist recommendation | ✅ Detailed | ✅ Detailed | ⚠️ Vague | | Audit log design advice | ✅ Good | ✅ Strong | ⚠️ Minimal | | Cost | Moderate | Moderate | Low | Related - · · · · Changelog - v2 (2026-04): Full expansion

title: Audit Logging
description: Record security-relevant agent actions in a structured, tamper-evident audit trail without logging secrets or unnecessary personal data.
body: Audit Logging Description Audit logging gives an agent system an attributable record of security-relevant actions: tool calls, resource access, authorization decisions, approvals, failures, and externally visible side effects. The log should support investigation and accountability without becoming a second data-leak channel. Use structured events with stable event types, actor identity, correlation IDs, timestamps, outcome, and a minimal resource reference. Do not record API keys, passwords, session cookies, full prompts containing sensitive data, or raw tool responses by default. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Agent, service, or human identity responsible for the event | | | string | yes | Stable action name such as or | | | string | yes | Minimal resource identifier; avoid embedding sensitive payloads | | | string | yes | , , , or | | | string | no | Identifier linking related events across a workflow | | | dict | no | Non-sensitive structured context | Output is a structured audit event containing timestamp, identity, action, resource reference, outcome, and an integrity field. Runnable Example The example demonstrates an append-only hash chain primitive. A production implementation also needs protected storage, clock handling, access controls, retention policy, and key management where stronger authenticity guarantees are required. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Secret leakage | Raw tool input/output is logged | Allowlist fields and redact secrets before serialization | | Unattributed action | Shared or missing actor identity | Require authenticated actor/service identity | | Broken correlation | Each component invents unrelated IDs | Propagate a workflow correlation ID | | Log tampering | Logs are writable by the workload being audited | Separate writer and reader permissions and use append-only storage | | Excessive retention | Logs become a privacy/security liability | Define retention by purpose and data class | | Clock ambiguity | Host clocks differ | Store UTC timestamps and use a trusted event ordering strategy | | High-cardinality noise | Every internal operation becomes an event | Log security-relevant state transitions, not arbitrary debug output | Design Rules 1. Treat logs as sensitive data. 2. Log decisions and outcomes rather than secrets or complete payloads. 3. Make actor and correlation identity explicit. 4. Separate operational debugging from compliance/security audit records. 5. Define retention and deletion rules before deployment. 6. Test that denied actions generate auditable events. 7. Never treat a hash chain alone as proof of external authenticity. References - OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LoggingCheatSheet.html - NIST AI Risk Management Framework: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework - Python documentation: https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html Evidence status: implementation guidance is grounded in the cited security guidance; no compliance certification or performance claim is made. title: Dependency Integrity Verification
description: Verify third-party package artifacts against pinned digests, signatures, and provenance attestations before installation so the build consumes exactly the artifacts that were reviewed.
body: Dependency Integrity Verification Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A dependency declaration names what you want; the artifact that arrives is what you run. Integrity verification closes that gap: versions pinned to exact hashes, digests recomputed at install time, signatures checked against a known identity, and provenance attestations matched to the build that produced the artifact. Anything that cannot be verified is rejected rather than installed and inspected later. When to Use Use before installing any third-party package in build, CI, or runtime environments — especially in automated pipelines that install without a human reading the output. Do not treat integrity verification as vulnerability scanning: a verified artifact is exactly the reviewed bytes, which can still contain a reviewed vulnerability. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency to install | | | | Yes | The pinned hash from the reviewed lockfile | | | | No | Detached signature over the artifact | | | | No | Build provenance statement for the artifact | Procedure 1. Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile; floating ranges bypass review by construction. 2. Fetch the artifact and recompute its digest locally; never trust the registry's advertised hash alone. 3. When a signature is available, verify it against a pinned signing identity, not a key fetched at verify time. 4. When provenance is available, check that the attestation's build matches the expected source and workflow. 5. Reject on any mismatch — digest, signature, or provenance — and fail the install. 6. Record the verification result (package, digest, verdict) so the decision is auditable later. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether the artifact matched its pinned integrity data | | | | First failed check when rejected | | | | Package, version, digest, and verdict for the audit trail | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating versions | ranges install whatever resolves today | Pin exact versions with hashes in the lockfile | | Registry substitution | Artifact swapped between resolve and install | Recompute the digest at install time | | Keys fetched at verify time | Signing key taken from the channel it vouches for | Pin the signing identity independently | | CI cache poisoning | Cached artifacts skip verification | Verify after cache restore, not only on download | | Mirror drift | Internal mirror serving different bytes | Verify digests from mirrors exactly like upstream | Security and Authority Boundary Integrity verification proves the artifact is the one that was attested; it says nothing about the safety or quality of the code inside. Vulnerability scanning, license review, and human review remain separate, mandatory steps. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of supply chain attacks on software distribution (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplychainattack). 2. The Sigstore documentation on artifact signing and verification (https://docs.sigstore.dev/). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. Related Skills - Secret Scanning — the paired check that no credentials ride along with the code. - Sandboxed Execution — containment for artifacts that pass verification but stay unproven in behavior. title: Harm Detection
description: Triage potentially harmful agent inputs and outputs with explicit categories, thresholds, and escalation paths before high-impact actions.
body: Harm Detection Description Harm detection is a safety gate that classifies content or planned actions against an explicitly defined risk policy before an agent acts or responds. It should identify relevant categories, preserve uncertainty, and escalate ambiguous or high-impact cases instead of silently converting a classifier result into authorization. The detector can combine deterministic rules, specialist classifiers, and human review. It is a risk-control layer, not a universal guarantee that content is safe. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Content to classify | | | string | no | Intended agent action if action-aware screening is used | | | dict | yes | Categories, thresholds, and escalation behavior | | | dict | no | Minimal context required for classification | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | string | , , or | | | list[str] | Policy categories triggered | | | float | Classifier confidence when available | | | string | Safe explanation of the decision | Runnable Example This deterministic example is intentionally conservative and incomplete. Production classifiers require a documented taxonomy, evaluation set, threshold policy, false-positive/false-negative analysis, and an escalation path. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False negative | Classifier misses harmful content | Use layered controls and action-specific authorization | | False positive | Benign content matches a category | Provide review/escalation rather than silent rejection when appropriate | | Context loss | Classification sees too little context | Pass only the minimum context required for the policy decision | | Classifier prompt injection | User content manipulates a classifier | Treat classifier input as untrusted and constrain its output schema | | Policy drift | Categories or thresholds become outdated | Version the policy and evaluate changes before rollout | | Over-trust | A classifier result is treated as authorization | Keep safety screening separate from identity/permission checks | Design Rules - Define categories and actions before implementing the classifier. - Keep and semantics explicit. - Do not expose hidden classifier prompts or sensitive evidence in user-facing messages. - Log policy decisions without storing unnecessary harmful content. - Re-test thresholds when models or policies change. - Use human review for ambiguous high-impact cases. References - NIST AI Risk Management Framework: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework - NIST AI RMF FAQs: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/ai-risk-management-framework-faqs Evidence status: the cited NIST material supports AI risk-management and trustworthiness guidance; this skill does not claim that any classifier is universally accurate. title: Human In Loop
description: Pause high-risk agent actions for explicit human approval with deny-by-default timeouts, auditable decisions, and safe resume or abort behavior.
body: Human In Loop Description Human-in-the-loop control inserts an explicit approval boundary before actions whose risk, authority, cost, or irreversibility exceeds an established threshold. The agent should prepare the proposed action and evidence, then wait for a decision from an authorized reviewer. Approval must be bound to the exact action being approved. A generic approval such as "yes, continue" should not authorize a different action later in the workflow. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Canonical action identifier | | | string | yes | Resource or target affected | | | string | yes | Policy risk classification | | | dict | no | Facts needed by the reviewer | | | int | no | Maximum approval wait | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | bool | Explicit approval result | | | string | Audit correlation identifier | | | string | Reviewer decision reason when supplied | Runnable Example The demo deliberately denies by default. A production implementation should use an authenticated, durable approval channel and bind the reviewer decision to an immutable action summary. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Approval replay | Old approval reused for a new action | Bind approval to action, target, parameters, and expiry | | Wrong reviewer | Reviewer lacks authority | Check reviewer identity and required scope | | Timeout bypass | Agent continues after timeout | Timeout must produce a deny/escalate state | | Approval fatigue | Too many low-risk approvals | Use explicit risk thresholds and batch only equivalent safe actions | | Missing evidence | Reviewer cannot understand the action | Present concise, relevant evidence and expected effects | | Race condition | Target changes after approval | Revalidate target state immediately before execution | Design Rules - Deny by default on timeout or unavailable approval service. - Never interpret silence as approval. - Make approvals single-purpose and time-bounded. - Re-check permissions and target state after approval. - Record who approved what, when, and under which policy version. - Provide an explicit abort path. References - NIST AI Risk Management Framework: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework - NIST AI RMF FAQs: https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework/ai-risk-management-framework-faqs Evidence status: guidance is based on general AI risk-management and accountability principles; no claim is made that human review alone guarantees safe behavior. title: Input Sanitization
description: Validate and clean every untrusted string before it reaches an LLM, a tool call, or a filesystem/SQL/HTTP boundary. Layered defense against prompt injection, SQL injection, path traversal, command injection, and PII leakage.
body: Input Sanitization Description Every string that enters your agent is untrusted: user messages, tool outputs, retrieved documents, file contents, web fetches. Each one is a candidate vector for prompt injection ("ignore previous instructions"), SQL injection ( ), path traversal ( ), command injection, and data exfiltration. This skill is the layered defense: (1) structural validation (Pydantic / JSON schema) for shape, (2) boundary-specific escaping (parameterised SQL, , ), (3) content-level analysis (PII detection, classifier, allowlist), and (4) isolation (separate LLM call to triage suspicious input). Defense is layered because any single check is bypassable. When to Use - Any time untrusted text is going to be: (a) concatenated into a prompt, (b) passed to a tool, (c) used as a path/filename, (d) interpolated into SQL/shell. - Even when the input "comes from your database" — if it was originally typed by a user, it's untrusted. - Don't skip for "internal" tools — most prompt-injection attacks today come via retrieved documents, not the user message. Inputs / Outputs | Field | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The untrusted input (str, dict, list, …) | | | | What's allowed (max length, charset, allowed paths, …) | | → | | Passed every layer | | → | | Cleaned version safe to forward | | → | | Specific rules tripped (for audit logs) | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Layer 1 passes; layer 2 still vulnerable | Defence-in-depth bypass at the SQL/path/shell boundary | All four layers must run; never skip the boundary-specific layer | | Allowlist too loose | Charset allows control chars, RTL overrides ( ) | Pin to printable ASCII + curated Unicode ranges | | Allowlist too strict | Drops legitimate non-English | Test on real i18n samples; whitelist ranges | | PII regex misses unusual formats | International phones, IBAN | Add a classifier (e.g. Microsoft Presidio) for tail PII | | Unicode normalisation differs | vs (combining) bypasses match | NFC-normalise before any regex check | | Indirect prompt injection via tool output | Trusted tool returned attacker-controlled text | Re-run sanitization on EVERY message into the LLM, not just the user's | | Sanitization log itself leaks PII | includes the matched span | Keep counts, not values | Variants | Variant | When | |---|---| | Allow-list (above) | Default for structured inputs; strict and auditable | | LLM-classifier triage | Pass suspicious input to a separate cheap model that scores attack-likelihood | | Sandboxed eval | Tool outputs run in a container; sanitize before piping back to the LLM | | Constitutional / guardrail libraries | LlamaGuard, Microsoft Presidio for PII, OpenAI Moderation | | Two-LLM pattern | Privileged planner + unprivileged executor, the latter never sees user text directly | Frameworks & Models | Framework | Notes | |---|---| | Direct (above) | Maximum control; small audit surface | | Pydantic | Schema validation for structured inputs | | Microsoft Presidio | Production-grade PII detection | | LlamaGuard / NeMo Guardrails | Classifier-based content moderation | | OpenAI Moderation API | Cheap safety classifier | Model Comparison | Capability | claude-opus-4-5 | gpt-4o | claude-haiku-4-5 | |---|---|---|---| | Resists prompt injection | 4 | 4 | 4 | | As an attack-classifier | 4 | 5 | 5 | | Cost-as-classifier | 2 | 3 | 5 | Related Skills - Output Guardrails — outbound counterpart - Permission Checking — authorisation layer above sanitization - Sandboxed Execution — isolation when the input becomes code - Audit Logging — record every refused payload Changelog | Date | Version | Change | |---|---|---| | 2025-03 | v1 | Stub | | 2026-04 | v3 | Battle-tested: 4-layer defence, prompt-injection regex, path/SQL/shell escaping, PII redaction, model comparison |

title: JWT Validation
description: Validate JSON Web Tokens by verifying the declared algorithm, signature, and claims in a fixed order so access decisions rest on cryptographic evidence instead of unverified payload strings.
body: JWT Validation Category: Security | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A JWT is three base64url parts and a lot of trust. Skipping the verification order — algorithm, signature, then claims — is how alg=none and algorithm-confusion attacks happen. This skill defines validation as a fail-closed sequence: pin the expected algorithm, verify the signature with a constant-time comparison, then evaluate claims (expiry, audience, issuer) with an injectable clock. When to Use Use whenever an agent or service accepts a JWT as evidence of identity or authorization, before any decision is made on its contents. Do not use JWTs as long-term session storage; validation is per-request evidence, and revocation needs server-side state. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The compact serialized JWT | | | | Yes | The verification key for the pinned algorithm | | | | Yes | The single algorithm accepted; anything else is rejected | | | | No | Injectable clock for expiry claim evaluation | Procedure 1. Pin the expected algorithm in configuration; accept only that value from the token header. 2. Reject tokens whose header declares a different algorithm, a missing algorithm, or none — before any signature math runs. 3. Verify the signature over the exact signing input (header.payload) with a constant-time comparison. 4. Only after the signature holds, parse the payload and evaluate claims: expiry against the injected clock, audience, issuer. 5. Fail closed on every check; a token that fails any step is rejected without partial trust. 6. Log the validation outcome — verified or rejected with reason — without logging the token itself. 7. Never decode the payload for authorization before the signature check passes; unsigned payload is attacker input. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The verified payload claims | | | | Whether the token passed the full sequence | | | | First failed check when rejected | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Algorithm confusion | Attacker-chosen alg trusted from the header | Pin one expected algorithm in configuration | | alg=none acceptance | Unsigned tokens treated as valid | Reject missing or none algorithms before signature math | | Claim skipping | Payload trusted without signature verification | Verify the signature before parsing any claims | | Expiry clock skew | Wall clock read during validation | Inject the clock and evaluate exp deterministically | | Token leakage in logs | Rejected tokens logged verbatim | Log outcomes and reasons, never the token string | Security and Authority Boundary Token validation is the enforcement point, not the policy. A cryptographically valid token still bounds only what its claims assert: authority comes from the issuer’s policy, and every downstream action must pass its own permission checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. RFC 7519 defining JSON Web Tokens (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519). 2. The jwt.io introduction to JWT structure and signature verification (https://jwt.io/introduction). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Least-Privilege Scoping
description: Scope every agent action to the minimum permission set the current step needs, with deny-by-default grants, explicit expiry, and per-action audit records so lateral movement stays contained.
body: Least-Privilege Scoping Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential that can do everything will eventually do something you did not intend. Least-privilege scoping treats authorization as a narrow, expiring grant instead of ambient power: each step names the capability and resources it needs, receives exactly that, and loses it on completion. Deny-by-default evaluation, per-grant expiry, and revocation mean a compromised step can only reach what that step was already allowed to touch. When to Use Use when an agent or automation holds credentials that can read, write, or delete beyond the single action it is performing — tool tokens, cloud roles, or API scopes. Do not use as a substitute for permission checks at the point of use; scoping narrows what a grant covers, and each call still needs its own decision. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The capability the step wants to invoke | | | | Yes | The specific objects the action targets | | | | Yes | The standing policy grants are checked against | | | | No | Lifetime of the grant; defaults to the step boundary | Procedure 1. Start from deny-by-default: an unlisted action is rejected before any tool call is attempted. 2. Enumerate the exact capability and resource IDs the step needs; wildcard scopes require explicit justification. 3. Check the request against the standing policy, then issue a grant scoped to those resources with an expiry. 4. Evaluate each subsequent tool call against the active grant — resource by resource, not by coarse role. 5. Revoke the grant at step completion, and treat any post-revocation call as a policy violation to log. 6. Record issued grants and their use in an audit trail that answers: who, what scope, which resources, how long. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The issued grant, or null when denied | | | | Allow or deny with the policy rule that decided it | | | | Issuer, scope, resources, expiry, and usage count | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Standing admin token | One long-lived credential reused across steps | Issue per-step grants with expiry | | Wildcard scope | Convenience grants like resource | Require explicit justification and review | | Scope creep | Step reuses a grant for adjacent resources | Evaluate each call against the grant, not the role | | Orphaned grants | Completion paths that skip revocation | Revoke in a cleanup path and audit usage after expiry | | Silent denies | Denials logged nowhere | Record every decision with the deciding rule | Security and Authority Boundary Scoping limits what a compromised step can reach; it does not decide whether an action is correct. A perfectly scoped grant can still perform a wrong action — purpose review and destructive-action approval remain separate, human-owned checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. RFC 6749 defining scoped OAuth 2.0 access (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749). 2. Wikipedia's overview of the principle of least privilege (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principleofleast_privilege). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: MCP OAuth Authentication
description: Authenticate remote MCP and agent tools with OAuth while keeping credentials outside skill definitions and enforcing explicit authorization boundaries.
body: MCP OAuth Authentication Description Authenticate a remote MCP server or agent-facing service through OAuth without embedding credentials in a skill, tool schema, repository, or generated artifact. Treat authentication and authorization as separate contracts: OAuth establishes identity/session state; authorization determines which tools and operations the agent may invoke. When to Use - A remote MCP server requires OAuth/OIDC authentication. - Tokens rotate or expire during long-running agent sessions. - A skill must describe authentication requirements without carrying secrets. - Tool availability depends on the authenticated principal. Inputs / Outputs | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Authorization-server metadata, client configuration, redirect policy, requested scopes, runtime identity, and protected-resource metadata when available. | | Outputs | Authenticated session state, token metadata needed for runtime use, granted scopes, and explicit authorization status. | | Never output | Client secrets, refresh tokens, access tokens, or other credentials in skill text, logs, prompts, or generated indexes. | Procedure 1. Discover protected-resource and authorization-server metadata from authoritative configuration. 2. Validate redirect URI, issuer, audience/resource, PKCE requirements, and requested scopes. 3. Complete authorization using the approved client and user interaction boundary. 4. Store tokens only in the runtime credential store; never in skill files or prompts. 5. Before each privileged tool call, verify that the identity and granted scope authorize the operation. 6. On expiry or invalidation, fail closed and require the defined re-authentication path. 7. Record non-secret authentication evidence sufficient to diagnose failures. Runnable Example Failure Modes - OAuth succeeds but the MCP session exposes no authorized tools. - Stale or revoked refresh token. - Redirect URI mismatch. - Wrong audience/resource or scope. - Authentication succeeds but authorization is insufficient. - Tokens or authorization codes leak into logs or model context. Security Boundary OAuth does not grant permission to perform arbitrary tool actions. Tool authorization remains authoritative and must be evaluated independently. Evidence Public 2026 ecosystem evidence includes recurring MCP OAuth interoperability and failure reports, including remote MCP authentication contract discussions and client-side OAuth failures. These are demand corroboration, not adoption measurements. Related - mcp-tool.md - permission-checking.md - approval-before-destructive-tools.md - secret-scanning.md

title: Password Hashing
description: Store passwords as salted, iterated hashes with a declared cost parameter and constant-time verification so credential material is never stored in recoverable form.
body: Password Hashing Category: Security | Level: basic | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A password stored in plaintext is a breach waiting for a date; a password hashed once without salt is a rainbow-table lookup. This skill defines credential storage as a contract: a per-user random salt, a slow memory-hard or iterated hash function, a declared cost parameter, and constant-time comparison on verification. The stored record keeps the algorithm and cost with the digest so migration to stronger parameters is possible. When to Use Use whenever a system stores a user-provided secret for later verification — passwords, PINs, API secrets — and must never recover the plaintext. Do not use for non-recoverable-but-high-entropy tokens like OAuth client secrets; those can be stored as plain fast hashes since entropy does the work. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The secret being stored or verified | | | | Yes | Per-user random salt, generated at first store | | | | Yes | Iteration count or hardness parameter, declared in policy | | | | Yes | The existing record for verification | Procedure 1. Generate a fresh random salt per credential at first store; reuse of salts across users is a defect. 2. Derive the digest with a salted slow hash and a cost parameter declared in policy, never chosen per call. 3. Store the salt, cost, and algorithm identifier alongside the digest so verification and migration are unambiguous. 4. Verify by re-deriving with the stored parameters and comparing in constant time; early-exit comparison leaks timing. 5. Reject passwords below the declared minimum entropy policy before hashing; the hash cannot repair a weak secret. 6. Rehash transparently on next successful login when the policy cost rises, and record the migration. 7. Never log the password, its digest, or the comparison result beyond pass/fail. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The stored credential record | | | | Constant-time comparison result | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Rainbow-table recovery | Digests computed without per-user salt | Generate a random salt per credential | | Cost stagnation | Iteration count frozen as hardware speeds up | Raise the policy cost and rehash on next login | | Timing leaks | Comparison short-circuits on first mismatch | Compare derived digests in constant time | | Weak secrets admitted | Short passwords hashed as-is | Enforce a minimum-length and entropy policy before hashing | | Digest logging | Credential records written to logs | Log only pass/fail outcomes, never the material | Security and Authority Boundary Hashing protects stored credentials, not the channel or the policy: transport still needs TLS, verification still needs rate limiting, and a verified password grants only what its account’s policy allows. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/PasswordStorageCheat_Sheet.html). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of Argon2, the winner of the Password Hashing Competition (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argon2). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Permission Checking
description: Authorize agent actions against explicit identities, capabilities, resource scopes, and policy constraints before executing tools or accessing data.
body: Permission Checking Description Permission checking is the authorization boundary between an agent's intent and an executable action. Evaluate the authenticated actor, requested action, target resource, granted scope, and policy constraints before invoking a tool or mutating state. Prefer deny-by-default authorization with narrowly scoped capabilities. Authentication identifies the actor; authorization decides what that actor may do. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Authenticated agent/service identity | | | string | yes | Requested operation | | | string | yes | Target resource | | | set[str] | yes | Granted capabilities/scopes | | | dict | yes | Resource and action constraints | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | bool | Whether the action may proceed | | | string | Safe decision explanation | | | string | Policy version used for the decision | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Privilege escalation | Broad wildcard permissions | Use least-privilege scopes and resource constraints | | Confused deputy | Agent uses a privileged service on behalf of an untrusted caller | Propagate caller identity and intent | | TOCTOU | Resource changes between check and use | Revalidate immediately before sensitive operations | | Stale grants | Long-lived cached authorization | Bound cache lifetime and invalidate on policy changes | | Missing tenant boundary | Resource ID alone does not encode ownership | Include tenant/owner scope in authorization | | Fail-open behavior | Authorization service unavailable | Default to deny for sensitive actions | Design Rules 1. Keep authentication and authorization separate. 2. Use explicit action/resource scopes. 3. Deny when the identity or policy cannot be established. 4. Revalidate high-risk operations immediately before execution. 5. Log authorization outcomes without leaking sensitive policy data. 6. Test both allowed and denied paths. References - OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/AuthorizationCheatSheet.html - OWASP API Security Top 10: https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/ Evidence status: guidance is grounded in the cited OWASP authorization material; no framework-specific security guarantee is implied.
