title: Privacy Preservation
description: Minimize, detect, and redact sensitive personal data before agent inputs, outputs, logs, storage, or external transmission.
body: Privacy Preservation Description Privacy preservation reduces unnecessary collection and propagation of personal or sensitive information through an agent system. Apply data minimization first, then detect and transform sensitive values at explicit trust boundaries. Pattern matching is useful for known formats but is incomplete. Production systems should combine deterministic detection with domain-specific validation, access controls, retention rules, and appropriate privacy governance. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Content to inspect | | | mapping | yes | Named detection patterns | | | string | no | Redaction marker | | | dict | no | Minimal policy context | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | Sanitized content | | | list[str] | Detected data classes | | | int | Number of replacements | Runnable Example The example uses deliberately generic test data. It is not a complete PII detector. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Missed PII | Format is not covered by a regex | Add domain-aware detectors and test representative samples | | Over-redaction | Pattern is too broad | Use validation and context before replacing | | Sensitive logs | Original input is copied before redaction | Redact before logging and before external transmission | | Re-identification | Several harmless fields combine into identity | Apply data minimization and access controls | | Unicode bypass | Normalization differences | Normalize consistently before detection | | Retention leak | Redacted output retained indefinitely | Apply explicit retention and deletion policy | Design Rules - Collect only what the task requires. - Redact before crossing a trust boundary. - Never assume a regex provides complete privacy protection. - Keep detection results free of the sensitive values they describe. - Define retention, access, and deletion policies. - Test international formats where relevant. References - NIST Privacy Framework: https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework - OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SecretsManagementCheat_Sheet.html Evidence status: references support privacy and secret-handling practices; no legal compliance determination is implied. title: Rate Limiting
description: Bound agent and tool request frequency to control abuse, runaway loops, concurrency spikes, and resource cost.
body: Rate Limiting Description Rate limiting constrains how frequently an agent, user, tool, or endpoint may perform an operation during a defined interval. In agent systems it is also a control against runaway tool loops and unbounded external API cost. Choose a limiter according to the failure mode: token bucket for bursts, sliding windows for straightforward request counts, or provider-side quotas when the external service is authoritative. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Identity/resource bucket | | | int | yes | Maximum allowed rate | | | float | yes | Time window or refill interval | | | int | no | Weighted request cost | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:| | | bool | Whether the request may proceed | | | float | Approximate delay when blocked | Runnable Example For distributed systems, use an atomic shared store or the upstream provider's quota mechanism; an in-memory limiter is process-local. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Bypass | Key can be changed by the caller | Derive identity from authenticated context | | Burst overload | Fixed window allows boundary bursts | Use sliding window or token bucket | | Distributed race | Multiple workers update counters independently | Use atomic centralized state | | Retry storm | Clients retry immediately after denial | Return bounded retry information and use backoff | | Starvation | One tenant consumes the whole quota | Partition limits by tenant/agent/resource | | Clock issues | Wall-clock adjustments | Use monotonic time for local windows | Design Rules - Apply limits at the earliest authoritative boundary. - Rate-limit expensive tools separately from cheap operations. - Combine request limits with concurrency and budget limits. - Make blocked requests observable without logging sensitive payloads. - Use provider-specific quotas when they are stricter than local limits. References - RFC 6585 (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585 - OWASP API Security: https://owasp.org/API-Security/ Evidence status: implementation guidance is grounded in HTTP/API rate-control conventions; no universal safe limit is claimed. Related Skills - Budget Management - Retry Backoff - Permission Checking

title: Rollback / Undo
description: Make high-impact agent mutations reversible with explicit snapshots, transaction boundaries, postcondition checks, and safe rollback semantics.
body: Rollback / Undo Description Rollback protects against failed or undesired agent actions by preserving enough state to restore a known-good condition. It is appropriate for multi-step mutations where partial completion could leave inconsistent state. Rollback is not equivalent to deletion or backup. A rollback design must define what state is captured, when it is captured, which operations are reversible, and how concurrent changes are handled. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | callable/object | yes | Reversible mutation | | | object | yes | State required to restore the prior state | | | object | no | Preconditions/postconditions | | | dict | no | Retry, timeout, and recovery rules | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | or | | | string | Failure reason when recovery occurs | | | string | Correlation identifier | Runnable Example The example is in-memory and does not address concurrent writers. Production systems need transactional storage, version checks, or compensating operations appropriate to the target system. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Partial rollback | Not all side effects are reversible | Use transactions or explicit compensating actions | | Stale snapshot | Another actor changed state after snapshot | Use version/ETag checks and conflict detection | | Rollback failure | Recovery path has its own failure | Make recovery observable and escalate to an operator | | Irreversible side effect | Email/payment/external call cannot be undone | Require approval before execution and use compensating actions | | Lost snapshot | Snapshot stored in same failure domain | Store recovery state separately with controlled access | | Silent divergence | State restores but external side effects remain | Verify postconditions and record residual effects | Design Rules - Capture state immediately before mutation. - Bind rollback to the exact action/version being reverted. - Prefer native transactions when available. - Use compensating actions for irreversible external effects. - Never claim successful rollback without a postcondition check. - Audit both commit and rollback outcomes. References - OWASP Transaction Authorization guidance: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/TransactionAuthorizationCheat_Sheet.html - Python context manager protocol: https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#context-managers Evidence status: guidance is grounded in transaction and recovery principles; rollback completeness is system-specific. title: Sandboxed Execution
description: Execute untrusted agent-generated code inside a separately enforced isolation boundary with resource, filesystem, network, and timeout controls.
body: Sandboxed Execution Description Sandboxed execution separates untrusted code from the agent host and limits what the code can read, write, execute, and connect to. A timeout alone is not a sandbox. Production isolation should be enforced by an operating-system, container, VM, or dedicated execution service boundary. Treat the sandbox policy as part of the security contract: filesystem visibility, network egress, CPU/memory limits, process privileges, runtime image, and cleanup must all be explicit. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Untrusted program | | | int | yes | Maximum execution duration | | | string | yes | Explicit network policy such as | | | path | no | Isolated working directory | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---:| | | string | Captured standard output | | | string | Captured standard error | | | int | Process result | | | bool | Whether the execution exceeded the limit | Runnable Example This example demonstrates timeout-bounded subprocess execution only. It is not a security sandbox and must not be used as isolation for hostile code without an additional OS/container/VM boundary. title: Secret Scanning
description: Detect credentials and secret-like material before it reaches source control, logs, prompts, artifacts, or external systems, with validation and remediation controls.
body: Secret Scanning Description Secret scanning detects API keys, access tokens, private keys, passwords, and other credential material before it propagates through an agent system. Pattern matching is useful for fast detection, but production controls should combine provider-aware detectors, validation, push protection, and incident response. Never store a real secret in a skill example or test fixture. Inputs / Outputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---:|---| | | string | yes | Content to scan | | | mapping | no | Custom patterns in addition to provider detectors | | | dict | no | File/source metadata used for policy | | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | list | Secret type and location metadata without exposing the secret | | | bool | Whether policy requires stopping the operation | | | list[str] | Actions such as revoke, rotate, or remove | Runnable Example The patterns are illustrative and intentionally incomplete. Provider-specific scanners should be preferred where available. Failure Modes | Failure | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | False negative | New or provider-specific token format | Keep detectors updated and use provider validation | | False positive | Random high-entropy text matches | Use contextual validation and allowlisted test fixtures | | Secret exposure in findings | Scanner stores the matched value | Store type/location/hash, not the credential | | Already leaked secret | Detection occurs after publication | Revoke/rotate immediately and remove from affected history | | Bypass abuse | Developer bypasses push protection | Require documented reason and review for exceptions | | Secret in generated artifacts | CI only scans source files | Scan generated files and release artifacts too | Design Rules - Scan before commit and again in CI. - Prefer provider-aware detectors and push protection. - Never print the matched secret in logs. - Treat detection as an incident trigger, not proof that the credential is harmless. - Rotate/revoke exposed credentials before cleanup work. - Keep test fixtures obviously synthetic. title: Session Management
description: Create, rotate, and expire agent sessions with server-side state, opaque identifiers, and re-authentication on privilege change so identity evidence stays fresh instead of indefinitely trusted.
body: Session Management Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A session is a server-side record plus a token that points at it; the token is evidence, not the identity itself. Session management keeps the record authoritative: opaque identifiers, rotation on login and privilege change, idle plus absolute expiry, and invalidation that actually invalidates. A leaked old token stops working because the record moved on — not because someone hoped it would. When to Use Use when an agent or service maintains state across requests on behalf of an identity — web sessions, agent run sessions, or API tokens issued per engagement. Do not use sessions as long-term authorization storage; a session says who someone was recently, and privilege should be re-established when the risk window grows. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Authenticated identity the session represents | | | | Yes | Max gap between requests before expiry | | | | Yes | Max total lifetime regardless of activity | | | | Yes | Server-side session state | Procedure 1. Store session state server-side; issue only an opaque, high-entropy identifier to the client. 2. Set both idle and absolute expiry; whichever fires first ends the session. 3. Rotate the identifier on login, on privilege change, and on any suspected disclosure. 4. Invalidate the server record on logout; a client-side cookie clear is not invalidation. 5. Require re-authentication for sensitive operations even inside a valid session. 6. Record creation, rotation, and expiry events in the audit log with actor and time. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Opaque identifier for the active session | | | | active, expiredidle, expiredabsolute, or revoked | | | | Session lifecycle events for auditing | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Client-side session trust | State stored where the client can edit it | Keep the record server-side; issue opaque IDs | | Eternal sessions | Only idle expiry configured | Enforce absolute TTL on top of idle timeout | | Missing rotation | Same identifier across privilege changes | Rotate on login and privilege change | | Predictable identifiers | Sequential or low-entropy session IDs | Use high-entropy random identifiers | | Logout theater | Cookie cleared client-side, record alive | Invalidate the server record on logout | Security and Authority Boundary A session carries recent identity evidence; it is not proof of continued presence or intent. Re-authentication, step-up verification, and the decision to trust a session at all remain with the identity provider and the calling service. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SessionManagementCheat_Sheet.html). 2. MDN's reference on the Set-Cookie header and session attributes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie). title: Threat Modeling
description: Model a system’s components against a structured threat taxonomy with per-interaction mitigations so security work is driven by an enumerated, reviewable threat list instead of ad-hoc paranoia.
body: Threat Modeling Category: Security | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Security without enumeration becomes either paralysis or theater. Threat modeling imposes order: decompose the system into components and interactions, walk a fixed taxonomy — spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege — per component, and record a mitigation or an explicit acceptance for every threat found. The model is the artifact; fixes are tracked against it. When to Use Use when designing or changing a system that handles untrusted input, credentials, or privileged operations, and when the security posture must be explainable to a reviewer. Do not use as a substitute for testing; a model guides where to test and review, and unverified mitigations are intentions, not protections. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | System decomposition under review | | | | Yes | Recorded threats and their handling per component | | | | Yes | The threat classes walked per component | Procedure 1. Decompose the system into components and their interactions before naming a single threat. 2. Walk the declared taxonomy for every component, in a fixed order, so classes are never skipped silently. 3. Record each threat with its entry point and a mitigation, or an explicit accepted-risk note — never an empty cell. 4. Treat missing mitigations as findings with owners and deadlines, not as future hopes. 5. Update the model whenever the decomposition changes; a model of the old system protects nothing. 6. Re-test mitigations that the model claims; an untested mitigation is a documented guess. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Enumerated threats and their handling status | | | | Taxonomy classes with no recorded interaction | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Taxonomy skipping | Only familiar threat classes examined | Walk the full taxonomy per component in fixed order | | Empty-cell acceptance | Threats noted without mitigation or decision | Require a mitigation or an explicit accepted-risk note | | Stale model | System changed, model unchanged | Re-model on every decomposition change | | Untested mitigations | Controls recorded but never verified | Track mitigations as testable findings with owners | | Paralysis inversion | Enumeration replaces remediation | Every finding needs an owner and a deadline | Security and Authority Boundary The model itself is sensitive: it enumerates exactly where the system is soft. Treat threat models as need-to-know artifacts and protect them with the same care as the codebase. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/ThreatModelingCheatSheet.html). 2. Wikipedia’s overview of the STRIDE threat classification (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STRIDE(security)). title: Capability-Based Skill Selection
description: Select and sequence canonical skills for a task by matching required capabilities, discriminating competing candidates, checking eligibility and dependencies, and using execution evidence to choose the next skill.
body: Capability-Based Skill Selection Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Capability-based skill selection turns a task into an explicit skill decision rather than treating retrieval as selection. It identifies the capabilities required by the current task, compares competing canonical skills, checks evidence, compatibility, authority, and prerequisites, then selects an executable skill and determines what should happen next from the observed result. This skill is intended for agent runtimes and orchestrators that consume a canonical skill registry. It does not replace search, the registry, dependency graph, or execution runtime. When to Use Use when an agent must decide which skill to invoke for a concrete task and more than one plausible skill may match. Do not use this as a substitute for simple deterministic lookup when the canonical skill ID is already known. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | / | Yes | Current task, objective, or unresolved subtask | | | | Yes | Project state, constraints, environment, prior results, and available tools | | | | Yes | Candidate canonical skills discovered from the registry/search boundary | | | | No | Required capabilities already inferred by an upstream goal/capability resolver | | | | No | Skills already executed successfully for the current task | | | | No | Available benchmark, provenance, freshness, compatibility, or runtime evidence | Selection Procedure 1. Normalize the task into the capabilities required to make progress. 2. Resolve candidate skills through the canonical registry and reject unknown or non-canonical IDs. 3. Separate direct matches from merely related skills. 4. Compare competing candidates using task fit, required capability coverage, eligibility, compatibility, evidence quality, freshness, and known limitations. 5. Resolve mandatory prerequisites before selecting a dependent skill. 6. Prefer the smallest sufficient skill set; do not select skills merely because they are related. 7. Produce an explicit selection rationale and rejected-candidate reasons. 8. Invoke the selected executable skill only when its prerequisites and authority conditions are satisfied. 9. Verify the result against the task acceptance criteria. 10. If verification fails, classify the failure and select the next justified skill or recovery action rather than blindly repeating the same invocation. 11. Stop when the task is verified complete, blocked by an external condition, or requires escalation. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Canonical skill ID/version selected for the current step | | | | Dependencies that must be satisfied before invocation | | | | Plausible candidates rejected with explicit reasons | | | | Next invocation, verification, recovery, escalation, or terminal decision | | | | Evidence needed to verify the selected action | | | | , , or | Decision Contract A valid selection must answer all of these questions: - What capability is required now? - Which canonical skill satisfies it? - Why is it better than the competing candidates? - Which prerequisites must run first? - Is the skill eligible in the current context? - What evidence will verify the invocation? - What result causes the agent to invoke the next skill? - What result causes recovery, substitution, escalation, or termination? A skill must not be selected solely because it contains matching keywords. Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Retrieval mistaken for selection | Top search result is treated as authoritative | Evaluate competing candidates against task requirements | | Ambiguous candidates | Several skills satisfy overlapping capabilities | Require explicit discrimination reasons and tie-break evidence | | Hidden prerequisite | Dependent skill selected before required capability exists | Resolve prerequisite/dependency graph before invocation | | Stale or weak evidence | Candidate has outdated or insufficient proof | Prefer fresher, provenance-backed evidence and surface the gap | | Ineligible candidate | Compatibility, authority, or runtime constraints are unmet | Reject candidate and continue with an eligible alternative | | Repeated failed invocation | Same action is retried without new evidence | Classify failure and choose recovery, substitution, or escalation | | Premature completion | Selection succeeds but task outcome is unverified | Require outcome evidence before | | Over-selection | Agent invokes related skills without causal need | Select the smallest sufficient skill set | Security and Authority Boundary Skill selection does not grant permissions. The selected skill must execute only within its declared authority, security boundary, compatibility constraints, and available runtime permissions. High-impact or irreversible actions must remain subject to the governing approval and policy controls of the consuming agent runtime. Evidence This skill is motivated by two complementary evidence classes: 1. Public demand signals around automated task breakdown, agent orchestration, and assignment based on skills/performance. 2. Skills Tree's current behavioral evaluation gap: retrieval quality is now measured, but task-specific skill discrimination, dependency-aware selection, invocation, and next-skill decisions are not yet comprehensively benchmarked. The demand evidence is recorded in ; it is not treated as popularity or adoption data. title: Circuit Breaking
description: Stop calling a failing dependency after a threshold, fail fast while the circuit is open, and probe with trial calls before closing so one slow or broken service cannot take the caller down with it.
body: Circuit Breaking Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Retries have a limit beyond which they become part of the outage. A circuit breaker converts persistent failure into a fast, local decision: after a threshold of consecutive failures the circuit opens and calls short-circuit immediately; after a reset window a limited probe tests the water; only a successful probe closes the circuit again. The caller sheds load and stays responsive while the dependency recovers. When to Use Use around any remote dependency whose failure or latency can exhaust the caller — model APIs, databases, downstream services called on a request path. Do not wrap workloads where every call must succeed; a breaker that skips required work turns degraded mode into silent data loss. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The dependency the breaker guards | | | | Yes | Consecutive failures that open the circuit | | | | Yes | Open period before a probe is allowed | | | | Yes | The single trial call used in half-open state | Procedure 1. Track consecutive failures per dependency, not globally; one bad endpoint should not open every circuit. 2. When the count reaches the threshold, open the circuit and fail fast — no call, no queue, no waiting. 3. While open, answer immediately with a defined degradation result, never with an exception shape callers have not agreed to. 4. After the reset timeout, move to half-open and allow exactly one probe call; the rest still fail fast. 5. Close on a successful probe and reset the counter; re-open and restart the timer on a failed probe. 6. Export circuit state as a metric; state transitions are the outage narrative. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Current circuit state | | | | What the breaker did with this call | | | | Consecutive failures at decision time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Flapping | Threshold or timeout tuned to noise | Calibrate to the dependency's real error profile | | No half-open state | Open circuits close on faith after the timer | Require one successful probe before closing | | Shared breakers | One circuit for heterogeneous calls | Track per dependency and per call class | | State lost on restart | Counters held in process memory only | Persist or re-warm counters; treat restart as probe | | Silent degradation | Short-circuits invisible to callers and operators | Export state metrics and log every transition | Security and Authority Boundary The breaker protects the caller's time and threads; it does not repair the dependency or verify its recovery. Post-incident validation of the dependency stays with its owner, and an open circuit is a degraded state, never a healthy one. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Circuit Breaker pattern on microservices.io (https://microservices.io/patterns/reliability/circuit-breaker.html). 2. Wikipedia's overview of fault tolerance (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_tolerance). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Cost-Aware Model Routing
description: Select an eligible model using task quality requirements, measured capability, latency constraints, and observed cost rather than defaulting every task to the most expensive model.
body: Cost-Aware Model Routing Description Route a task to the least-cost eligible model that satisfies quality, capability, latency, context, tool-use, and reliability constraints. Cost-aware routing is constrained optimization, not unconditional selection of the cheapest model. When to Use - Multiple models can satisfy the same task. - Model cost or latency materially affects runtime economics. - A workload has measurable quality requirements and fallback models. - Agent execution needs explicit routing and fallback policy. Inputs / Outputs | Area | Contract | |---|---| | Inputs | Task requirements, candidate models, capability evidence, context/tool constraints, observed quality, latency, and current pricing/cost telemetry. | | Outputs | Selected model, rejected candidates with reasons, routing evidence, and fallback policy. | | Safety | A cheaper model must never bypass capability, security, or authorization requirements. | Procedure 1. Translate the task into hard requirements and measurable quality thresholds. 2. Remove models lacking required capability, context, tool, safety, or availability constraints. 3. Compare eligible models using measured quality, latency, and observed cost. 4. Select the least-cost model that satisfies hard requirements. 5. Preserve a deterministic fallback policy for timeout, quota, or quality failure. 6. Measure actual outcome and cost; update routing evidence only from observed results. Runnable Example Failure Modes - Choosing a cheap but incapable model. - Using stale or guessed pricing. - Optimizing average cost while violating tail-latency or quality constraints. - Routing sensitive work to a model without required security controls. - Retrying across models without preserving task state or evidence. Boundary Routing selects among already-authorized models. It does not grant model access, change data permissions, or weaken safety policy. Evidence Public 2026 ecosystem work requests multi-model routing and cost optimization, including MCP inference routing and cost-aware LLM gateways. title: Dead-Letter Queuing
description: Route repeatedly failing messages to a dedicated dead-letter queue with full failure metadata so poison payloads are quarantined for inspection instead of blocking the pipeline or vanishing.
body: Dead-Letter Queuing Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Some messages cannot be processed, and retrying them forever converts one bad payload into a stuck pipeline. Dead-letter queuing draws the line: after a bounded number of attempts, the message moves to a dedicated dead-letter queue carrying its attempts, errors, and original payload. The main queue keeps flowing, the failure stays inspectable, and a replay path exists for after the cause is fixed. When to Use Use with any task queue or event pipeline where a malformed or failing message must not block subsequent messages. Do not use a dead-letter queue as a trash bin: entries are quarantined pending diagnosis, and unbounded growth without review hides an outage in plain sight. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The message being processed | | | | Yes | Processing attempts before dead-lettering | | | | Yes | Prior failures for this message id | | | | Yes | The dead-letter destination with its metadata schema | Procedure 1. Track attempts per message id; the count travels with the message, not with worker memory. 2. On each failure, record the error and timestamp; retry only while under the attempt bound. 3. At the bound, move the message to the dead-letter queue with its payload, attempts, and error history attached. 4. Surface dead-letter depth and entry age as operational alarms; a growing dead-letter queue is a failing pipeline. 5. Diagnose entries before replay: fix the consumer or correct the payload, then replay deliberately. 6. Re-run replayed messages through the same accounting so a still-failing replay dead-letters again, visibly. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Disposition of the message | | | | The quarantined message with metadata when dead-lettered | | | | Attempts made before the disposition | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Infinite retry | No attempt bound on failing messages | Count attempts per id and enforce the bound | | Silent drop | Failures discarded without a dead-letter queue | Every non-processed message lands somewhere inspectable | | Unreviewed backlog | The dead-letter queue grows with no alarm watching it | Alarm on depth and oldest entry age | | Blind replay | Messages replayed before the cause is fixed | Fix first, replay deliberately, re-account on failure | | Metadata loss | Entry stored without errors or attempt count | Attach payload, attempts, and error history to the entry | Security and Authority Boundary The dead-letter queue quarantines and preserves; it does not diagnose. Root-cause analysis, payload correction, and the decision to replay remain operator work, with the quarantine treated as evidence, not as a fix. title: Deadline Propagation
description: Carry one absolute end-time deadline through every orchestration hop so each step budgets its remaining time, children inherit a tightened deadline, and late results are discarded rather than delivered.
body: Deadline Propagation Category: Orchestration | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Relative timeouts do not compose: three sequential steps with a 5-second timeout each can stall a caller for 15 seconds. Deadline propagation fixes the arithmetic by carrying one absolute end time: each hop computes remaining time against the same clock, children receive the tighter of their own budget and the parent's remaining time, and results that arrive after the deadline are discarded instead of patched into the run late. When to Use Use in any multi-hop orchestration — service calls, subagent trees, pipelines — where a caller's total wait must stay bounded. Do not substitute per-hop timeouts without checking the sum; a chain of local limits is not a global one. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The absolute end time for the whole run | | | | Yes | Injectable current time for deterministic decisions | | | | No | The step's own preferred local budget | | | | No | Downstream hops inheriting the deadline | Procedure 1. Set one absolute deadline at run start, from the caller's wall-clock budget; it is a timestamp, not a duration. 2. At each hop, compute remaining time as deadline minus now; a hop with no remaining time fails fast without starting. 3. Give each child the tighter of its own budget and the parent's remaining time minus the parent's reserve. 4. Reject late results even if they eventually complete; a result after the deadline is not a result for this run. 5. Record per-step time consumption so postmortems can show where the budget went. 6. Reserve a margin for serialization and cleanup; a deadline with no reserve fails at the packaging step. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Time left at the decision point | | | | The tightened deadline handed to a child | | | | Whether the step or result is usable | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Relative-only budgets | Per-step timeouts whose sum exceeds the caller's budget | Propagate one absolute deadline | | Deadline-blind queues | Enqueued work starts without checking the clock | Check remaining time at dequeue, not just enqueue | | Children outliving parents | Children keep their local budget after the parent expired | Hand children the tighter of own budget and parent remaining | | Late results accepted | Stragglers patched in after expiry | Classify post-deadline results as late and discard | | No time accounting | Postmortems cannot say where time went | Record per-step consumption against budget | Security and Authority Boundary Deadline propagation bounds wall-clock time; it does not certify the quality of what was rushed to fit. Quality gates, evaluation, and review apply the same standards regardless of how much budget a step had. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The gRPC core concepts documentation on deadlines and cancellation (https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/core-concepts/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of timeouts in computing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeout_%28computing%29). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Documentation Drift Resolution
description: Detect, reconcile, and document drift between implementation and authoritative repository documentation.
body: Documentation Drift Resolution Description Reconcile implementation state with the repository's authoritative documentation without inventing history or silently changing strategic decisions. Documentation is updated only from verified implementation and decision evidence. 1. Identify the authoritative document for the affected concern. 2. Inspect live implementation and verification evidence. 3. Classify the mismatch as stale documentation, stale implementation, or unresolved strategic conflict. 4. Correct authoritative documentation to verified state when the decision is already established. 5. Record historically significant changes in the decision log. 6. Update only the relevant current-state, roadmap, architecture, security, testing, or deployment documents. 7. Do not declare completion until the documentation gate passes. title: Idempotency Keys
description: Assign client-generated idempotency keys to state-changing requests so retries and at-least-once delivery produce one effect, with duplicate calls returning the recorded first result.
body: Idempotency Keys Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description At-least-once delivery means the same request will sometimes arrive twice; idempotency keys turn that from a bug into a non-event. The client attaches a unique key to each operation intent, the server checks the key before executing, and a replayed key returns the stored first response instead of executing again. The stored response plus a payload fingerprint closes the gap between "same key" and "same request". When to Use Use for any state-changing request that may be retried — payment calls, task creation, webhook handlers, queue consumers under at-least-once semantics. Do not bother for pure reads or naturally idempotent operations; the machinery earns its cost only where duplicates have effects. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Client-generated unique key for this operation intent | | | | Yes | Digest of the payload the key refers to | | | | Yes | Server-side record of executed keys | | | | Yes | How long replayed keys resolve to stored results | Procedure 1. Generate the key client-side, unique per operation intent — not per session, not per process. 2. Before executing, look the key up: a hit with a matching fingerprint returns the stored response; a hit with a mismatching fingerprint is an error. 3. On a miss, execute once, then store the response keyed by the key and fingerprint. 4. Keep the TTL at least as long as the client's longest retry window; shorter expiry quietly reintroduces duplicates. 5. Keep keys out of URLs and logs; they identify operations and may correlate to sensitive intents. 6. Treat in-flight keys as locked: concurrent duplicate calls wait for the first execution rather than racing it. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The first execution's response, returned on every replay | | | | Whether this call returned a stored result | | | | When the key record expires | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Key reuse across payloads | Same key sent with different request bodies | Store and compare a payload fingerprint | | Server-generated keys | Key minted per attempt, not per intent | Generate the key client-side per operation intent | | No stored response | Key existence recorded, result discarded | Store the response, not just the key | | TTL shorter than retries | Key expires while the client is still retrying | Keep the TTL above the retry window | | Keys in URLs | Idempotency keys landing in access logs | Send keys in headers or bodies, never the path | Security and Authority Boundary Idempotency protects the server's effect from duplication; it does not order distinct operations. Sequencing two different calls — even related ones — needs explicit ordering, which this skill does not provide. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Stripe's API documentation on idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests). 2. Wikipedia's overview of idempotence (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idempotence). Honest boundary: these are implementation references, not adoption or demand evidence; this entry was added under the owner-directed corpus expansion recorded in , and no demand signal is claimed for it. title: Kanban Task Management
description: Maintain a persistent, file-backed Kanban board as the shared source of task truth between a coding agent, its orchestrator, and a human reviewer: an explicit task lifecycle with receipted transitions, a blocked-by dependency DAG with a derived ready set, and a per-task merge gate whose completion evidence is verified before a task may be marked done.
body: Category: Orchestration Skill Level: Intermediate Stability: experimental Version: v1 Added: 2026-10 Last Updated: 2026-10 Description Kanban task management gives an agent a durable board it can read and mutate between sessions instead of holding the plan in context. The board is plain files under version control in the repository being worked, so task state survives crashes, context resets, and handoffs between agents and humans. This page defines a portable contract for lifecycle, dependencies, concurrency, and completion evidence; concrete implementations are references, not requirements. The Portable Contract Any conforming implementation must provide: - Board store: task records stored as files inside the repository (or a directory the repository's review surface can see). Never a side-channel database a code review cannot diff. - Task record: stable ID, status, summary, tags, edges (referencing other task IDs), an append-only list of transition receipts, and evidence references (commit SHAs, merge receipts). - Transition receipts: every status change must append a receipt (timestamp, old→new status, human-readable response message, optional evidence). Receipts are never rewritten or deleted. - Controller CLI: the only writer. Mutations happen through controller commands; direct hand-edits of board files are out-of-contract (see Concurrency Model). - Derived ready set: a query that returns, without mutating anything, the tasks an agent may legally pick up next (status eligible and all targets satisfied per the semantics below). Task Lifecycle: Legal and Illegal Transitions States: , plus (soft, orthogonal) and (a flag on , not a fifth state). | Transition | Legal? | Rule | |---|---|---| | | ✅ | Planning step; receipt required | | | ✅ | Fast-track pick; receipt required | | | ✅ | Only from the ready set (all blockers satisfied); receipt required | | | ✅ | Only if the task's merge gate is satisfied (see Completion Evidence); receipt + evidence | | | ✅ | Return: work stopped; receipt must say why | | | ✅ | Re-plan; receipt required | | | ✅ | Reopen: new receipt citing the defect/omission; prior receipts retained; task re-enters ready computation | | , | ❌ | Reopen must pass through so an owner takes the task again | | | ❌ | Skips execution evidence and the gate | | any → | ✅ | Soft archive: history and receipts stay queryable; never a delete | | | ✅ | Restore: new receipt; dependency edges re-validated against current IDs | | | ❌ | Restore first, then execute the normal gate | | any transition | ❌ | Without a response receipt, or via a hand-edit instead of the controller | Setting/clearing the flag on is always legal with a receipt; a blocked task leaves the ready set until cleared. Blocked-By Dependency Semantics Edges are validated at write time and re-validated by every ready-set computation: | Blocker state | Semantics | |---|---| | (completed) | Satisfied — does not gate the dependent task | | | Does not gate, but the controller emits a warning receipt | | Missing ID | Rejected at edge-creation time. If discovered later, the edge is unresolved: the dependent task is not ready and a validation error is surfaced | | Cyclic | Rejected at creation by cycle check over the DAG; late-discovered cycles make all members not-ready | | / / | Gates normally until the blocker reaches or | The ready set is always recomputed from the live DAG — cached orderings are never trusted. Concurrency Model Read-before-mutate is not concurrency control: two agents can both read the same state and then both write, losing one transition. The contract prescribes exactly one of: 1. Single controller: one controller process owns the board and serializes mutations, or 2. Optimistic CAS: every mutation carries the content hash of the board state it was computed against; on mismatch the controller aborts and the agent re-reads. Hand-edited board files are detected as drift and must be reconciled through the controller. Completion Evidence Implementations may declare a completion gate per task: | Level | requires | |---|---| | | Response receipt only | | | Receipt + at least one commit SHA on the task's work branch; the controller verifies the SHA exists | | | Receipt plus independently verified evidence that the relevant change reached the target branch, recorded with the resulting merge/target commit SHA | A gate must verify the repository's actual merge state. Reopening a completed task creates a new evidence cycle and never rewrites Git history. Example The following commands illustrate the contract using the YYLO Ledger, a git-native reference implementation. The dependency edge is added with the documented dependency command rather than as an option to task creation: The exact task ID returned by must be used when adding the dependency; do not assume a preselected ID. Third-Party Implementation Boundary YYLO Ledger and its related skills are external implementations of the pattern, not dependencies of this skill. References are not trusted repository policy. If adopting an external implementation, review its source and permissions independently and pin a known release or commit where reproducibility matters. Provenance and Contributor Attribution The original Kanban skill contribution was submitted by InsightFactoryAPP as PR #266, originating from the contributor fork . The original contribution commit was and is retained as provenance evidence. The Skills Tree maintainer subsequently refiled and normalized that contribution in PR #267 rather than merging the external fork directly. The resulting canonical skill is therefore maintainer-integrated work with InsightFactoryAPP credited as the original contributor. This attribution does not imply that every subsequent revision was authored by the original contributor. Implementations | Implementation | Form | Notes | |---|---|---| | YYLO Ledger | Git-native task CLI ( ) | Receipts, dependency DAG, ready set; reference implementation of this contract | | ledger-tasks-yylo | Portable for agents | Teaches board operations and source-of-truth boundaries to any skill-capable agent | | YYLO CLI | Orchestrator ( ) | Delegates ; adds worktree-per-task and merge-queue gating on top | When to Use vs Alternatives | Approach | Persistence | Dependency-aware ordering | Best for | |---|---|---|---| | In-process task queue | None (process lifetime) | Priority only | Single-session fan-out | | Database-backed tracker | External server | Usually yes | Team SaaS workflows | | File-backed Kanban board (this skill) | Git/repository | DAG + ready set | Coding agents sharing one repo with humans | Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Lost update | Two writers mutate from the same read state | Single controller or CAS; never hand-edit | | Lifecycle bypass | Direct edits skip validation | Controller refuses on drift | | Stale dependency edges | Blocker archived, renumbered, or removed | Ready set recomputed from the live DAG | | False completion | without verified evidence | Completion gate enforced at transition time | | Silent task loss | Archive treated as delete | Archive is soft and history remains queryable | | Cycle deadlock | Circular discovered late | All members not-ready + validation error | Prompt Patterns Notes - The board is local-first: no server, and the store lives in the repository, so reviews and merges see task state as first-class content. - The required response message on every transition is the audit trail humans review. - Cross-project routing should be opt-in and explicitly allow-listed. - This skill describes a capability contract; it does not prescribe a particular CLI, database, agent framework, or hosting service. title: Result Aggregation
description: Collect parallel task results into one ordered report with per-task status, explicit handling of failures and stragglers, and deterministic merge order so the combined output stays reproducible.
body: Result Aggregation Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Parallel execution multiplies results and failure shapes at the same time. Aggregation turns a cloud of futures into one report: each task contributes a (id, status, output) tuple, missing tasks appear as missing instead of vanishing, and the merge order is deterministic. The aggregate carries per-task provenance, so any claim in the combined output can be traced back to the task that produced it. When to Use Use whenever work is split across parallel subagents or workers and the caller needs one combined, trustworthy answer. Do not use unordered ad-hoc merging; a merge that depends on arrival order produces a different output on every run. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Every task the plan dispatched | | | | Yes | Completed results, keyed by task id | | | | Yes | How completed, failed, and missing tasks are merged | | | | Yes | How long the aggregate waits for stragglers | Procedure 1. Register the full expected task id set at dispatch time; the plan, not the arrival count, defines completeness. 2. Collect results as (id, status, output) tuples; failures are results, not exceptions to swallow. 3. On aggregation, subtract completed ids from expected ids; anything unaccounted is missing — with the timeout recorded. 4. Apply the merge policy per status: include completed, record failed, mark missing; the policy decides what missing means for the whole. 5. Merge in task id order, never arrival order, so identical inputs produce identical output. 6. Emit the aggregate with per-task provenance: which task produced which part of the combined result. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The combined result under the merge policy | | | | Per-task disposition with provenance | | | | Whether all expected tasks completed | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Arrival-order merges | Results folded in completion order | Merge in task id order | | Vanished tasks | Dispatched ids never checked again | Diff expected ids against collected ids | | Exception swallowing | Worker errors absorbed into nothing | Record failures as first-class results | | Unbounded waits | Aggregate blocks on stragglers indefinitely | Enforce the timeout and mark missing | | Provenance loss | Merge output loses task attribution | Carry per-task provenance into the aggregate | Security and Authority Boundary Aggregation preserves and reports what subagents returned; it cannot judge whether the content is correct. Validation of merged content — sources, calculations, claims — remains a separate, explicit step. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Workflow Versioning
description: Version workflow definitions explicitly and record the version in every execution so in-flight runs keep a stable identity while definitions evolve without silent breakage.
body: Workflow Versioning Category: Orchestration | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A workflow definition is code that runs many times. Versioning it explicitly — semantic bumps, a recorded version per execution, and a written rule for what counts as compatible — separates "the run behaved as defined" from "the definition changed underneath the run". Executions carry their definition version, so a result can always be traced to the exact steps that produced it. When to Use Use whenever a multi-step workflow runs repeatedly and its steps, prompts, tool wiring, or output schema may change over time. Do not use one mutable definition with in-place edits; every execution should be able to name the version that produced it. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The step graph and its metadata | | | | Yes | The edits being applied to the definition | | | | No | Executions still using earlier versions | | | | Yes | What the project classifies as breaking, additive, or fix | Procedure 1. Assign each definition an explicit version; an unversioned definition is a defect, not a default. 2. Classify every change against the written rule: step removal, output schema change, or semantic edits are breaking; additive steps are additive; wording fixes are fixes. 3. Record the definition version inside every execution at start; a result without a version cannot be interpreted later. 4. Pin in-flight executions to the version they started with; migrate only between runs, never during one. 5. For breaking bumps, provide an explicit migration or a compatibility window; never change a version in place. 6. Keep the definition history queryable so any past result can be replayed against its own version. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The bumped version after applying the change set | | | | What happens to executions started under the old version | | | | Change set, bump class, and timestamp | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | In-place mutation | Definition edited while executions reference it | Versions are immutable; changes are new versions | | Unlabeled executions | Runs that cannot name their definition version | Stamp the version into every execution at start | | Silent breaking changes | Output schema edited without a major bump | Classify changes against a written rule, not mood | | Migration drift | In-flight runs partially migrated mid-run | Pin in-flight runs; migrate only between runs | | Lost history | Old definitions deleted after the switch | Keep every version queryable for replay | Security and Authority Boundary Versioning preserves the structure of orchestration; it does not pin model behavior. Two executions of the same version can still differ from model sampling — output reproducibility needs seed, prompt, and model tracking of its own. description: Order learning units into a dependency-respecting path — prerequisites as edges, cycle detection, mastery gates — so study plans stay coherent, individually paced, and free of impossible orders.
body: Curriculum Sequencing Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A curriculum is a directed graph wearing a reading list's clothes. Sequencing it means extracting prerequisite edges from stated dependencies, verifying the graph is acyclic, ordering units topologically, and placing mastery gates between a unit and everything that depends on it. Placement tests adjust the entry point by skipping proven material — not by deleting it, since a skipped unit must remain visible in the path's record. When to Use Use when a set of lessons, modules, or skills must be ordered for a learner — course assembly, onboarding plans, or personalized study paths. Do not use for a flat list with no real dependencies; sorting adds ceremony without value when the graph has no edges. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | All learning units in scope | | | | Yes | Stated edges: unit before unit | | | | Yes | Placement results per learner | Procedure 1. Extract prerequisite edges exactly as stated; an assumed-but-unstated dependency is an edge nobody can audit. 2. title: Diagnosis Coding
description: Map clinical descriptions to standard diagnosis codes using literal text support, a supplied code index, and explicit unresolved-case flagging so every code emitted is traceable, never invented.
body: Diagnosis Coding Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Diagnosis coding is a lookup task with a discipline problem: the temptation to code what a clinician probably meant. This skill pins the process to text — a code may be emitted only when the clinical text literally supports it, lookups run against a supplied code index of the declared version, and cases that cannot be resolved are flagged for a human coder. Output pairs every code with its evidence span, so nothing in the coded record is unattributable. When to Use Use when clinical notes or symptom descriptions must be converted to a standard code system (ICD or a supplied local variant) for administrative structuring. Do not use to diagnose patients, and do not emit codes for what the text implies but does not say; implication is a clinical judgment, not a coding fact. Declare the code system and version before lookup; codes from mixed versions do not merge into one record. 2. Normalize the clinical text conservatively — case and whitespace, not paraphrase; the evidence span must survive. 3. Match only against the supplied index, restricted to the declared scope if one is given. 4. Emit a code only with a literal evidence span from the source text; the span is part of the output. 5. Flag unresolved cases explicitly for human coding; a near-miss is a flag, not a code with a lower bar. 6. Record code, span, code system version, and confidence; audits reconstruct every decision from these fields. title: Inventory Reordering
description: Compute reorder points and order quantities from demand history, lead time, and safety stock with every formula input recorded so replenishment decisions rest on stated math rather than gut feel.
body: Inventory Reordering Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Reordering is arithmetic pretending to be intuition. The skill makes the math explicit: demand statistics from history, a reorder point from demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, an order quantity from policy (economic order quantity or a stated rule), and a comparison against stock on hand that emits a concrete reorder list. Every input — history window, lead time, service level — is recorded with the decision, so the same numbers regenerate the same order. When to Use Use for any stocked item where running out has a cost and overstocking has another — spare parts, consumables, retail or warehouse inventory. Do not use on sparse or stale demand history; a reorder point computed from three data points is a guess with extra decimals. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Recent demand series for the item | | | | Yes | Expected replenishment delay | | | | Yes | Current available quantity | | | | Yes | Safety stock rule, service level, and order quantity rule | Procedure 1. Fix the history window and clean the series — stockouts and promotions are noted, not silently averaged in. 2. Compute demand rate and variability; record the window and both statistics with the decision. 3. Compute the reorder point as demand rate times lead time plus safety stock, from the recorded inputs only. 4. Derive the order quantity from the stated policy — economic order quantity or a rule — with its formula and inputs recorded. 5. Compare stock on hand against the reorder point; items at or below it enter the reorder list with the computed quantity. 6. Emit the decision record: item, inputs, formulas, quantities, and date, so the order is reproducible. title: Receipt Parsing
description: Extract merchant, date, line item, tax, and total fields from raw receipt text with arithmetic cross-checks so expense records rest on validated numbers rather than best guesses.
body: Receipt Parsing Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A receipt is unstructured text pretending to be a table. Parsing it means segmentation (header, items, totals), normalization (dates, currencies, decimal separators per locale), and — the part that separates data from guesswork — arithmetic verification: line items must sum to the subtotal, and subtotal plus tax must match the stated total. Every extracted field carries its raw span, so any number in the structured record can be traced to where it came from. When to Use Use when receipt text (typed or OCR output) must become structured expense data — bookkeeping automation, reimbursement workflows, spend analysis. Do not use when a structured source exists instead; supplier invoices with structured input are a stricter field contract handled by invoice processing. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Raw or OCR-extracted receipt text | | | | Yes | Expected date, currency, and number formats | | | | Yes | Fields the caller needs to be present | Procedure 1. Segment the text: header block, line-item block, totals block; totals are parsed from the bottom up, where receipts are most structured. 2. Normalize numbers per locale — decimal separator, currency symbol, thousands grouping — before any arithmetic. 3. Parse line items as (quantity, description, amount) triples; wrapped descriptions are joined, not split into items. 4. Cross-check: item sum against stated subtotal; subtotal plus tax against stated total; record the verdict per check. 5. When a stated total is missing, compute it and flag it as computed, never as extracted. 6. Output the structured record with per-field raw spans and confidence; unresolved fields are flagged, not invented. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Merchant, date, items, subtotal, tax, total | | | | Arithmetic cross-check results | | | | Fields that could not be extracted | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | OCR digit noise | Misread digits pass the regex but fail arithmetic | Run cross-checks; flag records whose math fails | | Locale confusion | parsed as | Normalize per the declared locale first | | Split line items | Wrapped descriptions become two items | Join continuation lines before matching | | Missing totals | Stated total absent from the slip | Compute and mark as computed, never as extracted | | Tax-inclusive pricing | Totals include tax the parser assumed was added | Detect tax-inclusive slips and adjust the checks | Security and Authority Boundary Parsed receipts are structured data for review, not financial records of record. Reimbursement approval, tax treatment, and fraud detection remain with the accounting workflow and its human checks. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. title: Resume Screening
description: Screen resumes against a written rubric with per-criterion evidence spans, anchored scoring, and explicit missing-information handling so ranking decisions stay auditable and bias-controlled.
body: Resume Screening Category: Domain-Specific | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Resume screening is a judgment task wrapped in an audit problem. The skill makes the judgment mechanical and the audit trivial: criteria are written before any resume is read, each criterion is scored only against quoted evidence from the document, missing information is recorded as missing rather than punished, and protected attributes are never inferred or used. The output is a structured verdict with provenance, not a ranking by feel. When to Use Use when a stack of resumes must be reduced to a ranked or triaged shortlist against a defined role, and the decision must be explainable afterward. Do not use to make hiring decisions; screening output is decision support that humans review before any candidate outcome. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The candidate document to screen | | | | Yes | Written criteria with anchored score levels | | | | Yes | The role definition the rubric was derived from | Procedure 1. Fix the rubric before reading resumes; criteria written after reading a candidate are advocacy, not screening. 2. For each criterion, quote the evidence span from the resume that supports a score, or record it as missing. 3. Score against anchored levels defined in the rubric; two screeners should reach the same score from the same span. 4. Treat missing information as missing — a gap is not a negative unless the rubric says so explicitly. 5. Never infer protected attributes from text, dates, or names; they are out of scope by construction. 6. Emit the structured verdict with every span, score, and gap, so the decision can be reconstructed or challenged. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Per-criterion scores with anchors | | | | The quoted text supporting each score | | | | Criteria the resume left unanswered | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Unanchored scoring | Scores reflect the screener's mood | Use rubric anchors any screener can apply | | Punishing gaps | Missing information read as weakness | Record gaps as gaps unless the rubric penalizes them | | Protected-attribute inference | Dates, names, or photos used as signals | Keep protected attributes out of scope by construction | | Keyword-only matching | Exact terms trump equivalent experience | Match synonyms defined in the rubric; keep humans in review | | Decision without provenance | Verdict with no quoted evidence | Emit spans with every score or the verdict is invalid | Security and Authority Boundary Screening output is decision support for a human decision governed by employment law and fairness review. Bias auditing, adverse-impact analysis, and candidate communication remain with the hiring process, not with the screener. title: Shift Scheduling
description: Build staff shift schedules as constraint problems — coverage demand, availability, rest gaps, fairness — with every constraint explicit and every violation reported instead of hidden in an unexplained roster.
body: Shift Scheduling Category: Domain-Specific | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A roster is a set of assignments that satisfies stated constraints — or it is a wish. This skill treats scheduling as constraint programming: enumerate shifts and coverage requirements, encode hard constraints (availability, max hours, minimum rest between shifts) and soft ones (fairness in weekends and unpopular shifts), search for a feasible assignment, and report every constraint that could not be satisfied rather than quietly producing a broken roster. When to Use Use for on-call rotations, support coverage, clinical or retail staffing — any recurring horizon where people must be assigned to shifts under rules. Do not use for one-off task allocation with no recurring structure or constraints; that is task assignment, not scheduling. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | People and the shifts they can work | | | | Yes | Minimum headcount per shift | | | | Yes | Hard and soft rules with priorities | | | | Yes | The scheduling window | Procedure 1. Enumerate the shift grid across the horizon; every slot that needs coverage appears in the problem. 2. Encode hard constraints first — availability, maximum hours, minimum rest gaps; soft constraints carry explicit priorities. 3. Search for a feasible assignment; prefer solutions that minimize weighted soft-constraint violations. 4. When no feasible roster exists, report which constraints conflict and at which slots — do not silently drop coverage. 5. Compute fairness per person (shift counts, weekends, unpopular slots) and include it in the output. 6. On any later edit, revalidate the full roster; an edited roster is a new solution, not an exception to check. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The assignment per slot | | | | Unsatisfied constraints, if any | | | | Per-person load and distribution metrics | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Hidden hard constraints | Rules applied verbally after publication | Encode every constraint before solving | | Fairness ignored | One person absorbs the unpopular shifts | Track distribution and include it in the output | | Missing rest gaps | Back-to-back night-then-day assignments | Encode minimum rest as a hard constraint | | Unreported coverage gaps | Solver returns an incomplete roster silently | Emit violations with slots, always | | Unvalidated edits | Manual fixes break constraints quietly | Revalidate the full roster after any edit | Security and Authority Boundary A feasible schedule satisfies the stated constraints; labor-law compliance depends on those constraints being complete and current. title: Alerting Design
description: Build alerts around user-visible symptoms and service objectives rather than raw causes, so a page means real impact and silence means real health.
body: Alerting Design Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description An alert on every metric is a pager that cannot be trusted, and a pager that cannot be trusted gets silenced — usually right before the one that mattered. This skill designs alerting from the top down: start from what users experience, define objectives with error budgets, and alert on the burn rate of those budgets. Cause-level signals become dashboards and debug entries, not pages, because a page is a claim that a human must act now, and every unactionable claim spends trust the system needs for the real ones. When to Use Use whenever a service is on call — user-facing or internal — and especially where pages have grown noisy enough that responders pre-filter them. Do not page on individual cause metrics with no user-visible symptom; a nearly full disk at three in the morning is a dashboard, not a human. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The user-visible service level being protected | | | | Yes | How fast the error budget is being consumed | | | | Yes | The signal that measures the user experience | Procedure 1. Define the objective first — what users experience, measured as availability or latency — before writing a single alert. 2. Alert on burn rate: page when the error budget would exhaust within a bounded window, not on any single bad sample. 3. Keep causes out of the pager: route saturation and dependency signals to dashboards and debug pages, not to humans. 4. Make every page actionable: name the runbook, the owner, and the first command to run, in the alert itself. 5. Review alert performance like code: page rate, action rate, and the fraction of pages that were real become metrics. 6. Retire or repair chatty alerts immediately; a noisy alert is not a safety margin, it is a removed one. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Symptom-based, budget-burning pages with runbooks | | | | Page rate, action rate, and precision over time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Cause paging | Humans notified of every unhealthy-looking metric | Page on symptoms and budget burn, not causes | | Unactionable pages | A page with no runbook and no owner | Name the runbook and first step in the alert | | Alert fatigue | So many pages that real ones get ignored | Retire chatty alerts; measure alert precision | | Missing objectives | Alerts exist but no user experience is defined | Define the service objective before alerting on it | | Static thresholds | A fixed line that pages nightly at low traffic | Use burn-rate windows instead of single thresholds | Security and Authority Boundary Alert content travels to the widest, least protected channel in an organization — phones and chat: alert payloads must not embed credentials, internal topology details, or user data, and access to the alerting configuration itself must be protected, because silencing rules are a prime target for an intruder who wants the quiet path. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Prometheus alerting documentation (https://prometheus.io/docs/alerting/latest/overview/). 2. The SRE Workbook chapter on alerting on service level objectives (https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/). title: Blue-Green Deployment
description: Run two production environments and switch traffic between them, so a release becomes a reversible routing change instead of a waiting period for breakage.
body: Blue-Green Deployment Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A deployment that mutates the live environment in place makes rollback a race against the damage. This skill keeps two full environments — blue, live, and green, idle — and makes the release a routing flip: the new version deploys to the idle color, is verified there, traffic switches to it, and the old color stays warm for exactly as long as the new one needs to prove itself. Rollback is then the same switch in the other direction, which is what makes the flip a decision rather than a gamble. When to Use Use for stateless or forward-compatible services where a full second environment is affordable and a fast, reversible cutover is worth the cost. Do not blue-green around breaking database changes: if the old color cannot run on the new schema, the switch is not reversible and the pattern is theater. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The version being deployed to the idle environment | | | | Yes | The traffic control between the two environments | | | | Yes | How long the old environment stays warm after the flip | Procedure 1. Keep two environments, with the idle one always ready to receive the next release. 2. Deploy the new version to the idle color only, and verify it there — health, smoke, readiness — while production is untouched. 3. Flip routing to the new color, gradually or at once by design, and watch the user-visible symptoms rather than the deploy logs. 4. Keep the old color warm for the soak period: rollback during soak is a routing change, measured in seconds. 5. Handle state carefully: the schema and its consumers must be forward-compatible with both colors, or the flip is one-way. 6. Retire the old version after soak, and immediately prepare the idle color for the next release — the pattern only works while it is always two environments. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The flip with time, direction, and verification evidence | | | | The reverse switch, ready during the entire soak | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | In-place drift | The idle environment quietly becoming non-redeployable | Rehearse deploys to the idle color regularly | | One-way schema | A migration the old color cannot survive | Forward-compatible schema changes before the flip | | Instant retirement | The old version destroyed before the soak ends | Keep the old color warm for the full soak | | Verification in production | Testing deferred until after the flip | Verify on the idle color before switching | | Stateful split | Session state trapped on the wrong color | Externalize state or drain sessions before the flip | Security and Authority Boundary The routing switch is a security boundary: whoever can flip traffic between environments can redirect production, so route changes require the same authorization and audit as production deploys, and the idle environment must hold production data protections even while idle. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Martin Fowler's article on blue-green deployment (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). 2. title: Container Image Tagging
description: Tag container images with immutable, traceable identifiers — semantic version tags, registry digests, and build provenance — so deployments reference an exact artifact auditable after the fact.
body: Container Image Tagging Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A tag is a label someone can move; a digest is an identity they cannot. This skill pins that difference into the pipeline: builds get version tags once, deployments reference images by digest, a tag is never reassigned to different bytes, and every artifact carries build provenance — source commit, build definition, timestamp. The result is that any deployed environment can answer "exactly which bytes are running, and where did they come from". When to Use Use for any container image that reaches a deployment — application services, tooling images, CI runner environments. Do not deploy floating tags such as or a bare branch name; a deployment that cannot name its bytes cannot be rolled back to them either. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The image being built and tagged | | | | Yes | The release version this build belongs to | | | | Yes | The content-addressed identity from the registry | | | | Yes | Source commit, build definition, and timestamp | Procedure 1. Build once per version; the artifact from one build receives all its tags at creation time. 2. Tag with the semantic version; tags are claims about content, applied once and never retagged. 3. Record the registry digest; deployments pin by digest, with the version tag kept for humans. 4. Attach provenance to the artifact — source commit, build definition, build time — as metadata or attestation. 5. Reject retag requests: a tag that points at new bytes is a new version, whatever it is called. 6. Keep tag-to-digest mappings queryable so an environment's running bytes can be resolved historically. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Version tag, digest, and provenance per image | | | | The digest deployments reference | | | | Who tagged what, when, from which build | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | in production | Environments reference a moving tag | Pin deployments to digests | | Retagged versions | The same version label naming different bytes | Refuse retags; new bytes get a new version | | Tag-only references | Digest never recorded at release time | Store tag-to-digest mappings per release | | Missing provenance | Artifact cannot be traced to source or build | Attach source commit and build definition | | Cross-registry drift | The same tag resolves differently per registry | Resolve and compare digests, not tag names | Security and Authority Boundary Tagging identifies artifacts; it does not make them safe.
