title: Declarative Infrastructure
description: Define infrastructure as reviewed, versioned code — desired state, applied by a controller — so environments are reproducible, diffable, and rebuildable from source alone.
body: Declarative Infrastructure Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Infrastructure described imperatively is infrastructure nobody can rebuild: the console clicks that made it exist live in a browser history. This skill makes the desired state the source of truth: resources are declared in code, the code is reviewed and versioned, and a reconciler applies the declaration — reporting a diff between what exists and what is wanted before it changes anything. The payoff is that the environment is no longer a memory; it is a file, with a history, that can be recreated in another region on a bad day. When to Use Use for any environment expected to outlive a single change — clusters, databases, networks, queues — and for anything that must be rebuilt identically elsewhere. Do not drive one-off break-glass resources through the declarative pipeline during an incident; make the manual change, record it, and reconcile the declaration afterward. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The desired state expressed as reviewed infrastructure code | | | | Yes | The recorded actual state the controller reconciles against | | | | Yes | The preview of changes between current and desired | Procedure 1. Declare desired state in code — resources, parameters, and their relations — with nothing that exists only as a console change. 2. Store the declaration in version control with review, so every infrastructure change has an author, a diff, and a reason. 3. Preview before applying: generate the plan and read it, because the apply step is where the diff meets production. 4. Apply through the reconciler, and let it record state — never mutate resources by hand where the controller watches them. 5. Treat drift as an incident: a manual change to a managed resource gets reconciled or recorded, not ignored. 6. Rehearse the rebuild: a declaration that has never created a fresh environment is a hypothesis, not a backup. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The proposed changes between recorded and desired state | | | | What the controller created, changed, or destroyed | | | | Divergences between declaration and reality | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Console drift | Manual edits silently diverging from the declaration | Detect drift and reconcile or record every divergence | | Apply-without-plan | Changes hitting production unread | Always generate and read the plan first | | Hand-edited state | State files mutated into folklore | Never hand-edit state; act through the reconciler | | Unreviewed changes | Infrastructure edited like scratch config | Same review bar as application code | | Unrehearsed rebuilds | The declaration has never built a fresh environment | Rehearse a clean rebuild periodically | Security and Authority Boundary Infrastructure code holds the shape of the estate and often the references to its most sensitive stores: declarations must be reviewed with the same scrutiny as application code, secrets referenced by identity rather than embedded, and reconciler credentials guarded as the master key to every resource it can create. title: Dependency Auditor
description: Audit declared skill dependencies and executable examples in isolated environments, producing reproducible pass/fail evidence without silently promoting trust state.
body: Dependency Auditor Description Audit declared external dependencies and executable skill examples in isolated environments. The auditor records pass/fail evidence and proposes badge artifacts without directly changing canonical trust state. > Phase 3 of the Dependency Watchdog pipeline. > Closes the gap between Package Exists (🟡 Yellow) and Code Runs (🟢 Green). The Execution Gap The AST Sweep (Phase 1) confirms that a skill's declared packages exist on PyPI and are free of known CVEs. But existence ≠ execution. A package might: - Have breaking API changes in its latest release - Require a native system dependency (e.g. , ) absent from the runner - Conflict with another skill's dependencies when installed together - Simply have a typo in its import path in the code example The Dependency Auditor solves this by running the code, not just scanning it. --- Architecture --- Isolation Strategy Each skill runs in a completely independent virtual environment. This prevents dependency bleed between skills — Skill A's cannot shadow Skill B's . > Why not a single shared venv for all skills? > Because conflicts between skill deps would produce false results. > Skill A might pass only because Skill B's dep happened to satisfy its import. > Isolation ensures every Green badge is independently earned. --- Verdict Logic The auditor distinguishes three outcomes. The distinction between and is the single most important design decision — it keeps the CI signal clean. | Verdict | Condition | Badge Action | |---|---|---| | | Snippet exits 0, no ImportError/RuntimeError | Promote Yellow → 🟢 Green (via PR) | | | Snippet exits non-zero, or raises on import | Stays Yellow, opens issue with traceback | | | No Python snippets found, or skill has no deps declared | No badge change, not flagged as broken | --- The Human-in-the-Loop Contract The badge is not written directly into canonical skill content. A passing audit produces a proposed badge artifact on a new branch and opens a Pull Request. The exact PR HEAD is merged only when required repository CI, security, tests, and invariants pass. This is the critical security feature. Without it, a snippet that passes due to a flaky network call or a temporary PyPI outage could silently award a Green badge that isn't earned. --- Recursive Dogfooding This skill ( ) is itself subject to the badge pipeline it describes. - Its own and imports are scanned by the AST Sweep → Yellow badge - The Dependency Auditor runs its own snippets in an isolated venv - If they pass → a verification PR is opened → exact-head repository CI gates the merge → Green badge The tool that audits the repository is itself audited by the repository. This is the self-healing property of the infrastructure. --- Security: Network Constraint Model > See for the full threat model. The short version: | Risk Level | Scenario | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Low (current) | Trusted contributor PRs, reviewed before merge | Ephemeral GH runner (discarded after job) | | Medium (community PRs) | Unreviewed code execution in audit | Require maintainer approval before audit workflow runs | | High (if abuse detected) | Adversarial snippet exfiltration | Docker container for execution | For the current scope — a curated, maintainer-reviewed repository — the ephemeral runner model is the primary and sufficient containment strategy. --- Related Infrastructure | Component | Role | |---|---| | | Phase 1: Extract imports, validate PyPI, write Yellow badges | | | Phase 2: Poll OSV CVE database every 15 min | | | Manual badge state transitions | | | Shared utility | | | Phase 3: CI runner for this auditor | | | Badge state machine reference |

title: Deployment Rollback
description: Restore the last known-good release through pre-verified rollback artifacts, recorded migration state, and a rehearsed procedure so a failed deployment recovers within a bounded time budget.
body: Deployment Rollback Category: Infrastructure | Level: advanced | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Rollback is a deployment you have already practiced — or a hope. The skill makes it an artifact: the previous release stays deployable, schema migrations carry their compensating steps, the rollback procedure is rehearsed in staging against the same artifact shape, and recovery runs in a defined order with health verification at the end. The measure of success is a bounded recovery time, not the absence of failures. When to Use Use for any release with state — services, migrations, configuration — where reverting to the previous good state must be possible within a stated time budget. Do not use rollback as the primary deployment strategy; a process that ships failures expecting to revert is a quality problem wearing recovery clothing. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The failing release and its artifacts | | | | Yes | The verified previous release, kept deployable | | | | Yes | Forward migrations with compensating steps | | | | Yes | The rehearsed recovery procedure | Procedure 1. Keep the last known-good release deployable — artifacts, configuration, and schema state — until the next one is verified. 2. Record every forward migration with its compensating step; a migration without a reverse is a decision to make rollback impossible. 3. Rehearse the rollback in staging with the same artifacts and order; an unrehearsed plan is a draft. 4. On the failure signal, execute in the recorded order: stop traffic, revert code, revert migrations step by step, restore configuration. 5. Verify health after rollback — probes, smoke checks, error rates — before declaring recovery. 6. Write the incident reference: trigger, release delta, migration state, recovery time against budget. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Whether recovery completed | | | | Each rollback step and its verification | | | | Time from signal to verified recovery | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | No retained artifact | Previous release deleted or unreferenced | Keep the last known good deployable until the next is verified | | Irreversible migrations | Forward-only schema changes | Record compensating steps with every migration | | Unrehearsed plan | Rollback procedure written during the outage | Rehearse in staging with real artifacts | | Config drift | Configuration differs between the two releases | Snapshot and restore configuration with the release | | Unverified recovery | Traffic restored without health checks | Verify probes and error rates before declaring done | Security and Authority Boundary Rollback restores service state; it does not reconcile data written by the failed release. Data repair, backfills, and customer-impact analysis stay with the data owner after service recovery. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. Wikipedia's overview of blue-green deployment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-green_deployment). 2. Martin Fowler's note on blue-green deployment (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). title: Health Check Endpoints
description: Expose separate liveness and readiness endpoints with dependency-aware checks so orchestrators restart dead processes while temporarily unready ones simply receive no traffic.
body: Health Check Endpoints Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description Liveness answers "is this process broken"; readiness answers "can it serve right now". Conflating them produces the two classic outages: restarts during a dependency blip (the process is fine, the database is not) and traffic routed to instances that cannot serve. This skill splits the endpoints, makes readiness check real dependencies with real timeouts, and degrades to unready instead of dead — because a restart loop solves nothing a moment of patience would. When to Use Use for any long-running service an orchestrator manages — web services, workers, agents behind a scheduler or platform that probes health. Do not run side effects in probes; a health check that writes, rotates, or caches changes system state on a timer nobody scheduled. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Dependency probes with timeouts for readiness | | | | Yes | How often the orchestrator checks | | | | Yes | Consecutive failures before action | | | | Yes | What liveness failure and unreadiness each do | Procedure 1. Implement two endpoints: liveness reports process health from in-process state only; readiness reports the ability to serve. 2. Make readiness walk the real dependencies with short timeouts; a dependency down means unready, not a restart. 3. Keep checks cheap and side-effect free — probing sits on the request path of every scheduling decision. 4. Tune probe intervals and thresholds above the noise floor; flapping thresholds convert blips into restart storms. 5. Degrade to unready under partial dependency failure, and report which dependency held the gate. 6. Log state transitions with the reason; restart and no-traffic events are only debuggable with that record. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | Process state from in-process evidence | | | | Ability to serve, per dependency | | | | Which dependency made the instance unready | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | One endpoint for both states | Restart policy and traffic policy share one signal | Split liveness from readiness | | Dependency blip restarts | Readiness failures routed to liveness | Degrade to unready, never to dead | | Heavy probe checks | Health checks loading dependencies | Keep checks cheap, cached, and side-effect free | | Restart storms | Thresholds tuned under the noise floor | Set thresholds above transient error rates | | Silent unreadiness | Unready with no recorded reason | Log the gating dependency with every transition | Security and Authority Boundary Health endpoints report process state; they do not validate data quality, security posture, or business correctness. Those belong to monitoring, security scanning, and SLOs — separate signals with separate owners. Evidence This skill is grounded in dated public implementation references: 1. The Kubernetes documentation on liveness, readiness, and startup probes (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/). 2. Wikipedia's overview of heartbeat signals in computing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartbeat_%28computing%29). title: Kubernetes Deployment
description: Build a Deployment manifest with pinned image tags, explicit resource requests and limits, distinct readiness and liveness probes, and a declared rollout strategy so container runs stay predictable.
body: Kubernetes Deployment Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A Deployment manifest is where container defaults become incidents: floating tags, unset resource bounds, identical probes, and an implicit rollout strategy. This skill defines the manifest contract: pin the image, declare requests and limits, give readiness and liveness probes distinct purposes, and state the rollout strategy and history bound explicitly. When to Use Use when authoring or reviewing a Kubernetes Deployment manifest for a long-running service. Do not use for one-off pods, batch Jobs, or StatefulSets; their lifecycle contracts differ and need their own manifests. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | Deployment and label name | | | | Yes | Fully pinned image reference including registry and tag | | | | Yes | Desired replica count | | | | Yes | CPU and memory requests and limits per container | | | | Yes | Distinct readiness and liveness probe definitions | Procedure 1. Pin the image to an immutable tag or digest; latest is not a deployable version. 2. Declare resource requests and limits for every container; unbounded containers share fate with their neighbors. 3. Give readiness and liveness probes different purposes and settings; identical probes detect nothing distinct. 4. Set the replica count and the rollout strategy explicitly, including max unavailable and max surge. 5. Configure a bounded revision history so rollback targets exist without growing forever. 6. Match label selectors to the pod template exactly; a mismatch strands replicas unsupervised. 7. Validate the manifest with a dry run before applying; schema errors belong in review, not in apply output. 8. Record the deploy outcome, including revision, conditions, and observed replicas, and compare against the declared intent. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The Deployment manifest conforming to the contract | | | | Dry-run rejections with the offending field | | | | The rollout revision after apply | | | | Observed replicas and conditions versus declared intent | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Floating tag | The image reference uses latest | Pin the tag or digest | | Identical probes | Readiness equals liveness | Tune each probe for its distinct purpose | | No limits | Requests and limits are unset | Declare both requests and limits | | Selector mismatch | Labels were edited after creation | Match selectors to the pod template exactly | | Unbounded history | revisionHistoryLimit is unset | Set an explicit history limit | Security and Authority Boundary Applying a Deployment manifest grants authority only within the cluster’s own RBAC. Image registries must be trusted, and credentials are supplied through declared secrets, never in the manifest. The manifest is code: it goes through the same review path as any change, and apply happens through the platform’s normal controls. The Kubernetes documentation on managing resources for containers (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/). title: Secrets Management
description: Store and deliver credentials through a managed system — never in code or config files — with scoped leases, rotation, and audit, so a leak has a blast radius and an end date.
body: Secrets Management Category: Infrastructure | Level: intermediate | Stability: experimental | Version: v1 Description A credential in a config file is a credential in a repository, a backup, and a log shipper forever. This skill routes around that: secrets live in a dedicated store, workloads fetch them at start time under an authenticated identity, each credential carries a scope and a lease, and rotation is routine rather than an incident. The audit trail closes the loop — who fetched what, when, under which role — because the question after a leak is never only what got out, but what it could reach and for how long. When to Use Use for any credential a workload needs — API keys, database credentials, signing material — delivered at runtime by identity, with rotation intervals that limit the lifetime of a stolen value. Do not build home-grown encryption schemes or stash credentials in environment files that outlive their leak; the managed path exists precisely so the shortcuts do not have to. Inputs | Input | Type | Required | Description | |---|---|---|---| | | | Yes | The logical name the workload requests | | | | Yes | The authenticated workload identity making the request | | | | Yes | Scope, duration, and renewal policy for the grant | Procedure 1. Inventory the credentials first: every secret gets an owner, a scope, and a rotation interval before it gets a store entry. 2. Store values only in the secrets system, addressed by logical name, with no copies in code, config files, or CI variables. 3. Deliver at runtime: the workload authenticates as itself and receives only the entries its scope allows. 4. Lease and rotate: credentials expire by policy, and rotation is a routine operation with a tested procedure, not an emergency. 5. Audit every fetch — identity, secret, time — and route the log somewhere a compromised workload cannot edit. 6. Revoke on suspicion, and drill revocation like backups: a rotation path never exercised will fail exactly when it matters. Outputs | Output | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | | | The scoped, time-bound credential issued to the identity | | | | Rotations and revocations with dates and owners | | | | Fetch events by identity, secret, and time | Runnable Example Failure Modes | Failure Mode | Cause | Mitigation | |---|---|---| | Config-file credentials | A secret committed, backed up, and shipped in logs | Store by logical name; deliver at runtime only | | Over-scoped grants | One credential reaching everything it never needed | Scope per identity; least privilege per fetch | | Eternal credentials | Values that live until the incident that rotates them | Lease and rotate on a fixed interval | | Unexercised rotation | The rotation path fails during the real event | Drill rotation and revocation routinely | | Unaudited fetches | No answer to who read what and when | Audit every fetch to an append-only log | Security and Authority Boundary The secrets system is the highest-value target in the estate: its stores must be encrypted at rest, its access decisions must run on workload identity rather than shareable credentials, and its audit logs must live outside the reach of the identities they record.
